0.title: Job: Does He Fear God for No Reason?
0.overview:
The book of Job turns on a question asked about a man behind his back. God points to his servant Job, blameless and upright, and the Accuser answers: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). Take away the hedge, the flocks, the children, the health, and see what the piety was really for. The next forty-one chapters answer that question, and Job is never told it was asked.

The book is set in Uz, outside Israel, in a world of tents and raiding parties where a man offers his own sacrifices: no temple, no law of Moses, no king, no date. Prose opens it (chs. 1-2) and closes it (42:7-17), with a long poem between: Job and three friends arguing about God in three rounds, then a fourth man, Elihu, then God himself out of the whirlwind.

Who wrote Job, and when? Scripture does not say. The setting is patriarchal; the book itself may have been written later. Job was a real man: Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel (Ezek 14:14), and James points to the steadfastness of Job (Jas 5:11). Some read the book as a parable or a drama. The better reading is that it records real events, with the speeches shaped into great poetry, as the Psalms shape real prayers. That shaping does not make it less true. With the historic confessions (the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 London Baptist Confession), this commentary receives Job as God's inspired and wholly true word: it records truly what each speaker said, though not every speaker spoke truly.

Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar come to comfort and sit seven days in silence, which is the best thing they do. Then they begin to explain. Their system is tidy: God is just, God repays, so suffering on this scale means sin on this scale, and Job must confess. By the third round they are inventing crimes for him (22:5-9). Much of it sounds orthodox. But God says to Eliphaz, twice, you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). A single line may be true in itself (Paul quotes one, 5:13, in 1 Corinthians 3:19), but none of their speeches may be quoted as God's verdict on a sufferer.

Job, meanwhile, says wild things. He calls God his enemy, demands a court, wishes he had never been born. And God commends his speech, because Job spoke to God and not merely about him, refused to tell a lie in God's favour, and would not stop coming. The friends never once address God. From his deepest pit Job reaches for someone to stand between: an arbiter (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), and then I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth (19:25).

God answers at last, and answers nothing. Out of the storm come questions about the sea and the snow, the wild donkey and the ostrich, Behemoth and Leviathan, and not one word about chapter 1. Job is given God instead of an explanation, and that turns out to be what he wanted: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you (42:5). The man they accused becomes the priest who prays for them, and his fortunes come back doubled, except the children: ten graves are not cancelled by ten cradles. The Accuser's question is answered by a man who has lost everything and still wants God.

All of this is unfinished until Christ. Job wanted a mediator and got one, long after: the Son of God, himself blameless, stripped, deserted by his friends and condemned by his enemies' theology, who went further than Job into the dark. God has given one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), who indeed is interceding for us (Rom 8:34). Job asked why the innocent suffer; at the cross God answers by suffering. And the empty tomb guarantees Job's hope that in his flesh he would see God.

A word to anyone reading this book from inside it. Job is not mainly a lesson about patience, though James calls him steadfast. The book gives permission: to say the true thing to God rather than the pious thing, to refuse the explanations of people who are sure they know why this happened to you, and to keep asking. Read the friends' speeches as what you need not believe about yourself, and Job's prayers as words you may borrow. The God of this book is not fragile. He can take what Job said, and he vindicates the man who said it. He does not owe an answer, and he came, which is more.

1.title: Does Job Fear God for No Reason?
1.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.<sup>2</sup>There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.<sup>3</sup>He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.<sup>4</sup>His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.<sup>5</sup>And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually.<sup>6</sup>Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?"<sup>9</sup>Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Does Job fear God for no reason?<sup>10</sup>Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.<sup>11</sup>But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face."<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,<sup>14</sup>and there came a messenger to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them,<sup>15</sup>and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>16</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>17</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>18</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,<sup>19</sup>and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>20</sup>Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.<sup>21</sup>And he said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."<sup>22</sup>In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
1.overview: Job of Uz is blameless and upright; he has ten children and great wealth, and offers a burnt offering for each child in case they have cursed God in their hearts (vv. 1-5). In the council of heaven the LORD commends him to Satan, who answers, Does Job fear God for no reason? The LORD puts all Job has into Satan's hand, but not Job himself (vv. 6-12). In one day four messengers report the loss of his herds, flocks and camels to raiders and fire, and of all ten children to a great wind (vv. 13-19). Job tears his robe, falls to the ground and worships: The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. In all this he does not sin or charge God with wrong (vv. 20-22).
1.theology:
The book's question is whether God deserves to be loved for himself, or only for his gifts. Satan's phrase for no reason will return in God's mouth (2:3), in Job's (9:17) and in Eliphaz's (22:6), and the gospel gives it its fullest sense (see on vv. 9-10).

God is sovereign over suffering without being the author of evil. Human wickedness, natural disaster and Satan's malice all act, and none acts outside God's permission and limit; the cross is the clearest instance of the same pattern (Acts 4:27-28).
1.examples: It is God, not Satan, who first mentions Job, and Job's trouble begins with God's delight in him. And the father who offered ten sacrifices after every feast never had the comfort of a sacrifice that was finished; Christian parents do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Man in the Land of Uz
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job of Uz is given four marks of true piety (v. 1), a full family and great wealth (vv. 2-3), and he prays and sacrifices for his children (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Scripture's verdict on Job comes before his trouble, so that no reader can explain the trouble by him.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book begins like a story told at a fireside: there was a man. Uz lies outside Israel; Lamentations sets it with Edom (Lam 4:21). Nowhere does the book mention Israel, Abraham, the covenant, the law or the temple, and Job offers his own sacrifices as head of his family, as the patriarchs did. He was a real man: Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel (Ezek 14:14), and James holds him up to Christians (James 5:11). His story is set outside Israel on purpose. It belongs to anyone who has ever suffered.

Then the verdict, in four parts. Blameless (Hebrew tam) means whole, all of a piece; its noun is the integrity God will say Job still holds fast (2:3). Upright means straight in his dealings. His fear of God showed in what he did: he turned away from evil. It does not mean sinless; Job himself will ask God to pardon his transgression (7:21) and speak of the iniquities of his youth (13:26). It means there was no hidden life behind the visible one.

God will repeat this verdict word for word (v. 8; 2:3). Whatever explains Job's suffering, it will not be Job's sin, and the reader is told so on the first line, so that he can never take the friends' side.
verseByVerse.note: Uz was probably in Edom or northern Arabia, east of Israel. The story seems set in the age of the patriarchs; the book’s author and date are unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: There were born to him seven sons and three daughters. He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven and three make ten, and the flocks follow the same pattern: seven thousand and three thousand, five hundred and five hundred. It is the storyteller's way of saying complete. The people of the east were famous for wealth and wisdom; when Scripture praises Solomon's wisdom, it says it surpassed theirs (1 Kgs 4:30). Job was the greatest of them.

Keep the list in mind. Every item on it is about to be taken, the children last of all. At the end of the book it will be read out again (42:12-13), every number doubled except the children: ten again, not twenty. Many have seen in this that the first ten were not lost to God; and the new children did not cancel the grief for the old.

verseByVerse.quote: His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them. And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is a happy family. The brothers take turns to host, and they do not leave their sisters out. And their father watches over their souls: when each round of feasting ends, he gets up early and offers a burnt offering for every one of them, ten sacrifices.

He has no evidence. He offers for sins he cannot see, in hearts he cannot read. The Hebrew actually says blessed God; the text avoids writing “curse God”, and the ESV rightly translates the sense. The same word will come back in Satan's mouth (v. 11) and in Job's (v. 21), and it is the hinge of the chapter.

Thus Job did continually. He was a good father, and a picture of the limit of every priest before Christ. He had to do it again after every feast, because no sacrifice he offered could finish the matter. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb 10:11-12). The Christian parent still prays for his children every day. He no longer has to wonder whether the sacrifice was enough.
verseByVerse.note: “Cursed” is literally “blessed” in Hebrew, a euphemism for cursing God (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the council of heaven the LORD points to Job (vv. 6-8), Satan asks the question the whole book will test (vv. 9-11), and the LORD lets him touch all Job has, but not Job himself (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Satan is real and malicious, and he is on a leash: nothing reaches Job that did not first pass through the council of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curtain goes up on a scene Job never sees. The sons of God are heavenly beings, the angels who shouted for joy when God laid the foundation of the earth (38:7). They come to present themselves, like officials reporting to a king, as Micaiah saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him (1 Kgs 22:19).

In Hebrew Satan has the article: the satan, the accuser or adversary. He appears in the same role in Zechariah, standing at his right hand to accuse him (Zech 3:1). Some read him here as a court prosecutor doing an unpleasant job for God. But his aim is that Job should curse God (v. 11), and that is not a servant's aim. The New Testament names him: that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the accuser of our brothers ... who accuses them day and night before our God (Rev 12:9-10). He is real, he is hostile, and he still has to come before the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: Compare the accuser of Zechariah 3:1-2, rebuked by the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."
verseByVerse.commentary: God asks, not because he needs to know, but because Satan must give an account. And the answer is restless: to and fro, up and down. Peter uses the picture to warn Christians: Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet 5:8). He is not everywhere at once, and he is not idle.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who raises Job's name? Not Satan: the LORD. Have you considered is literally "have you set your heart on". God points to Job the way a father points to a son he is proud of. My servant is the title Scripture gives to Abraham, Moses and David, and at last to the Servant of Isaiah who suffers for others (Isa 52:13). And God repeats the narrator's verdict, all four parts, and adds there is none like him on the earth.

This is an unsettling verse, and a deeply comforting one. Job's trouble does not begin with Job's failure, but with God's delight in him. That is not a rule for every suffering; much of our trouble we bring on ourselves, and Scripture says so. But it breaks the equation the friends will spend the debate defending, that a man in pain must be a man in the wrong. Some sufferings begin in heaven, with God's pleasure in a servant he means to show to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Does Job fear God for no reason? Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the question of the book. For no reason is one Hebrew word, chinnam: gratis, for nothing. Satan does not deny that Job is devout. He denies that Job's devotion is love. It is a wage, he says: Job serves God because God pays well.

Satan's own words admit that God has hedged Job in on every side. And his charge is aimed at God as much as at Job. If he is right, God is loved only for what he hands out, and no one would stay with him if the gifts stopped.

Watch the word as the book goes on. God will turn it back on Satan: you incited me against him to destroy him without reason (2:3). Job will use it, not knowing how true it is: he ... multiplies my wounds without cause (9:17). The Greek Old Testament renders it dorean, and the New Testament uses the same word of Christ, They hated me without a cause (John 15:25), and of us: we are justified by his grace as a gift (Rom 3:24). The gospel is God giving for no reason in us, and the faith it creates loves him back the same way.

Every believer is asked Satan's question sooner or later, usually by a loss: what would be left of your faith if the hedge came down? If the honest answer frightens you, take heart from the next verses. Job's faith held because he was held, and Christ prays for his people that their faith may not fail.

verseByVerse.quote: But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face." And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan does not ask to strike Job himself. He asks God to do it: stretch out your hand. And curse is again the Hebrew bless. Keep that word for verse 21.

People sometimes call this a wager. It is not. A wager is made when the outcome is uncertain, and God has just said what Job is. It is a demonstration, before an audience in heaven, that God can be loved for himself, as Paul says through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Eph 3:10).

And there is a limit, set before a single blow falls: only against him do not stretch out your hand. Jesus told Peter the same on the night of his arrest: Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31-32). Job did not know about the council. The Christian knows there is one, and that Jesus is in it, praying. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability (1 Cor 10:13).

Is God then responsible for the evil? He permits it and sets its limits (v. 12), and nothing happens outside his rule. But Satan and the raiders are the ones who do evil, and God is neither its author nor guilty of it. Job rightly says the LORD has taken away (v. 21) and did not sin or charge God with wrong (v. 22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On one ordinary day four servants arrive on each other's heels: raiders, fire, raiders again, and a great wind that brings the house down on all ten children (vv. 13-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The book never lets wicked men, weather, the devil or God's permission explain the others away.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and there came a messenger to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them, and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a day echoes verse 6. What was decided in heaven arrives on earth on an ordinary day, at a family meal. If the brothers hosted in order of age, the round of feasts had just begun again.

The work is ordinary, ploughing and grazing; then come raiders from Sheba, men who kill for livestock. The first blow is plain human wickedness. The Sabeans were not puppets; they chose their raid and will answer for it. But they have come because God allowed it and Satan wanted it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabeans came from Arabia; the Chaldeans (v. 17) from Mesopotamia.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you." While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was probably lightning. But the servant calls it the fire of God, the phrase used of the fire that fell at Elijah's word (2 Kgs 1:12). Even the messenger reads it as heaven turned against his master. That is how it looked from the ground, and Job will spend the rest of the book wrestling with that appearance.

Then come raiders again, this time from Mesopotamia. Men, then sky, then men: trouble comes from every side and through every kind of cause. No one explanation will cover it, and Job is not given time to look for one: while he was yet speaking, three times over. He cannot take in one loss before the next arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The storyteller has kept the worst till last. Ten children are under one roof, at the very meal their father used to pray over. A wind from the desert struck the four corners, every side at once, and there was nowhere to run. By the end of one day Job has ten graves to dig.

Two things must be said to any parent who reads this with a grave of his own. First, the book never says these children died for their sins. Bildad will say it (8:4), and the LORD will judge him and his friends for speaking what is not right (42:7). Second, Job's prayers for them were not wasted; nothing in the book suggests that a father loses his children because his prayers failed. What the book does is refuse to explain the loss, and then show that God can be trusted in it.

Was it just to take Job’s children for a test they knew nothing of? The book does not explain it from their side, and we should not pretend to. But the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Gen 18:25), and the manner of a death is no verdict on the one who died. Job, who had prayed and offered sacrifices for them (v. 5), never accuses God of injustice to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The LORD Gave, and the LORD Has Taken Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job grieves and worships (vv. 20-21), and in all this he does not sin (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The first round goes to God, and to the man who trusted him with nothing left in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are five verbs. The first four are the grief of his time: the torn robe, the shaved head, the body thrown on the ground. Job does not pretend; there is no brave face. Then the fifth, in the same sentence: and worshiped, bowed down, face to the earth.

Grief and worship are not opposites. A Christian at a graveside does not have to choose between weeping and trusting. Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend (John 11:35), and Paul tells the church not to stop grieving but not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13). Tears are not unbelief. Job's were on the ground, and so was his worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came with nothing and will leave with nothing; everything in between was loaned. The Preacher says the same (Eccl 5:15), and Paul: we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world (1 Tim 6:7).

Job does not blame the Sabeans or the Chaldeans or the weather, and he does not know about Satan. He goes straight past every second cause to the first, and he is right to: God will say to Satan, you incited me against him (2:3). This is not fatalism. His losses were not in the hands of chance, but of the one who gave him everything in the first place.

Blessed be the name of the LORD uses Satan's own word. He said Job would “bless” God to his face, meaning curse. Job blesses God, and means it, and Satan's theory has failed in a single verb.

This verse is not a formula to recite over someone else's grief, and it was not easy for Job. He said it with his head shaved and his clothes torn, and in chapter 3 the same man will curse the day he was born. Both are in him. But it shows what a person can say from the bottom. Long afterwards another man was stripped, and soldiers divided his clothes among them (John 19:23-24). He had nothing left, and he did not curse God: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46).

verseByVerse.quote: In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the verdict carefully, because the rest of the book depends on it. Job said that the LORD had taken away his children, and that was not sin. What he did not do was charge God with wrong. To say “God did this” is not sinful. To say “God did this and was wrong to” would be. The whole book lives between those two sentences.

Satan, raiders, fire and wind all had their part, and over it all stood the permission and purpose of God. The same pattern appears at the cross: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Wicked men did their worst, and God's hand and plan had predestined it (Acts 4:28). If God could rule the darkest day in history for good, he rules yours too, even when you cannot yet see how.

Satan asked whether anyone would love God for no reason. One man did it perfectly. Jesus loved the Father with nothing in his hands and suffered without a cause, and because of him the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down (Rev 12:10). He is worthy of such love.

2.title: Skin for Skin
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason."<sup>4</sup>Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life.<sup>5</sup>But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life."<sup>7</sup>So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.<sup>8</sup>And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.<sup>9</sup>Then his wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die."<sup>10</sup>But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.<sup>11</sup>Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him.<sup>12</sup>And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.<sup>13</sup>And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
2.overview: The heavenly court meets again. The LORD repeats his verdict on Job: he still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason. Satan answers, Skin for skin!, and the LORD gives Job into his hand but forbids him to take his life (vv. 1-6). Satan strikes Job with sores from head to foot; his wife says, Curse God and die, and he will not (vv. 7-10). Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar come to comfort him and sit with him on the ground seven days and nights without a word (vv. 11-13).
2.theology:
God rules over evil without doing evil: Satan incites, and God says you incited me (v. 3). The limit on Satan moves, but it remains.

Job is struck with the look of the law's curse though he has not disobeyed, so that every onlooker takes him for cursed; Christ bore the curse itself, and it was ours (see on vv. 6-7).
2.examples: Job's wife turns God's own words, he still holds fast his integrity, into a despairing question, and Job, answering her, rebukes the words and spares the woman. Then three friends do the wisest thing they will ever do: they sit in silence for seven days.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a second council the LORD repeats his verdict (vv. 1-3), Satan claims that Job will break if his body is touched (vv. 4-5), and he is allowed to strike Job, but not to take his life (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not keep his distance from Job's suffering. The evil is Satan's; the permission, and the limit, are God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD. And the LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene repeats almost word for word, with one addition. In chapter 1 Satan simply came among them (1:6). Now he comes to present himself before the LORD, like the others. He has lost the first round, and he has to report. However much he roams the earth, he cannot stay away from the throne. He answers to God, whether he likes it or not.

The question and the restless answer are the same. Nothing has changed for Satan. Everything has changed for Job, and he does not know why.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God repeats his verdict and adds two things. First, he still holds fast his integrity: the blameless of 1:1 again. His children are dead and his wealth is gone, and he has not let go.

The second is startling: you incited me against him. God does not say Satan did it while he looked away. He says Satan moved him. Samuel says the LORD incited David to number Israel (2 Sam 24:1); Chronicles says Satan ... incited David (1 Chr 21:1). Both are true. Satan means evil by it, and God rules over it for his own ends. God owns what happened to Job, and he does not let Satan off.

And without reason is Satan's word from 1:9, handed back to him. There was nothing in Job that called for this. Whatever the friends are about to argue, the LORD has already ruled: this suffering was not deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Skin for skin is a proverb, probably from trading: a man will give one hide to save another, and anything to save his own. Satan's argument is that the first test did not go deep enough. Job still had himself. Touch that, and you will see what he really loves.

Again Satan asks God to do the striking. It is the cynic's creed, and it sounds shrewd: in the end everyone looks after number one. Satan has never met a love that would not save itself. He is about to watch one in Job, and one day he will watch it perfectly, in a man who saved others and would not save himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The limit moves, but there is still a limit. Satan may touch Job's body, not take his life. God draws the line before the blow, as he did the first time (1:12).

Any Israelite reader would feel it at once. The sentence echoes one of the law's curses on a disobedient people, word for word at the end: The LORD will strike you ... with grievous boils of which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head (Deut 28:35). Job has done nothing to earn that curse, but he looks exactly like a man who has. Everyone who sees him will draw the obvious conclusion, and three men are about to.

That is the pattern of the cross. The prophet says of the Servant, we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted (Isa 53:4). The onlookers were right that he bore a curse and wrong about whose. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). Job bore the look of the curse without the guilt. Christ bore the curse itself, and it was ours.

Is all sickness, then, from Satan? This is a particular case, permitted and limited by God, and the book shows it to us so that we will not assume it of every illness. Sickness comes in many ways in a fallen world, and God rules over all of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job sits in the ashes (v. 8). His wife urges him to curse God and die (v. 9); he answers that we must receive evil from God as well as good, and does not sin with his lips (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The body that Satan was sure would break is the place where Job holds on. The second round goes to God as well.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He scrapes the itching, running sores with a shard from a broken pot, one small picture of how far he has fallen. The greatest man in the east sits in the ashes, the place of mourning, with a piece of rubbish in his hand.

Jesus told of a poor man at a rich man's gate, covered with sores, and even the dogs came and licked his sores (Luke 16:20-21). God's people have often looked like that. And their Lord did not stay away from that place: Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Heb 13:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then his wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her first question is God's own sentence from verse 3, he still holds fast his integrity, turned into a question. God said it with pride. She says it in despair, or scorn. The one thing God delights in is the one thing she wants him to let go of. And her advice is Satan's goal to the letter: curse God, and then die and be done with it.

She has been hard judged, and she has earned some of it. But remember what she has lost: ten children in the ground, the wealth gone, her husband scraping his sores in the ashes. Hers are the words of someone who thinks faith has failed and would rather see the suffering end in death. Plenty of believers have heard those words from someone they love, or said them to themselves. Job mentions her later (19:17), but she never speaks again.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foolish person in Scripture is not the stupid one but the one who lives as if God does not matter: The fool says in his heart, There is no God (Ps 14:1). And Job does not call her a fool. He says she is talking like one. He rebukes the words and spares the woman.

We: he takes her into the question with him. Evil here means calamity, not wickedness, as when God says, I make well-being and create calamity (Isa 45:7). Job has taken God's good gifts for years without asking whether he deserved them. Is he now to take only the good and hand back the rest? His faith is not a contract that lapses when the payments stop.

In chapter 1 Job worried that his children had cursed God in their hearts (1:5). Here the narrator speaks of his lips, because the test was whether he would curse God aloud. And the mouth shows the heart: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt 12:34). Satan has lost twice. He is not mentioned again in the book.
verseByVerse.note: “Evil” can also be rendered “disaster” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — Seven Days on the Ground
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three friends come to comfort Job (v. 11), weep at the sight of him (v. 12), and sit with him seven days without a word (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: When the friends begin to speak, they begin to go wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come from the lands around Edom and Arabia. Eliphaz shares his name with a son of Esau, whose own son was called Teman (Gen 36:10-11), and Teman was famous for its wise men: Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jer 49:7). Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25:2). These are serious men from the wisdom country, and they come as friends.

Their intentions were good: they took trouble and arranged to travel together to share his grief. Keep the two verbs in mind. Job will soon call them miserable comforters (16:2). And at the very end, when his brothers and sisters come to eat with him, the narrator will say they showed him sympathy and comforted him (42:11), the same pair of words. The friends came to do something the book finally sees done by others.
verseByVerse.note: Teman was a city of Edom, famous for its wise men.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They see a man on the ash heap and do not know him; the sores have changed his face. They weep aloud, tear their clothes as he tore his (1:20), and throw dust into the air so that it falls on their heads. It is real grief, and it is honest.

Isaiah's Servant is described the same way: his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance (Isa 52:14). There is a suffering that makes a man unrecognizable, and the Son of God went into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph mourned his father seven days (Gen 50:10), and the friends mourn Job as though he were already dead. They sit on the ground with him, day and night, and say nothing, because they can see that nothing would be big enough for his pain. They let him speak first.

This is the best thing the friends do in the whole book, and it is still the right place to begin with anyone in deep grief: go, sit on the ground, and do not explain. Weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). When the friends open their mouths, from chapter 4 on, they will do great harm, and God will say they did not speak rightly of him (42:7). Their silence never needed to be forgiven.

And this is what God did for us. He did not send an explanation from a distance. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). He sat in our dust, and so we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15). He has been on the ground with us, and he stays; his comfort is what we bring when we go and sit with others.
verseByVerse.note: Compare Ezekiel 3:15, where the prophet sits overwhelmed among the exiles seven days.

3.title: Let the Day Perish
3.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.<sup>2</sup>And Job said:<sup>3</sup>"Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A man is conceived.'<sup>4</sup>Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it.<sup>5</sup>Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.<sup>6</sup>That night—let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months.<sup>7</sup>Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.<sup>8</sup>Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan.<sup>9</sup>Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning,<sup>10</sup>because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes.<sup>11</sup>"Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?<sup>12</sup>Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?<sup>13</sup>For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest,<sup>14</sup>with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves,<sup>15</sup>or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.<sup>16</sup>Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light?<sup>17</sup>There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest.<sup>18</sup>There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster.<sup>19</sup>The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.<sup>20</sup>"Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul,<sup>21</sup>who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,<sup>22</sup>who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?<sup>23</sup>Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?<sup>24</sup>For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water.<sup>25</sup>For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me.<sup>26</sup>I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes."
3.overview: After seven days of silence Job speaks, and curses the day of his birth. He wishes that day darkness and that night barren, struck from the calendar, because it did not keep him from being born into trouble (vv. 1-10). He asks why he did not die at birth: then he would be at rest with kings and princes, where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest (vv. 11-19). And he asks why light is given to the miserable who long for death, to a man whom God has hedged in; he has no rest, but trouble comes (vv. 20-26).
3.theology:
Lament is not rebellion. Job curses his day, not his God, and Scripture places the same cry in the mouth of a faithful prophet (Jer 20:14-18), lets whole psalms end in darkness, and hears the lament of Psalm 22 on Christ's own lips.

Job tries to un-create his day, and when God answers he will begin with creation. The rest Job seeks in the grave is answered in Christ.
3.examples: Many of Job's words here will come back later in the book with their meaning turned: the Leviathan he wants roused, God will show him on a lead (41:1), and the man who digs for the grave as for treasure will later ask where wisdom, deeper than any treasure, can be found (ch. 28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job breaks the silence by cursing the day of his birth (vv. 1-2) and wishing it unmade, dark and barren (vv. 3-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief this deep is not the same thing as rebellion, and Scripture keeps the two apart.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. And Job said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven days of silence end, and it is Job who breaks them. And the first thing he does is curse, not God, but the day. Satan twice predicted that Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). He does not. He curses the day he was born, and the difference is the whole difference between a man in agony and a man in rebellion.

He is not the only servant of God to say it. Jeremiah, in the middle of his calling, cried, Cursed be the day on which I was born! (Jer 20:14). Scripture does not tidy these cries away. It prints them, so that the believer who has felt the same will know he is not the first, and that God has heard it before.

Two things change here. The book changes from prose to poetry: from And Job said until 42:6 almost everything is set out in lines, like the Psalms, meant to be heard as the speech of a man in extremity, not as a statement of doctrine. And Job himself seems to change. The man who said blessed be the name of the LORD now wishes he had never been born. It is the same man, after seven days on the ash heap. When James holds Job up to Christians, the word he uses is steadfastness (James 5:11): not calm, but endurance, the refusal to let go while everything in you is shouting. This chapter is part of what James meant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A man is conceived.' Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it. Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes back to the beginning, his birth and before that his conception, as if he could reach into the past and unmake it. The night is imagined speaking, announcing a boy. He wishes it had never spoken.

Anyone who knows Genesis will hear it. On the first day God said, Let there be light (Gen 1:3). Job uses the same Hebrew form in reverse: let that day be darkness. He wants to un-create his own day.

May God above not seek it. To seek a thing, in this sense, is to care for it: Israel's was a land that the LORD your God cares for (Deut 11:12). Job asks God to take his eyes off one day, so that it falls out of existence. It is the prayer of a man who still believes that nothing lasts unless God keeps it.

He piles up every word for dark he has. This is what grief does to a man's world: it runs back over his whole life and puts out the lights one by one.

One of those words matters for the rest of the book. Deep darkness is the Hebrew tsalmaveth, which older translations rendered “the shadow of death”, as in the valley of the shadow of death (Ps 23:4). The same man who here asks the deep darkness to swallow his day will say that God brings deep darkness to light (12:22), and God will ask him, have you seen the gates of deep darkness? (38:17). The darkness Job calls on is not beyond God's reach. God has seen its gates.

When God finally answers Job, he will not start with Job's suffering, but with creation: Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? (38:4). Job has tried to undo a day. God will show him the One who made every day there is.

verseByVerse.quote: That night—let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months. Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He wants the night struck off the calendar, so that it never comes round again. And he wants it barren: the joyful cry would have been the shout when a boy was born.

He is not saying his life was always misery; chapter 29 will show how rich it was. He is saying that if this is where it was heading, it would have been better never to have begun. Deep grief can reach back and poison the happy years too. That is not a verdict on the years. It is a measure of the wound.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan. Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning, because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ancient world believed in men who could curse a day and make it unlucky, and told stories of Leviathan, the monster of the sea and of chaos. Job reaches for any power at all that might undo his day, even the monster.

That name will come back. God will ask Job, Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook? (41:1), and describe the creature Job wanted roused as something God made and holds on a lead. Scripture elsewhere uses the name for every power that opposes God: In that day the LORD ... will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent (Isa 27:1). Job calls on chaos. God will show him that chaos has a master.

The eyelids of the morning are the first glimmer at dawn. He wants that night to wait for a morning that never comes, because it let him be born, and so let him see trouble.

That word, 'amal, is what Job calls his life now (v. 20; 7:3). And Eliphaz will seize on it in his first reply: man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward (5:7). Job says trouble came because he was born. Eliphaz will say trouble is what being born means, and that it does not come from nowhere. The argument of the next twenty chapters is already starting.
verseByVerse.note: Leviathan was a sea monster of ancient myth, a picture of chaos; God later describes it as his creature (ch. 41).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — Why Did I Not Die at Birth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks why he did not die at birth (vv. 11-12), and pictures the grave as rest (vv. 13-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Job longs for the grave as a place of rest. The New Testament does not deny the longing; it points it to a person.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire? Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first why of the book, and there will be many. The knees may be a father's, taking the newborn on his lap as his own; the breasts are the mother's. Every kindness that kept the baby alive, Job now counts as a cruelty.

This is not a philosopher's question. It is the question people ask in hospital corridors and at three in the morning. The Bible does not forbid it. Job asks it, and God will answer him, though not in the way he expects.

verseByVerse.quote: For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest, with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves, or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Quiet, sleep, rest: the three things he cannot have, and in his pain the grave looks like the only place to find them. He pictures himself among the great, kings who built monuments and princes who hoarded gold. What they built for themselves did not keep them. Death has made them equal, and Job would rather be equal with the dead than go on living.

The Old Testament saints saw the grave dimly, as a place of silence, and Job speaks of it as a desperate man does, as mere relief. The New Testament gives the longing its real answer. There is a rest for the weary, and it is not the grave but a person: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light? There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest. There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster. The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stillborn baby is buried quietly, unnamed; the light never touches it. Job envies it.

These lines have been carved on many gravestones, and they are true as far as they go. In the grave nobody bullies anyone. The taskmaster is the word Exodus uses for Egypt's slave drivers (Exod 3:7). The weak and the powerful, the slave and his owner, lie side by side. For a man in unending pain it sounds like freedom.

But Scripture's fuller word about the rest of the dead is for those who die in the Lord: Blessed indeed ... that they may rest from their labors (Rev 14:13). The rest Job longed for in the dark is real, and it belongs to those who belong to Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks why life is given to those who long for death (vv. 20-23), and ends with no rest, only trouble (vv. 24-26).
verseByVerse.theology: For the first time Job's question turns toward God. He does not doubt that God gives life. He cannot understand why God goes on giving it to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul, who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures, who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the question turns. It is no longer only about Job's birth but about everyone in misery, and it is aimed, carefully, at God, though it does not name him. Job still believes that God gives life. That is exactly his problem.

Some who read this will know the longing from the inside, the wish to go to sleep and not wake. Look at what Job does with it. He says it aloud, to God. And he never takes his life into his own hands; he will ask God to end it (6:8-9), because he knows it is God's (1:21). If that is where you are, do what Job did: say it aloud, to the God who has not let go of you, and to someone who will sit with you on the ground.

Is the wish to die a sin? Job, Elijah (1 Kgs 19:4) and Jonah (Jon 4:3) all wished it, and God did not condemn them for saying it. But taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment; life is God’s to give and to take. Depression and despair are real, and they call for help: from God in prayer, from the church, and from doctors where needed. Anyone who is thinking of ending their life should tell someone today: a pastor, a doctor, a friend, or a crisis line. And if someone you love has died this way, this book, which records Job's darkest words without condemning him, does not ask you to sit in judgment; leave them with the God who knows the heart.

And look at the picture of digging for death more than for hidden treasures. In chapter 28 men will dig for treasure, and Job will ask where wisdom, dearer than all of it, can be found (28:1-13). The man digging for the grave has not yet found what is buried deeper.

verseByVerse.quote: Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now God is named. Whose way is hidden: Job cannot see where his road goes or why it turned. Hedged in is close cousin to the word Satan used: God had put a hedge around Job to protect him (1:10). Job feels the hedge as a prison wall. The same hand that once guarded him now seems to be shutting him in.

The reader knows what Job does not: that God is still guarding him, and the limit set in heaven still stands (2:6). Every believer walks, some of the time, where his way is hidden. The hedge he feels as a prison may be the very thing that is keeping him.

verseByVerse.quote: For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water. For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me. I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sighing is his food; groaning runs out of him like water from a jar. The sores, the loss, the sleeplessness have taken over the ordinary things of life.

People sometimes take the thing that I fear comes upon me to mean that Job's fears brought the disaster on him. The book says nothing of the kind; chapters 1 and 2 have told us exactly how this began. Job had always known how fragile his blessings were, and rose early to pray for his children (1:5). Now the thing he dreaded has happened, and his dread did not cause it.

Ease, quiet, rest: the words he used of the grave (vv. 13, 17-18), now with not in front of each one. The dead have what he lacks. And the last word of his first speech is trouble.

The chapter ends there, in the dark, with no word of hope. Psalm 88 ends the same way: my companions have become darkness (Ps 88:18). Job's lament is not the sin Satan wanted; he has not cursed God. But it is not the whole truth either, and God will call some of his later words words without knowledge (38:2). Scripture lets a chapter end in darkness because some of God's people have to sit there for a while, and the Son of God sat there too: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Heb 5:7), and on the cross he prayed, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone into ours, in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

4.title: Who That Was Innocent Ever Perished?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?<sup>3</sup>Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands.<sup>4</sup>Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees.<sup>5</sup>But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed.<sup>6</sup>Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?<sup>7</sup>"Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off?<sup>8</sup>As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same.<sup>9</sup>By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.<sup>10</sup>The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken.<sup>11</sup>The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.<sup>12</sup>"Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it.<sup>13</sup>Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men,<sup>14</sup>dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.<sup>15</sup>A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up.<sup>16</sup>It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice:<sup>17</sup>'Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?<sup>18</sup>Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error;<sup>19</sup>how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth.<sup>20</sup>Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it.<sup>21</sup>Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom?'
4.overview: Eliphaz, the first and most courteous of the friends, begins gently: Job has strengthened the weak hands of others, but now that trouble has touched him he is dismayed (vv. 1-6). Then he states the friends' case: who that was innocent ever perished? Those who sow trouble reap it (vv. 7-11). He tells of a spirit that came to him stealthily in the night: no mortal can be in the right before God, and men in houses of clay are crushed like the moth (vv. 12-21).
4.theology:
The friends' case, stated here for the first time, is that suffering proves sin, and God will say at the end that they did not speak rightly of him (42:7). Their error is a true rule (the wicked reap what they sow, Gal 6:7) read backwards from the harvest to the seed, a reading Jesus himself refused (Luke 13:2-5; John 9:2-3). The innocent do perish, and the cross is the proof.

The vision's question, Can mortal man be in the right before God?, is the right one, but it is asked here to crush. The gospel is its answer.
4.examples:
Watch how Eliphaz works. He quotes Job's good works back to him as a rebuke, and he turns Job's fear of God and integrity into a guarantee that nothing bad could happen. His picture of how the wicked die happens to be the way Job's children died.

Then he claims a night vision with no face and no thus says the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Strengthened the Weak Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz begins gently (vv. 1-2): Job has strengthened weak hands (vv. 3-4), but now trouble has touched him (v. 5). Should not his fear of God be his confidence (v. 6)?
verseByVerse.theology: The first friend to speak is the kindest, and his courtesy is real. But a gentle voice can carry a false message.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The debate begins, and it will run for twenty-four chapters. Before a word of it is read, the reader should know how it ends. The LORD will say to this man by name: My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). Everything Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar say must be read in that light. They will say many true things about God. They will be wrong about Job, and wrong about God's ways with him. A line of theirs may be true in itself, but their speeches are never to be quoted as God's verdict on a sufferer.

Eliphaz speaks first, probably as the eldest, and he is the most courteous, asking permission almost apologetically. But who can keep from speaking? The friends' seven days of silence were their best hour, as this speech is about to show.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands. Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees. But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribute is real. Job had been the man others went to in trouble, and Eliphaz uses words Isaiah would later use of God's comfort to his people: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees (Isa 35:3). Hebrews takes up the same words to rally tired Christians (Heb 12:12).

Then the tribute turns: now it has come to you. You gave advice to others; now take it yourself. It is easier to counsel suffering than to bear it, and that much is true. But Eliphaz has not measured what has come to Job. Ten children and his health are not the troubles Job used to talk people through. The comforter who says "you of all people should cope with this" has not yet understood the size of the grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the narrator's words from 1:1, and God's own from 2:3. Eliphaz does not deny Job's piety. He assumes it, and turns it into a guarantee: if you really fear God, you cannot come to real harm.

It has a true root: those who fear God are safe in him for ever. But Eliphaz means safe from loss and grief in this life, and God never promised that. Job's integrity was on trial, not his insurance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — Who That Was Innocent Ever Perished?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz states the case the friends will hold to the end (v. 7): those who sow trouble reap it (vv. 8-9); even the strong lion perishes (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: A true rule about the end of the wicked is turned here into a law about every sufferer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off? As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the friends' whole case, and the rest of their speeches only repeat it: the innocent do not perish; therefore, if you are perishing, you are not innocent.

Scripture answers the question on almost every page. Abel was innocent and was killed in a field. Zechariah the priest was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD for speaking God's word (2 Chr 24:21). And a Roman officer would stand at the foot of a cross and say, Certainly this man was innocent! (Luke 23:47). Where were the upright cut off? At Golgotha. Jesus refused Eliphaz's reasoning in so many words. Of the Galileans Pilate killed and the eighteen crushed by a tower: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others ...? No, I tell you (Luke 13:2-5). Of a man born blind: It was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:3).

Paul says something that sounds the same: whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7). But Paul warns the one doing the sowing. Eliphaz reads it backwards, from the harvest to the seed. Trouble is Job's own word from 3:10, and the blast of God's anger is the Hebrew word for the wind that brought the house down on Job's children (1:19). Whether he means it or not, Eliphaz has described how Job's children died.
verseByVerse.note: The friends never move off this ground; every later speech builds on it.

verseByVerse.quote: The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken. The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
verseByVerse.commentary: The poet uses five different Hebrew words for lion in two verses, a showpiece of his art. The most powerful beast grows old, its teeth break, it starves, and its cubs are scattered: the mighty cannot keep their strength or their children when God is against them. Eliphaz does not say "you". He does not need to. The strong man of the east has lost his wealth, and his children are gone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A spirit glides past him in the night (vv. 12-16), and its message is that no mortal is right before God; if even angels are charged with error, how much more men in houses of clay (vv. 17-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The book gives us no reason to trust where this voice came from, and it asks a true question only to leave a man without hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it. Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake. A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz now claims something more than experience: a revelation. It is written to make the reader's skin crawl, and it does. But look at what is missing. There is no thus says the LORD. The spirit has no face. It comes by stealth. The book does not say where it came from, but it sets this scene beside the end, when the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (38:1): openly, in person, to the man himself. God does not need to creep up on anyone. A believer who is told "God showed me in the night what your suffering means" is right to ask what Scripture says.

Was Eliphaz’s vision from God? What the spirit says in verse 17 is true as far as it goes: no one is righteous before God. But Eliphaz uses it to accuse Job, and God says the friends did not speak of him what is right (42:7). No vision outside Scripture binds anyone, and every claim to one must be tested by the word of God (1 John 4:1).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice's question is true: no one can stand before God on his own merits. Job will ask it himself (9:2), and Bildad again (25:4). It is the question the whole Bible asks.

That is what makes the friends dangerous: they speak true sentences in a false speech. Because no one is pure before God, Eliphaz reasons, Job's suffering must be the fruit of Job's sin. But the question was never meant to condemn one man above others. It is the question the gospel answers. God set forth Christ so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). Eliphaz leaves it hanging over Job like a sword. The cross answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error; how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth. Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it. Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even angels fall short before God, what hope for men of clay? It is a picture of how frail we are: bodies of mud, founded on dust, as easily crushed as a moth. Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it. Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom? The body is a tent; pull up the cord and it collapses.

Paul uses the same pictures, and the difference is the gospel. We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God (2 Cor 4:7). If the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor 5:1). Eliphaz's vision ends with men dying without wisdom, unnoticed. Paul's ends with a house in heaven. Same clay, same tent. The difference is Christ, raised from the dust.

Do the angels sin? Some did, and fell (2 Pet 2:4; Jude 6), but Scripture calls the rest holy angels and elect angels (Mark 8:38; 1 Tim 5:21). Eliphaz’s point is that no creature is righteous in itself before God; he stretches it to make every creature suspect, in order to condemn Job.

5.title: Blessed Is the One Whom God Reproves
5.text: <sup>1</sup>"Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?<sup>2</sup>Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple.<sup>3</sup>I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling.<sup>4</sup>His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them.<sup>5</sup>The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.<sup>6</sup>For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground,<sup>7</sup>but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.<sup>8</sup>"As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause,<sup>9</sup>who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number:<sup>10</sup>he gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields;<sup>11</sup>he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.<sup>12</sup>He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success.<sup>13</sup>He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end.<sup>14</sup>They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night.<sup>15</sup>But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty.<sup>16</sup>So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.<sup>17</sup>"Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty.<sup>18</sup>For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal.<sup>19</sup>He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you.<sup>20</sup>In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.<sup>21</sup>You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes.<sup>22</sup>At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth.<sup>23</sup>For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.<sup>24</sup>You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing.<sup>25</sup>You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth.<sup>26</sup>You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.<sup>27</sup>Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good."
5.overview: Eliphaz goes on. No heavenly being will answer Job; vexation kills the fool, and man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward (vv. 1-7). He would seek God, who lifts the lowly and catches the wise in their own craftiness (vv. 8-16). Blessed is the one whom God reproves: if Job accepts his discipline he will see peace, many children and a ripe old age, and the friends have searched it out (vv. 17-27).
5.theology:
Eliphaz speaks true things falsely. God does catch the wise in their craftiness (1 Cor 3:19), does discipline those he loves (Prov 3:11-12; Heb 12:5-6), and does wound and heal (Deut 32:39). But Eliphaz applies these truths to a man God has declared innocent, and in the end the wise man caught in his own wisdom is the speaker.

A comforter must hold both what God has revealed and the limits of what he himself knows. God's works are unsearchable (v. 9), yet Eliphaz claims to have searched out Job's case (v. 27).
5.examples: Small details carry the argument. The fool's children are crushed, and so were Job's. The first Almighty in the book is on Eliphaz's lips, and so is the promise no evil shall touch you, made to a man evil has touched twice. Paul quotes one of his lines as Scripture, but turns it on the man who thinks himself wise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Man Is Born to Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one will answer Job (v. 1). Vexation kills the fool, whose house is cursed and children crushed (vv. 2-5). Trouble does not sprout from the ground (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every picture Eliphaz chooses of the fool's end is a picture of what has happened to Job.

verseByVerse.quote: "Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy ones are heavenly beings, the angels. Eliphaz is mocking the idea that Job might find anyone in heaven to take his side. If God puts no trust even in his angels (4:18), who would stand up for a man like Job?

It is a cruel question, and Job will spend the rest of the book reaching for an answer. He will wish for an arbiter between himself and God (9:33); he will say my witness is in heaven (16:19); he will say I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25). Eliphaz says there is no one. The Christian knows the name of the one there is: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple. I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling. His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them. The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vexation is exactly what Job poured out in chapter 3, and Eliphaz warns him that fools die of it. Job will throw the word back: Oh that my vexation were weighed (6:2).

Eliphaz has seen a fool prosper and then fall: his home cursed, his children crushed, his harvest carried off by others, and he himself pronounced the house cursed when he saw it. The friend who came to comfort is a man ready to pronounce curses, where Job, in chapter 1, pronounced a blessing. He tells it as a general lesson, but Job's children were crushed when a house fell on them, and his flocks were carried off by raiders. Eliphaz does not need to say "you are the fool". The friends will work this way throughout.

verseByVerse.quote: For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground, but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last line is often quoted as a sad truth about life, and it is true: we are all born to trouble. But look at the line before. Trouble does not grow out of the ground like a weed; it has a root, and the root is in man. Eliphaz means: your trouble came from somewhere, and it came from you.

Trouble is Job's own word again, from 3:10. Scripture agrees that suffering entered the world through sin (Rom 5:12). It refuses to say that each sufferer's pain can be traced to his own sin. That is the step Eliphaz takes, and the step God will judge.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz would seek God (v. 8), who does unsearchable things and lifts the lowly (vv. 9-11), catches the wise in their own craftiness (vv. 12-14), and saves the needy (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: A true and beautiful hymn. Yet Job, not Eliphaz, is the one who will actually take it to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause, who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number: he gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields; he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I would seek God is good advice: take it to God. Here is the irony of the whole debate: Job is the one who does it.
