Again and again in the chapters to come he will turn from the friends and speak to God directly, pleading, protesting, asking for a hearing. Not once in the whole debate do the friends speak to God. They only speak about him. When the LORD judges between them, that difference will matter.

Mary will sing the gospel fulfilment of the lifting of the lowly: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52). God will lift this mourner, and Eliphaz will be standing by with a sacrifice in his hands when he does (42:8).

But look again at the first line. God gives rain on the earth. Jesus drew a lesson from the rain that cuts straight across Eliphaz's system: God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matt 5:45). Rain is not a wage paid to the good. It falls on everyone's field, out of kindness. If God's gifts are not handed out strictly by merit, neither are his losses. Eliphaz has quoted the evidence against his own case.

verseByVerse.quote: He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success. He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end. They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night. But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty. So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes this line: For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, He catches the wise in their craftiness (1 Cor 3:19). It is one of only two places where the New Testament clearly quotes Job, and it quotes Eliphaz. The book is inspired as a whole, it records his words truly, and this sentence is true. Eliphaz's error was never the sentence. It was aiming it at Job.

And Paul aims it rightly, at the man who thinks that he is wise (1 Cor 3:18). Read to the end of Job and the wise man caught in his own wisdom is Eliphaz, to whom God says, My anger burns against you (42:7).

Groping at noonday is Deuteronomy's curse on the disobedient (Deut 28:29), from the same chapter as the sores of 2:7. Job is sitting in the dark at noon. The friends keep reaching for the covenant's curses to describe the wicked, and each time the description fits the man in front of them.

God rescues the needy from the sword of their mouth. Before long, the sword aimed at this needy man will be the friends' own words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Blessed Is the One Whom God Reproves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not despise the Almighty's discipline (v. 17). He wounds and heals, and delivers from every trouble (vv. 18-23); your tent will be safe, your children many, your grave in ripe old age (vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Much of it will come true for Job. None of it will come true for the reason Eliphaz gives.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty. For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first time the book calls God the Almighty (Shaddai), a name it will use thirty-one times. And the sentence is true: the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights (Prov 3:12), and Hebrews tells Christians under pressure that the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb 12:6). A believer in trouble may rightly ask whether God is showing him something to put right, and he asks it as a son already loved, with the Spirit of adoption in him to help him turn. For one who is in Christ, discipline is a Father's training for his good, never the punishment of sins that Christ has already borne (Romans 8:1; Hebrews 12:10).

Hebrews gives this truth to sons as comfort: your pain is not a sign that you are unloved. Eliphaz gives it to Job as a diagnosis, and in Job's case it is false, because God has already said his suffering was without reason (2:3).

The wounding hand is the healing hand: Moses sang it (Deut 32:39) and Hosea preached it (Hos 6:1), and it will prove true of Job, though not by the route Eliphaz prescribes.

verseByVerse.quote: He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six troubles, then seven, means every trouble, however many. Touch is Satan's word: touch all that he has (1:11), touch his bone and his flesh (2:5). Evil has touched Job twice, and he will cry, Have mercy on me ... for the hand of God has touched me! (19:21).

Eliphaz paints perfect safety: no famine, no sword, no stone in the plough-land, no wild beast. It is the peace God promised Israel for obedience. One line stands out. Job will be hidden from the lash of the tongue. He is being lashed by one now.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing. You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth. You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imagine hearing this beside ten new graves. Your offspring shall be many. Eliphaz means it kindly; it is the reward he offers if Job will only confess. But Job has nothing true to confess, and every line of the promise names something he has just lost.

The last picture is the loveliest: like a sheaf gathered up in its season. A good death is a harvest, the grain brought in when it is ripe and not before. Job's children were cut down green. Eliphaz holds out the ripe sheaf as the reward of the righteous, and does not see the field behind Job.

And here is the strangest thing: it comes true. At the end of the book Job will have seven sons and three daughters again, and Job died, an old man, and full of days (42:17). Eliphaz promised the right blessings for the wrong reason. They came to Job not as the wage for a false confession, but as the free gift of a God who had vindicated him. New children did not replace the ten he buried, and no reader who has lost a child should hear it so. God's kindness is larger than the friends' theology, and it does not run on their terms.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We: Eliphaz speaks for the three of them, for the whole tradition. Searched out: they have studied the matter and settled it. But listen to what he said in verse 9: God does things unsearchable. In Hebrew it is the same word. God's ways cannot be searched out, says Eliphaz; and we have searched this out, says Eliphaz. He has not noticed the contradiction.

Job will take up the line about God's unsearchable works and say it almost word for word himself (9:10). Paul will cry, How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33). That is the right response to the God of Job. Whoever sits with a sufferer should be slow to say, "we have searched this out." There is a proper confidence about what God has said, and a proper humility about what he has not. The friends had the first without the second.

6.title: Oh That My Vexation Were Weighed
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!<sup>3</sup>For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.<sup>4</sup>For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.<sup>5</sup>Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder?<sup>6</sup>Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow?<sup>7</sup>My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me.<sup>8</sup>"Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope,<sup>9</sup>that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!<sup>10</sup>This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.<sup>11</sup>What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?<sup>12</sup>Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze?<sup>13</sup>Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?<sup>14</sup>"He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.<sup>15</sup>My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away,<sup>16</sup>which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself.<sup>17</sup>When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place.<sup>18</sup>The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish.<sup>19</sup>The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope.<sup>20</sup>They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed.<sup>21</sup>For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid.<sup>22</sup>Have I said, 'Make me a gift'? Or, 'From your wealth offer a bribe for me'?<sup>23</sup>Or, 'Deliver me from the adversary's hand'? Or, 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?<sup>24</sup>"Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray.<sup>25</sup>How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove?<sup>26</sup>Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind?<sup>27</sup>You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend.<sup>28</sup>"But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face.<sup>29</sup>Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake.<sup>30</sup>Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity?
6.overview: Job answers Eliphaz: weigh his calamity before his rash words, for the arrows of the Almighty are in him (vv. 1-7). He asks God to crush him; his comfort would be that he has not denied the words of the Holy One (vv. 8-13). His friends have withheld loyal love, like a desert stream that fails the caravans in summer (vv. 14-23). Let them teach him, look at him and turn, for his vindication is at stake (vv. 24-30).
6.theology:
Loyal love to a suffering friend belongs to the fear of God (v. 14), and it is the friends, not Job, who are failing it. Christ is the spring that does not fail (John 4:14).

Job is right that God's hand is in his trouble and wrong about its intent. His strength is gone, but he has not denied God's word, and God's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9).
6.examples: Notice the order Job asks for: weigh the pain before you judge the words. He admits his words were rash, and the only time he calls God the Holy One is while asking to die. His picture of his friends is a desert wadi, full in winter and dry in summer, and all he had asked of them was themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh That My Vexation Were Weighed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks that his calamity be weighed (vv. 1-3). The Almighty's arrows are in him, and a donkey does not bray without cause (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks that his pain be weighed before his words are judged. It is a fair request, and the friends never grant it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances! For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz warned that vexation kills the fool (5:2). Job takes the word and asks them to put his trouble on the scales before they judge what he said. It would outweigh the sand of every shore. Later he will ask God for the same thing: Let me be weighed in a just balance (31:6).

And he admits it: my words have been rash. He does not claim that chapter 3 was measured speech. He says it was wild, and that the wildness is the size of the pain. That is honesty, not defiance, as anyone who has sat with the bereaved knows. The first thing to do with rash words from a crushed person is to weigh the crushing, not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job says plainly who is behind it: not raiders or bad luck, but the Almighty, an archer with poisoned arrows, and Job is the target. Lamentations says the same: he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow (Lam 3:12).

Job is right that God's hand is in it; the LORD said so in heaven (2:3). He is wrong about what the hand intends. He thinks he is God's enemy; the reader knows he is God's delight. Many believers have felt exactly this, that God has turned against them, and the book lets them say it, while showing them what Job could not see: the arrows he feels are not the verdict of an enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder? Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow? My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder? Animals do not complain when they are fed. When a donkey brays, something is wrong. Job's cries have a cause, and it is not weakness of character.

Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow? My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me. The mallow's juice was slimy and flavourless, perhaps like raw egg white. Job may mean the food of suffering he is forced to eat every day; or he may mean the advice he has just been served, which has no salt in it. Either way he cannot swallow it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — That It Would Please God to Crush Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He asks God to end his life (vv. 8-9); his one comfort would be that he has not denied God's word (v. 10). He has no strength left to wait (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Even wishing to die, Job holds on to the one thing Satan tried to take: he has not denied God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off! This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His one request is that God would finish it. Cut me off: King Hezekiah, sick to death, used the same words, with a weaver's picture: like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom (Isa 38:12). Job does not reach for the knife himself. He asks God, because his life is God's to end.

Here is the one thing he still has. If he died now, he would die without having denied the words of the Holy One. That was exactly what Satan wanted (1:11; 2:5), and he has not done it. It is the only time in the book that Job calls God the Holy One. Even while asking to die, he names God by his holiness and clings to his word. That is not the speech of a man who has lost his faith. It is faith at the end of its strength.

verseByVerse.quote: What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze? Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?
verseByVerse.commentary: What is my strength, that I should wait? Eliphaz told him to be patient. Job asks, with what? He is not made of stone or bronze, and there is nothing left in him to hold on with. He is right that the strength is not in him, and Scripture never says it should be. They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:31); the strength comes from the one waited for. Paul learned it in his own weakness: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). Job has reached the end of himself. That is not the end of the road.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Withholding kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty (v. 14). His friends have proved a desert stream in summer, though he asked them for nothing (vv. 15-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The friends are afraid of what Job's innocence would mean for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kindness is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness that holds when holding is costly. Eliphaz told Job that his fear of God should be his confidence (4:6). Job turns it round. A man who withholds loyal love from a suffering friend is the one who has abandoned the fear of the Almighty. The friends think they are defending God, but in failing their friend they are failing him.

That is a test for every church: the measure of our fear of God is not how firmly we hold our doctrine while a brother suffers, but whether we stay with him. We can, because Christ stayed with us when we had nothing to give, and his Spirit pours out the love that holds (Gal 5:22).

The ESV's note says one Hebrew word here is uncertain, and several translations read: "a despairing man should have kindness from his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty". Then Job says something more searching still: if his faith did falter, that is exactly when a friend's loyalty is owed. Either way, the one going under needs love, not a verdict, most of all when his grip on God is weakest.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away, which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself. When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place. The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish. The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope. They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed. For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A desert wadi roars with water in winter, when no one needs it, and is bone dry in summer, when everyone does. Traders of Tema and Sheba (the raiders who took his oxen came from Sheba, 1:15) leave their route for the stream they remember, and find stones. So are his friends: full when he prospered, dry now.

Jeremiah once said the same thing to God himself: Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail? (Jer 15:18). God is not. Jesus offered a woman at a well water ... welling up to eternal life (John 4:14), a spring that does not dry up in the heat.

Here is the heart of it: you see my calamity and are afraid. If a man like Job can lose everything without deserving it, so can they. Their theology is their shelter, and Job's innocence would blow the roof off, so they need him to be guilty. That is still why people blame the sufferer: it keeps them safe.

In Hebrew see and be afraid sound almost the same. A friend afraid of what your suffering means for him cannot help you with it. The Christian can afford to look, because his safety was never in having deserved his blessings. It is in Christ, and nothing that happens to a brother can take it away.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I said, 'Make me a gift'? Or, 'From your wealth offer a bribe for me'? Or, 'Deliver me from the adversary's hand'? Or, 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job had asked them for no money, no ransom, no rescue: nothing but themselves, which would have cost nothing.

The last word is redeem. Job is not asking the friends to redeem him; he will look much higher (with a different Hebrew word, the kinsman's word), and find it: I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — Teach Me, and I Will Be Silent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teach me, says Job, and I will be silent (vv. 24-27). Look at me: my vindication is at stake (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is willing to be corrected, if anyone will show him where he went wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray. How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove? Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind? You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job is teachable: show me where I went wrong and I will stop talking. It is the prayer of Psalm 139 turned to his friends: see if there be any grievous way in me (Ps 139:24). He does not claim to be sinless. He asks to be shown his fault, not to have it presumed.

Honest words have force. Theirs prove nothing: they correct Job's words as if they were a lecture on doctrine, when they were the cry of a man in despair, wind. Bildad will throw the word back: the words of your mouth are a great wind (8:2). The lesson stands for every counsellor: hear grief as grief before you correct it as theology.

The harshest line in the chapter says that people who can treat a suffering friend as a case to be argued would cast lots over the fatherless. Job had been the man who delivered ... the fatherless who had none to help him (29:12), and he will stake his life on it (31:17, 21). Before the debate is over, Eliphaz will accuse him of exactly this (22:9): the charge that fits the accusers will be laid on the accused.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face. Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake. Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks them to look at him; they have been looking at a theory. To your face is Satan's phrase (1:11): Job will not curse God to his face, and he will not lie to his friends' faces either. My vindication is his standing as an innocent man. That, not his health, is what he fights for from here on.

Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity? The palate that knew the mallow's juice was tasteless (v. 6) can taste the difference between a lie and the truth. Job knows his own heart better than they do. And the reader knows he is right, because God has said so (2:3).

7.title: What Is Man, That You Make So Much of Him?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand?<sup>2</sup>Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages,<sup>3</sup>so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.<sup>4</sup>When I lie down I say, 'When shall I arise?' But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn.<sup>5</sup>My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh.<sup>6</sup>My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope.<sup>7</sup>"Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good.<sup>8</sup>The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone.<sup>9</sup>As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up;<sup>10</sup>he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.<sup>12</sup>Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?<sup>13</sup>When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,'<sup>14</sup>then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions,<sup>15</sup>so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones.<sup>16</sup>I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.<sup>17</sup>What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him,<sup>18</sup>visit him every morning and test him every moment?<sup>19</sup>How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit?<sup>20</sup>If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you?<sup>21</sup>Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be."
7.overview: Job describes human life as hard service, and his own as months of emptiness, sleepless nights and broken skin, his days running out without hope (vv. 1-6). Then he turns to God: remember that my life is a breath (vv. 7-10). He will not restrain his mouth; is he the sea, that God must guard him? (vv. 11-16). What is man, that you make so much of him? Why does God not pardon him before he is gone (vv. 17-21)?
7.theology:
Job's first words to God are complaint, and they are prayer; the friends never pray at all. The Psalm 8 he turns into a groan is fulfilled, Hebrews says, in Jesus, made lower than the angels to taste death for everyone (Heb 2:6-9).

His two cries, hard service and unpardoned sin, are answered together in the gospel (Isa 40:2; John 1:29).
7.examples: Job calls life hard service, a soldier's term of duty, and watches his days run out like thread on a shuttle. Yet his first word to God is Remember, and his last line, you will seek me, carries faith inside the complaint.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Hard Service on Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human life is hard service (vv. 1-2). Job has been given months of emptiness and nights of misery (vv. 3-5), and his days run out without hope (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job describes the life of a sufferer from the inside: the long night, the body, the days that go nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand? Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages, so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hard service is the Hebrew word for a soldier's term of duty. A labourer longs for his pay, a slave in the sun for shade; they at least have something to wait for. Job's shift has no end and no wage, and the illness has gone on for months, not days.

Hold on to that first phrase, hard service, and to the last request of this chapter, why do you not pardon my transgression? (v. 21). Isaiah was sent with a message that answers both at once: cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned (Isa 40:2). It is the gospel in one sentence, spoken to exhausted people. In Christ the service is over and the pardon is given.

verseByVerse.quote: When I lie down I say, 'When shall I arise?' But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn. My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh. My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I lie down I say, When shall I arise? But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn. Anyone who has been ill or grieving knows this night. He goes to bed longing for morning; the hours do not move; he turns over and over until grey light comes. Scripture does not think sleeplessness too small to record.

Then he describes the sores of 2:7 from the inside: crusting, cracking, weeping again, and maggots in the wounds.

The shuttle flies across the loom until the thread runs out. The Hebrew for hope, tiqvah, also means a cord or thread, the word for Rahab's scarlet cord (Josh 2:18). Job's days come to the end of the thread, and of hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — Remember That My Life Is a Breath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job turns to God: remember that my life is a breath (vv. 7-10). He will not restrain his mouth (v. 11). Is he the sea, that God sets a guard over him (v. 12)? Even sleep brings terrors; leave me alone (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is honest with God about his nights, his body and his dread of the grave. That honesty, spoken to God and not merely about him, is itself a kind of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good. The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone. As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up; he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the chapter turns, and so does the book. Remember is spoken to God, Job's first words to him since his troubles began, and from here on he will keep speaking to him. Eliphaz said, I would seek God (5:8). Job does. The friends never once will.

His first prayer is: remember what I am. A breath. The psalmist says God does remember it: He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again (Ps 78:39). Sheol is the grave, the place of the dead. Psalm 103 says the wind passes over us and its place knows it no more (Ps 103:16), and adds the comfort Job cannot yet see: he remembers that we are dust (Ps 103:14).

Job sees no way back from the grave, only a door that closes. Later he will begin to hope past it (14:14; 19:25-27). The Christian stands where Job could not, on the far side of an empty tomb.

God is looking at him, and he will vanish while God looks: while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone. The chapter will close the same way (v. 21): Job cannot stop believing that God's eyes are on him. His fear is only that God will look away too long, or look again too late. James takes up the vanishing and asks, What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes, and draws a different lesson: say If the Lord wills (James 4:14-15). The shortness of life is a reason not to despair of God but to lean on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore: since life is this short, he will not waste it in silence. This is a decision, not an outburst. Better an honest complaint to God than a polite silence that has given up on him.

The ancient world pictured the sea as chaos that God had to hold back. Job feels treated like that: watched, penned in, a danger to creation. When God answers, he will speak of exactly this: who shut in the sea with doors and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther (38:8, 11). God does set bars for the sea, but Job is not the sea; he is a man God is holding.

verseByVerse.quote: When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,' then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions, so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even sleep, when it comes, is not rest. It brings nightmares, and Job lays them at God's door too. He would rather choke than go on in this body.

Set this beside Eliphaz. He too had visions of the night (4:13), and came away from his with a doctrine he was sure of. Job's come to him as terror, and teach him nothing. Neither man's nights are a safe guide to what God is doing. Neither has the last word; God will speak openly, from the storm (38:1).

A breath is hevel, Ecclesiastes' word for everything that vanishes like vapour. Leave me alone is desperate, but he does not want God gone for good, only to stop pressing. Soon he will beg God to come near and answer (13:22; 23:3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is man, that God sets his heart on him and tests him every moment (vv. 17-19)? If Job has sinned, why does God not pardon him before he is gone (vv. 20-21)?
verseByVerse.theology: The answer to this complaint is a Son of Man who was tested for us, and a God who takes iniquity away.

verseByVerse.quote: What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him, visit him every morning and test him every moment? How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here Psalm 8 is turned inside out: what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him? (Ps 8:4). The psalmist marvels that God pays attention to tiny man. Job groans that God will not stop. The same fact is wonder in one mouth and torment in another.

And there is an echo only the reader can hear. Set your heart on him recalls the LORD saying, Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). Job is right that he is tested every moment. He does not know that God's own heart was set on him in delight.

Hebrews takes up Psalm 8 and finds its answer in one man: we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:9). What is man? The Son of Man was tested every moment, on our behalf, and did not fail.
verseByVerse.note: Job asks God to look away from him even for the moment it takes to swallow (v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you? Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if he has sinned, Job asks, how could that harm God, and why aim at him? Your mark is the archer's target of 6:4. Watcher: a keeper, a guard. Job gives God the name and hears it as surveillance.

Two things here are worth holding on to. First, Job does not claim to be sinless. He asks for pardon. His complaint is not that he has never done wrong but that nothing he has done can account for this, and that God, if he is holding something against him, could forgive it.

Second, listen to the last line. You will seek me. Even in his complaint Job assumes that God will come looking for him, and grieves that he will be gone. It is the faith hidden inside the protest: he believes God cares enough to search. He was right. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). And the prayer to take away my iniquity was answered by name on the banks of the Jordan: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29).

8.title: Does God Pervert Justice?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?<sup>3</sup>Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?<sup>4</sup>If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.<sup>5</sup>If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy,<sup>6</sup>if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation.<sup>7</sup>And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great.<sup>8</sup>"For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out.<sup>9</sup>For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow.<sup>10</sup>Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?<sup>11</sup>"Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water?<sup>12</sup>While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant.<sup>13</sup>Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.<sup>14</sup>His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web.<sup>15</sup>He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure.<sup>16</sup>He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden.<sup>17</sup>His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones.<sup>18</sup>If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, 'I have never seen you.'<sup>19</sup>Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring.<sup>20</sup>"Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers.<sup>21</sup>He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting.<sup>22</sup>Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
8.overview: Bildad calls Job's words a great wind and asks whether God perverts justice. Job's children must have sinned; if Job pleads for mercy, God will restore him (vv. 1-7). The fathers teach that the godless wither (vv. 8-19). God will not reject a blameless man; he will fill Job's mouth with laughter (vv. 20-22).
8.theology:
God does not pervert justice, but his justice is not read off each person's circumstances. Bildad's inference that Job's children died for their sins is the kind of speech the LORD rejects at the end. Tradition deserves honour, but it cannot overrule God's word.

Bildad's promises come true for the opposite of his reasons, and in the end the friends need Job's prayers.
8.examples: Bildad's speech is full of ironies he cannot see. He says we know nothing, yet claims to know why ten people died. His promise that Job's latter days will be great comes true almost word for word, and his warning that God will not reject a blameless man turns out to be good news for Job.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad calls Job's words wind and asks whether God perverts justice (vv. 1-3). Job's children were given over to their sin (v. 4); if Job pleads for mercy, God will restore him (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God is just, and Bildad is right to say so. The error is the step he takes next.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?
verseByVerse.commentary: The second friend has none of Eliphaz's courtesy. Job asked them to hear the speech of a despairing man as wind (6:26), a cry and not a doctrine. Bildad turns the word into an insult. He repeats the friends' case, and adds something harder: he brings in the dead, and he brings in the fathers.

verseByVerse.quote: Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer is no, and Bildad is right to insist on it: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen 18:25). A believer in Job's position needs to keep hold of that.

But see what Bildad does with it. God is just; Job is suffering; therefore Job deserves it. The first two are true and the third does not follow, because God's justice is not measured out day by day in each man's circumstances. The whole debate turns on this one verb. Job will answer it later with the same verb turned round: God has put me in the wrong (19:6). Bildad reasons that God cannot pervert justice, so Job must be guilty; Job, that he is not guilty, so God seems to have perverted it. Both men are trapped by the same assumption, that suffering is a verdict. The prologue has already told the reader it is not.

verseByVerse.quote: If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the cruellest sentence yet. The if is a courtesy; Bildad means since. Your children are dead and God is just, so they had it coming: God simply handed them over to the consequences of their own sin.

Say it to a father who rose early after every feast to offer a burnt offering for each of them (1:5), and who has ten graves to visit. Bildad has no evidence at all; his system requires it, so he says it. The narrator never suggests it, and the LORD will name what Bildad has done: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:8). Jesus refused the same reasoning about eighteen people killed when a tower fell: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others ...? No, I tell you (Luke 13:4-5).

If you have been told that someone you loved died because of their sin, or yours, hear the verdict of this book. That was Bildad's speech, and God did not accept it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy, if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation. And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the offer: plead for mercy, be pure and upright, and God will act for you. It sounds like the gospel and is a bargain. Bildad cannot see the irony: upright is the narrator's word for Job in 1:1. By Bildad's own conditions, God should restore Job. He will.

Read the last chapter: And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning (42:12). Bildad's promise comes true in almost the same words, but not because Job confessed the sins Bildad imagined. It comes true after God has declared Bildad wrong and Job right: God kept the promise and threw away the reasoning.

He will rouse himself for you, as though God were asleep toward Job until he repented. Psalm 44 uses Bildad's very verb and turns his theology upside down. It is the prayer of people who have not sinned their way into trouble, who say, All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant (Ps 44:17); and they cry, Rouse yourself! (Ps 44:23). Paul quotes that psalm about Christians and answers it: in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Rom 8:36-37). God never sleeps (Ps 121:4). When the disciples woke Jesus in the storm (Mark 4:38), he had been in the boat with them all along.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ask the fathers, says Bildad (vv. 8-10). All who forget God wither like papyrus without water (vv. 11-13); the godless man's trust is a spider's web (vv. 14-15), and the uprooted plant is forgotten (vv. 16-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Every picture is true of the godless. Every picture is also a portrait of Job, and that is the point of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out. For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow. Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz appealed to his experience and a vision. Bildad appeals to the fathers. We are young and know little, he says, so ask the generations before us. Searched out is Eliphaz's confident word again (5:27).

There is real wisdom in that: ask your father, and he will show you (Deut 32:7). But tradition cannot overrule what God has said. Jesus rebuked men for making void the word of God by your tradition (Mark 7:13). And Bildad says we know nothing, and in the same breath knows exactly why ten young people died. David used the same words in prayer: Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding (1 Chr 29:15). In David's mouth they lead to humble dependence on God. In Bildad's they lead to a lecture.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water? While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant. Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? The papyrus reed of the Nile grows tall and green, but only in the marsh. Take away the water and it withers before it can even be harvested. So, says Bildad, the man who forgets God: flourishing one day, dead the next.

True, and the prophets say it better: the man who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes (Jer 17:8). But the point of Bildad's reed is its sudden withering, and Job has withered suddenly. The hidden sentence is: you must have forgotten God. Job has not. He is the one still speaking to him.

verseByVerse.quote: His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web. He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Hebrew it is a spider's house: built with care, beautiful in the morning light, and useless when you lean on it. Isaiah says of the works of the wicked, their webs will not serve as clothing (Isa 59:6).

Job's house did not stand; it fell on his children (1:19). Bildad could hardly have chosen a sharper picture.

Jesus' story of two houses answers Bildad. One was built on rock, one on sand, and almost the same words are said of the storm that beat on both (Matt 7:25, 27). The difference was not whether the storm came but what stood afterwards. Job's roof fell in; his faith did not. By Jesus' measure, he built on the rock.

verseByVerse.quote: He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden. His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones. If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, 'I have never seen you.' Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring.
verseByVerse.commentary: Bildad's next plant is a creeper spreading green in the sun, its roots wrapped round the stones, looking settled and strong. Pull it up and the garden forgets it was ever there. This is the joy of his way is bitter irony: this is all his flourishing came to. Job said of the dead, nor does his place know him anymore (7:10). Bildad agrees, and adds that the wicked deserve to be forgotten. The Christian holds a better promise than either of them. The one who does the will of God abides forever (1 John 2:17), and God does not forget his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — God Will Not Reject a Blameless Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not reject a blameless man (v. 20); he will fill Job's mouth with laughter and shame those who hate him (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Bildad means it as a warning; it turns out to be a promise.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers. He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting. Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blameless is the very word God used of Job (1:1, 8; 2:3). Bildad means it as a warning: God does not abandon the blameless, so if you have been abandoned, you are not blameless. But his sentence is simply true, and it is the truest thing he says. God will not reject Job, because Job is exactly what Bildad doubts he is.

The laughter is that of the restored, as in the psalm of the returning exiles: Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy (Ps 126:2). It will happen. And the ones clothed with shame at the end will be Job's friends, sent to him with seven bulls and seven rams so that he can pray for them, not to deal with you according to your folly (42:8). God is kinder to Bildad than Bildad was to Job.

9.title: There Is No Arbiter Between Us
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God?<sup>3</sup>If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times.<sup>4</sup>He is wise in heart and mighty in strength— who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded?—<sup>5</sup>he who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger,<sup>6</sup>who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble;<sup>7</sup>who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars;<sup>8</sup>who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea;<sup>9</sup>who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south;<sup>10</sup>who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.<sup>11</sup>Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him.<sup>12</sup>Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, 'What are you doing?'<sup>13</sup>"God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab.<sup>14</sup>How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him?<sup>15</sup>Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser.<sup>16</sup>If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice.<sup>17</sup>For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause;<sup>18</sup>he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness.<sup>19</sup>If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?<sup>20</sup>Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse.<sup>21</sup>I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.<sup>22</sup>It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.'<sup>23</sup>When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent.<sup>24</sup>The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges— if it is not he, who then is it?<sup>25</sup>"My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good.<sup>26</sup>They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey.<sup>27</sup>If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer,'<sup>28</sup>I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent.<sup>29</sup>I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain?<sup>30</sup>If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye,<sup>31</sup>yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.<sup>32</sup>For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together.<sup>33</sup>There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.<sup>34</sup>Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me.<sup>35</sup>Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.
9.overview: Job agrees that no man can be in the right before God, but means that no one could win a case against him. God moves mountains, tramples the sea and made the stars; he passes by unseen (vv. 1-13). Though in the right, Job could only plead for mercy; God multiplies his wounds without cause, and no court can summon him; if it is not he, who then is it? (vv. 14-24). Though he washed with snow, God would plunge him in the pit, for there is no arbiter between us (vv. 25-35).
9.theology:
Job's cry for an arbiter who could lay a hand on God and on man describes the mediator God provided (1 Timothy 2:5). The God who walks on the sea and passes by unseen (vv. 8, 11) later walked on the sea in the flesh, and spoke (Mark 6:48-50).

Job is right that his wounds are without cause, and wrong that God mocks the innocent. No one can wash himself clean, but God washes whiter than snow.
9.examples: Job repeats Eliphaz's hymn to God's power and draws the opposite conclusion. The Rahab he names is a sea monster, not the woman of Jericho. And his bitterest question, if it is not he, who then is it?, is one the reader of the prologue can answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — How Can a Man Be in the Right Before God?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job agrees that no man is in the right before God, for no one could answer him once in a thousand (vv. 1-3). God moves mountains, tramples the sea and made the stars (vv. 4-10); he passes by unseen, and no one can question him (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's hymn to God's power is as true as Eliphaz's. For Job it is not a comfort, because a God this great cannot be taken to court.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God? If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job agrees with the friends' premise. This is the question Eliphaz's night visitor asked (4:17). But Job means something sharper. Be in the right is courtroom language: win your case. How could anyone take God to law and win?

God would ask a thousand questions and a man could not answer one. Job is more right than he knows. When God does speak, he will ask Job question after question (chs 38-41), and Job will say, I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4).

The question is still the one every human being must face. Job sees only a courtroom he cannot win. The gospel announces that the Judge himself has provided the righteousness (Rom 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: He is wise in heart and mighty in strength— who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded?— he who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger, who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble; who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has hardened himself against God and succeeded? Pharaoh tried, and the sea closed over his army (Exod 14:27-28).

Earthquakes, eclipses, stars hidden by storm: Job has watched the world shake, and he knows who shakes it. He does not doubt God's power for a moment, and that is what makes his position so hard: a weak god could be excused, but this one could stop Job's suffering with a word.

verseByVerse.quote: who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea; who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south; who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trampled the waves of the sea: God walks on the sea as a man walks on the ground. Keep that picture; it will come back in a moment. The constellations he names are the ones God will name when he answers: Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion? (38:31). Amos praised the same Maker (Amos 5:8).

The last line is Eliphaz's, almost word for word (5:9). Job and the friends agree about God's greatness; they disagree about what it means for a man in pain. For the friends it proves that everything is in order. For Job it means there is no one above God to appeal to.
verseByVerse.note: The Bear, Orion and the Pleiades are constellations; the identifications are probable, not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him. Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, 'What are you doing?' "God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is at work all around him, and Job cannot see him. He feels the effects and never the presence. Many believers in the dark have said exactly this.

Now put two verses together. God trampled the waves of the sea (v. 8), and he passes by me, and I see him not (v. 11). Mark's account of one night seems to echo both. On the Sea of Galilee, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them (Mark 6:48). They took him for a ghost. But immediately he spoke to them and said, Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid (Mark 6:50). The God who passes by unseen in Job's complaint walked the waves in a body, and was seen, and spoke. Job longed for God to come near in a form he could meet. In Christ he did.

No one can ask God what he is doing; Nebuchadnezzar learned the same: none can stay his hand or say to him, What have you done? (Dan 4:35). This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho but a sea monster, a picture of chaos and every power set against God: was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces? (Isa 51:9). If the monsters of chaos bow to him, what hope has Job of standing up to him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — If It Is a Matter of Justice, Who Can Summon Him?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Though in the right, Job must plead for mercy (vv. 14-16). God multiplies his wounds without cause, and no one can summon him (vv. 17-19). Job is blameless, yet God destroys blameless and wicked alike (vv. 20-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is right about one thing here and wrong about another, and the reader needs to see both.

verseByVerse.quote: How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser. If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An innocent man would normally demand justice. Before God, says Job, even the innocent could only beg for mercy. The one he would have to plead with is the one he feels is prosecuting him.

This is the despair of unanswered prayer: even if God answered, I would not believe he had heard. And yet Job keeps summoning him. He does not stop talking to God because he doubts God listens. That is faith of a kind the friends never show.

verseByVerse.quote: For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause; he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness. If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without cause. Satan had asked, does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9), and God had said, you incited me against him to destroy him without reason (2:3). Job has no idea those words were spoken, yet he says exactly what God said: his wounds really are without cause in him. On that point Job is right and the friends are wrong.

And the tempest that crushes him is, in Hebrew, the same word as the whirlwind out of which the LORD finally answers him (38:1). The storm he complains of is the storm God will speak from.

No court can issue God a summons, and that is Job's dilemma.

From here on, Job's speeches are a lawsuit, in the words of a court: contend, answer, summon, in the right, arbiter. He asks less for his health than for a hearing and a verdict that he is innocent: I have prepared my case (13:18), I would lay my case before him (23:4), and at last, Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me! (31:35). The book's climax is that God does answer, not with a verdict on the charges but with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse. I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.
verseByVerse.commentary: I am blameless: God's own word for him (1:1, 8; 2:3), and Job says it of himself. He is not boasting. He is refusing to confess what is not true, even though a false confession might end the argument. But he is afraid that under God's cross-examination he would be tripped up and made to look guilty. I regard not myself is the exhaustion of a man who no longer cares what happens to him.

verseByVerse.quote: It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.' When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges— if it is not he, who then is it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here Job says too much, and the reader must see it. That the same disasters fall on good and bad alike is true; the Preacher says so (Eccl 9:2). But that God mocks the innocent in their calamity is not true, and God will call such talk words without knowledge (38:2) and ask Job, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8). A sufferer may say this in the dark. He must not build a theology on it.

And look at Job's last question: if it is not he, who then is it? The reader can answer it. It was the accuser (1:12; 2:7), acting under God's permission and within God's limit. Job sees only two possibilities, that God is doing this or no one is. The prologue shows a third that he cannot see. God rules over it all, and God does not mock.

Even his complaint that the earth is given into the hand of the wicked is truer than he knows. In the council God said to Satan, all that he has is in your hand (1:12). John says the same of the world as a whole: the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). But the hand that gave it can take it back, and the same letter says, The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–35 — There Is No Arbiter Between Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His days flee and he cannot feign cheer (vv. 25-29). Though he washed with snow, God would plunge him in the pit (vv. 30-31). God is not a man, and there is no arbiter between them (vv. 32-33). If God took away his rod, Job could speak without fear (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Job describes exactly the one he needs: someone who belongs both to God and to him, and could put a hand on each.

verseByVerse.quote: "My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good. They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey. If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer,' I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A royal runner, a papyrus boat, a diving eagle: speed on land, on water and in the air. His life is rushing past and all of it is bad.

Every sufferer has been told to cheer up. Job has tried to put off my sad face, and the fear comes back, because nothing has changed. Forced cheerfulness is no cure for grief, and the church should never demand it.

verseByVerse.quote: I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain? If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Snow water, the cleanest there is; lye, the strongest soap. Scrub as he may, God would push him back into the filth, and his very clothes would be disgusted to wear him. Whatever he does, Job means, the verdict is fixed.

He has stumbled on a truth bigger than his case. No one can wash himself clean before God. Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me (Jer 2:22). But the same God who says so offers the washing himself: Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isa 1:18). David prayed for it: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Ps 51:7). The snow Job cannot wash with, God washes with.

verseByVerse.quote: For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together. There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the heart of the chapter and one of the great moments of the book. Job's problem is not only that God is strong, but that God is not a man. There is no common ground on which they could meet. He needs an arbiter, a mediator who could lay one hand on God and one on Job, belonging to both, trusted by both. (The Greek Old Testament and a few Hebrew manuscripts read the line as a wish, would that there were an arbiter; either way Job longs for one.)

The word arbiter comes from the verb God uses in Isaiah 1:18. Job thinks a hearing is impossible. God himself proposes one, let us reason together (Isa 1:18), and ends it with snow-white cleansing.

And Job has described, without knowing it, the one God would send. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). God, who is not a man as Job is, became one, so that the hand that holds God's throne could also be laid on us. Job cries that there is no arbiter. Every Christian can answer him by name. And Job will reach higher still: to a witness in heaven (16:19), and to a Redeemer who lives (19:25). And for the sufferer who feels God is too high to hear him, the one between us has felt our pain from the inside, a merciful and faithful high priest, able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:17-18).
verseByVerse.note: The KJV's daysman is an old word for an umpire.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me. Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If only the beating would stop and the terror lift, Job could speak his case calmly. It is dread, not guilt, that silences him.

The gospel does what Job asks. The rod was not simply taken away; it was laid on another: upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace (Isa 53:5). And so the Christian can do what Job could not, and speak to God without dread: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16). Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

10.title: Your Hands Fashioned and Made Me
10.text: <sup>1</sup>"I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.<sup>2</sup>I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.<sup>3</sup>Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?<sup>4</sup>Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees?<sup>5</sup>Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years,<sup>6</sup>that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin,<sup>7</sup>although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?<sup>8</sup>Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether.<sup>9</sup>Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?<sup>10</sup>Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?<sup>11</sup>You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.<sup>12</sup>You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.<sup>13</sup>Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose.<sup>14</sup>If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity.<sup>15</sup>If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction.<sup>16</sup>And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me.<sup>17</sup>You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.<sup>18</sup>"Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me<sup>19</sup>and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.<sup>20</sup>Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer<sup>21</sup>before I go—and I shall not return— to the land of darkness and deep shadow,<sup>22</sup>the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness."
10.overview: Job speaks to God in the bitterness of his soul: do not condemn me; tell me why you contend with me. Why search out his sin, when God knows he is not guilty (vv. 1-7)? God's hands made him like clay, knit him with bones and sinews, and granted him life and steadfast love; yet God hunts him like a lion (vv. 8-17). Why did God bring him out of the womb? Let God leave him alone a little before he goes to the land of deep shadow (vv. 18-22).
10.theology:
Job never learns the reason for his suffering, and the book shows it is possible to rest in God without it. God does not despise the work of his hands; he completes it. The care Job feels as scrutiny is the care that has preserved his spirit (v. 12).

Job's own words point beyond the grave: the God who knit him in the womb will knit the dead together again, and the land of deep darkness has seen a great light (Matt 4:16).
10.examples: Job's picture of the womb (milk, cheese, skin, flesh, bones and sinews) uses the same materials Ezekiel sees gathered again in the valley of dry bones. Even his bitterest line, about a purpose hidden in God's heart, turns out to be true in a way he could not guess.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Let Me Know Why You Contend Against Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks God not to condemn him but to tell him why (vv. 1-2). Why would God despise his own work, or search out a sin he knows is not there (vv. 3-7)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks God for the charge against him, and he is right that God knows he is not guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job goes on straight from chapter 9, still speaking to God. He asks God not to condemn him, and to tell him the charge. He will ask for it again at the end: Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary! (31:35).

Here is something that matters for anyone who suffers. Job never gets his answer: not here, not from the whirlwind, not in the happy ending. He is never told about the council in heaven. He has to come to rest in God himself without ever learning why. Many believers in deep suffering live and die in the same place, and the book shows that it is possible to be at peace there.

verseByVerse.quote: Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A craftsman does not smash his own best work, so why would God? Job is appealing to God's own character, and he is right to. The psalmist prays in the same way: Do not forsake the work of your hands (Ps 138:8). Isaiah says, we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand (Isa 64:8).

And the New Testament gives the answer Job reaches for: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:6). God does not despise the work of his hands. He finishes it.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees? Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years, that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin, although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A human investigator has limited sight and time, so he presses a suspect hard. But God does not see as man sees (1 Sam 16:7), and he has all eternity. Why, then, interrogate Job?

Although you know that I am not guilty. It is exactly true; God said it himself, twice (1:8; 2:3). Job's mistake is only in thinking that God's hand on him means God doubts him.

None to deliver out of your hand is from the song of Moses: I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand (Deut 32:39). Eliphaz quoted the first half (5:18); Job quotes the second. The hand that holds him is the only hand that could heal him, and Job knows it. He has nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Your Hands Fashioned and Made Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's hands made Job and granted him life and steadfast love (vv. 8-12), yet hid a purpose in his heart (v. 13). Guilty or innocent, Job cannot lift his head; God hunts him like a lion (vv. 14-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Job remembers God's tenderness and cannot square it with his suffering. The chapter's answer is in his own words: the care that preserved his spirit has not stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether. Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?
verseByVerse.commentary: Job remembers where he came from. God formed man of dust from the ground (Gen 2:7), and said that to dust he would return (Gen 3:19). Job asks whether, after taking such care to make him, God will simply grind him back into dust. It is a plea from the potter's own workmanship.

verseByVerse.quote: Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the ancient world's picture of a child forming in the womb: something liquid set into shape, like milk thickening into cheese, then clothed in skin and flesh, then bound together with bone and sinew. The psalmist sings the same wonder: you knitted me together in my mother's womb (Ps 139:13). Job knows he is not an accident. God made him, carefully, from the inside.

And there is a hope hidden in that list which Job cannot yet see. Ezekiel, looking at a valley of dry bones, heard God promise, I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live (Ezek 37:6). The same materials are gathered again: the God who knit Job together in the womb can knit him together again from the grave.

You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit. This, in the middle of his complaint, is the loveliest line in the chapter. Steadfast love is chesed, God's covenant loyalty. And your care comes from the same Hebrew root as the complaint of 7:18, that God would visit him every morning and test him. The visiting that Job felt as surveillance is, in his own better words, the care that has kept his spirit alive. He has the answer in his mouth and cannot yet see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose. If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity. If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job suspects that God's kindness was a trap: that all along, behind the care, God was planning this. And he is half right. God did have a purpose hidden from him, settled in heaven before a single blow fell. But the purpose was not malice. It began with God saying, Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). What God hid in his heart was delight in Job, and a purpose to show the world a man who would trust him for no reason. For those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28). A believer may be sure of that hidden purpose even when, like Job, he never sees it.

Job feels trapped either way: guilty, and he is lost; innocent, and he still cannot lift up my head. But Scripture has a name for God that answers this line: you, O LORD, are ... the lifter of my head (Ps 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me. You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he tried to stand, God would stalk him like a lion. The witnesses are his wasted body (16:8): everyone who sees his sores assumes his guilt. Job describes God as hunter, prosecutor and general at once. It is how things look from the ash heap, not how they are.

Eliphaz praised God who does marvelous things without number (5:9). Now the wonders seem turned on Job. The same power that fills the psalms with praise feels, from inside the pain, like an ambush. It is the same God and the same power; what Job cannot yet see is its direction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why was he born (vv. 18-19)? Let God leave him alone a little before he goes to the land of darkness and deep shadow (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's land of deep shadow is not the last word about death.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.
verseByVerse.commentary: He returns to the wish of chapter 3, but with a difference that matters. In chapter 3 he cursed his day and asked the dark to swallow it. Now he says you: why did you bring me out? The question is the same; it has become a prayer. That is movement. Job is still in the dark, but he is now talking to God in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer before I go—and I shall not return— to the land of darkness and deep shadow, the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not my days few? He asks only for a little cheer, the word of 9:27, the brighter face he could not put on, a short breathing space before he dies. Then he describes the grave: darkness piled on darkness, without any order, where even the light is dark. It is creation undone, the world before God said Let there be light, the dark Job wished on his birthday (3:4-5).

But hear what the prophets say about that land. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone (Isa 9:2). Isaiah's deep darkness is Job's deep shadow, the same Hebrew word, tsalmaveth. And Matthew says the light dawned when Jesus began to preach in Galilee: for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned (Matt 4:16). The land Job dreads has been visited. Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10).

11.title: Less Than Your Guilt Deserves
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right?<sup>3</sup>Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?<sup>4</sup>For you say, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.'<sup>5</sup>But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you,<sup>6</sup>and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding. Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves.<sup>7</sup>"Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?<sup>8</sup>It is higher than heaven —what can you do?
