Deeper than Sheol—what can you know?<sup>9</sup>Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.<sup>10</sup>If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back?<sup>11</sup>For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it?<sup>12</sup>But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man!<sup>13</sup>"If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him.<sup>14</sup>If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents.<sup>15</sup>Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.<sup>16</sup>You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away.<sup>17</sup>And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning.<sup>18</sup>And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security.<sup>19</sup>You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor.<sup>20</sup>But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last."
11.overview: Zophar will not let Job's many words go unanswered. Job claims to be clean; if only God would speak, Job would learn that God exacts of him less than his guilt deserves (vv. 1-6). The deep things of God are beyond finding out, and a stupid man will understand when a wild donkey is born a man (vv. 7-12). If Job will pray and put away iniquity, his darkness will be like the morning; but the hope of the wicked is to breathe their last (vv. 13-20).
11.theology:
That God punishes us less than our sins deserve is a truth for confession, not a verdict to pass on a sufferer. God had said Job suffered without reason, and in the end he judged Zophar's speech.

God's depth and height are beyond finding out (vv. 7-9). Zophar uses them to silence Job; Paul uses the same four dimensions for the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.
11.examples: Zophar mocks Job's claim to be clean in God's eyes, which is what God himself said of him. He wishes God would speak, and God will, against Zophar. And he turns Job's own picture of the wild donkey into an insult.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — God Exacts of You Less Than Your Guilt Deserves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar will not let Job's words go unanswered (vv. 1-3). If only God would speak, Job would learn that he is getting less than his guilt deserves (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The third friend goes further than the other two: Job, he says, is getting off lightly.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right? Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third friend is the bluntest. Eliphaz appealed to a vision and Bildad to the fathers; Zophar appeals to nothing but his own certainty. What he adds to the friends' case is harsher: Job deserves worse than he is getting.

He hears Job's speeches as babble, and his questions to God as mockery. That is how lament often sounds to people who have not suffered: too long, too loud, irreverent. But the man who has lost ten children has not said too much. He has said what he feels, to God, and God will take his words more seriously than Zophar does.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Zophar summarises Job, and not fairly. Job never claimed his doctrine was pure; he has been pleading with God, not lecturing on theology. He claimed to be innocent of anything that could explain this (9:21; 10:7). And here is the irony again: clean in God's eyes is exactly what God said of him, a blameless and upright man (1:8). Zophar mocks as arrogance the verdict heaven has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you, and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding. Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar wishes God would speak, sure that God would take his side. His wish will be granted: the LORD will speak (38:1), and when he has finished speaking to Job, he will turn to the friends and say, you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7).

This is Zophar's hardest line: you have earned more. It is true of every sinner before God. Ezra confessed, you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved (Ezra 9:13), and the psalmist, He does not deal with us according to our sins (Ps 103:10). A believer may say that about himself on his knees, and should, knowing that what his sins deserved was laid on Christ. No one may say it about another person in pain. Zophar has taken a truth for confession and made it a weapon.

The secrets of wisdom Zophar wished God would tell were told in the end, and they were not what he expected. We impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory (1 Cor 2:7), and Paul's secret wisdom is Christ crucified, the innocent one who suffered for the guilty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Can You Find Out the Deep Things of God?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's depths are beyond finding out (vv. 7-9). Who can stop him when he summons the court (vv. 10-11)? A stupid man will understand when a wild donkey is born a man (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: These are true words about God's greatness, used to shut a sufferer's mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than heaven —what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can you find out the deep things of God? Up to the sky, down to the grave, out to the ends of the earth and across the sea: God's wisdom fills every direction, and no man can measure it. This is true, and Zophar means it as a gag: you cannot understand God, so stop arguing with him. He does not notice that it applies to him too. If God's ways cannot be found out, Zophar cannot find out why Job is suffering.

Paul uses the same four dimensions, and uses them the other way. He prays that Christians may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Eph 3:18-19). God's depth is not a wall to keep sufferers quiet. It is the size of the love that holds them.

verseByVerse.quote: If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back? For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it? But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back? Job said these very things: he passes by me and who can turn him back? (9:11-12). Zophar hands Job's words back to him: if Job admits God can do as he pleases, let him accept the verdict.

God does see what men hide, and the one thing he has seen in Job is integrity (2:3).

The wild donkey born a man is a proverb for the impossible. Job had compared his cry to a wild donkey's bray (6:5); Zophar throws the image back as an insult. When God speaks, he will talk about the wild donkey too, with pleasure, as a creature he set free (39:5). God is gentler with donkeys than Zophar is with his friend.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — If You Prepare Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Job will pray and put away iniquity, his darkness will be like the morning (vv. 13-17); he will have hope and rest (vv. 18-19). But the wicked hope only to die (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar's promises will largely come true, though not on his terms.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him. If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents. Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hands stretched out toward God is the posture of prayer. Zophar's advice is good for anyone who has sinned: set your heart right, pray, put away what is wrong, and find the God who promised to forgive (Ps 32:5). But it assumes the thing in question. Job's hands are not full of iniquity (9:30).

Without blemish uses the word for the defect that barred an animal from sacrifice. Job will look God in the face again, but not because he confessed Zophar's list.

verseByVerse.quote: You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away. And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning. And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security. You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The misery will be like a flash flood that roared through the wadi and is gone. Zophar reverses Job's own words. Job described the grave as the place where light is as thick darkness (10:22). Zophar says that if he repents, his darkness will be like the morning. For those who belong to God it is even truer than he knew: night will be no more ... for the Lord God will be their light (Rev 22:5).

Zophar promises hope, which Job said his days had run out of (7:6), and rest, which he could not find (3:26). As for many will court your favor, read the last chapter. The first to come asking for Job's favour will be Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, with seven bulls and seven rams, needing his prayers (42:8-9).

None will make you afraid is the covenant blessing of Leviticus (Lev 26:6). Eliphaz reached for Deuteronomy's curses to describe the wicked (5:14); Zophar reaches for Leviticus' blessings to describe the repentant. Both treat Job's life as a ledger read off his circumstances. The blessings are real, and Micah sees them at last for all God's people, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid (Mic 4:4). But they are gifts of grace, not a receipt for a confession.

verseByVerse.quote: But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sting is in the tail: the wicked have only one hope left, to die. Job had said, Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me (6:8-9). Zophar has taken a sufferer's cry of despair and entered it as evidence against him.

That is a warning to every comforter. The things a person says in the worst hour are not a confession to be used against him. They are a cry to be answered. God answered Job's, and he answers ours in Christ, who by his death came to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:15).

12.title: With God Are Wisdom and Might
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you.<sup>3</sup>But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?<sup>4</sup>I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock.<sup>5</sup>In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip.<sup>6</sup>The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand.<sup>7</sup>"But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you;<sup>8</sup>or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you.<sup>9</sup>Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?<sup>10</sup>In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind.<sup>11</sup>Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food?<sup>12</sup>Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.<sup>13</sup>"With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding.<sup>14</sup>If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open.<sup>15</sup>If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land.<sup>16</sup>With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his.<sup>17</sup>He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools.<sup>18</sup>He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips.<sup>19</sup>He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty.<sup>20</sup>He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders.<sup>21</sup>He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.<sup>22</sup>He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light.<sup>23</sup>He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away.<sup>24</sup>He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste.<sup>25</sup>They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.
12.overview: Job answers with sarcasm: wisdom will die with the friends, but he knows all they know. He, a blameless man, is a laughingstock, while robbers are at peace (vv. 1-6). Every creature knows that the hand of the LORD has done this; in his hand is every life and breath (vv. 7-12). With God are wisdom and might, and he humbles the great (vv. 13-25).
12.theology:
Wisdom and might belong to God, not to the aged or the learned (v. 13), and he overturns every human wisdom that thinks it has him measured (1 Cor 1:19-20). Job's one use of the covenant name in the debate is to confess that the hand of the LORD has done this (v. 9).

Because God brings deep darkness to light (v. 22), no one should pronounce judgment on another's heart before the time.
12.examples: Job meets the friends with sarcasm, wisdom will die with you, and with a sharp observation: the comfortable always despise the man who slips. Elihu will later borrow a line of this speech almost word for word, and a psalmist joins two of its lines into one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wisdom Will Die with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job answers the friends' wisdom with sarcasm (vv. 1-3). He, a blameless man, is a laughingstock, while robbers live at peace (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's first answer to the friends' wisdom is to notice what it has made of him: a joke.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you. But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three speeches from three friends, Job answers with sarcasm, and then plainly: who does not know such things? The friends have been telling Job what he taught others for years (4:3-4). Their theology is not wrong because it is new. It is wrong because it is being used on the wrong man.

This speech closes the first round of the debate, and it is Job's longest yet, running to the end of chapter 14. Here he takes the friends' own subject, God's wisdom and power, and shows that it cuts against them.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock. In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip. The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who prayed and was answered, whom God himself called blameless (1:1), is now a joke to the men who came to comfort him.

Job observes sharply that contempt is always waiting for the man who stumbles. The psalmist knew it: Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease (Ps 123:4). The friends are at ease, their homes standing and their children alive. It is easy, from there, to explain why someone else's fell.

And look at the facts, says Job: plenty of wicked men are doing very well, their god their own strength, as the prophet said of Babylon, whose own might is their god (Hab 1:11). Asaph nearly lost his faith over the same sight: I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked (Ps 73:3). If suffering proves guilt, prosperity should prove innocence, and it plainly does not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every creature knows that the hand of the LORD has done this (vv. 7-9); every life is in his hand (v. 10). The ear tests words; wisdom is said to be with the aged (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The beasts know what the friends have missed: every life is in God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you; or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you. Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends claim wisdom, but every animal in the field knows as much. Creation itself testifies that everything that happens comes from God's hand. That is not a secret the friends discovered.

And mark the name. The LORD, God's covenant name, appears nowhere else in the debate from chapter 3 to chapter 37 (a few Hebrew manuscripts read God even here). Here, once, his deepest conviction breaks through in the name God gave his people, in the very words of Isaiah: that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it (Isa 41:20). His suffering came through the LORD's hand. That is his agony, and it is also the ground under his feet.

Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God gives to all mankind life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). Every breath Job draws on the ash heap is given by the God he argues with.
verseByVerse.note: “The bushes of the earth” may be rendered “speak to the earth” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food? Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food? Job said something like it before (6:30). The ear can tell good words from bad, as the tongue can tell good food from spoiled. Test what you are being told. Elihu will later quote this line almost word for word (34:3).

Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days. Taken alone it sounds like a proverb Job agrees with. But the next line answers it: With God are wisdom and might (v. 13). Job is probably repeating the grey-haired friends' confidence in their years, to set it beside the real source. Elihu, the youngest man present, will say it outright: It is not the old who are wise (32:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — With God Are Wisdom and Might
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With God are wisdom and might, and what he tears down no one rebuilds (vv. 13-16). He strips the great and raises and destroys nations (vv. 17-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's God overturns the wise and the powerful, and that includes any theology, the friends' among them, that thinks it has him measured.

verseByVerse.quote: "With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding. If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open. If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land. With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Job's thesis: wisdom is not with the old men but with God, and the rest of the chapter is a hymn to prove it.

If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open. No one reverses God. Isaiah uses these words of a steward given the key of David's house (Isa 22:22), and Jesus takes them as his own title: the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Rev 3:7). The one who holds the keys that no one can overrule is Christ, and for his people he holds them open.

Drought and flood are both his. Even deception is not outside his rule: the deceived and the deceiver are his. The reader thinks of the accuser in the council, whom Revelation calls the deceiver of the whole world (Rev 12:9). He too is on God's leash, going only as far as he is let.

verseByVerse.quote: He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools. He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips. He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty. He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders. He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job pictures a procession of the great, marched off in shame: counselors and judges made fools, kings stripped like captives, priests led away, elders who lose their judgment. It happened whenever empires fell.

The point is aimed at the friends: if they think wisdom guarantees their standing, God strips the wise. Paul says the same of every clever system that sets itself up against God: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? ... Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? (1 Cor 1:20). And the psalmist took two of Job's lines and joined them: he pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes (Ps 107:40; cf. vv. 21, 24).

The picture of the great led away stripped, in shame, is the picture Paul uses for the cross. There the rulers of this age did their worst, and none of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). And there God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15). The procession Job describes has a victor at its head, and it is Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light. He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away. He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste. They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deep darkness Job called down on his birthday (3:5) is the very thing God drags into the daylight. It is a warning to the friends and a promise to Job. Paul turns it on everyone who judges another's heart too soon: do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness (1 Cor 4:5). The friends have done exactly that. God will bring to light what was hidden, and what comes to light will be Job's innocence.

Whole nations rise and fall at his word, and their leaders grope in the dark like drunkards, the curse of Deuteronomy that Eliphaz used against Job (5:14). Job's reply is that it falls on kings and nations and wise men too, and no one can read a man's guilt from it. God rules the whole world, and that is exactly why no one can track his ways by counting who is suffering.

13.title: Though He Slay Me
13.text: <sup>1</sup>"Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it.<sup>2</sup>What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you.<sup>3</sup>But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.<sup>4</sup>As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all.<sup>5</sup>Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom!<sup>6</sup>Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips.<sup>7</sup>Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him?<sup>8</sup>Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?<sup>9</sup>Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man?<sup>10</sup>He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality.<sup>11</sup>Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you?<sup>12</sup>Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.<sup>13</sup>"Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may.<sup>14</sup>Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?<sup>15</sup>Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.<sup>16</sup>This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.<sup>17</sup>Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears.<sup>18</sup>Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right.<sup>19</sup>Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.<sup>20</sup>Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face:<sup>21</sup>withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me.<sup>22</sup>Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.<sup>23</sup>How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin.<sup>24</sup>Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?<sup>25</sup>Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff?<sup>26</sup>For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.<sup>27</sup>You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet.<sup>28</sup>Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
13.overview: Job knows all the friends know; he wants to argue his case with God. They whitewash with lies and are worthless physicians; will they speak falsely for God? God will rebuke them (vv. 1-12). Let them be silent while he speaks, whatever comes: though he slay me, I will hope in him; he has prepared his case (vv. 13-19). He asks God to lift his hand and speak, to show him his sin, and to say why he hides his face and counts Job an enemy (vv. 20-28).
13.theology:
God does not need lies told in his defence, and Job's warning that God will rebuke the friends for them is fulfilled at the end (42:7). Job will go to God even at the cost of his life (v. 15), and Paul borrows his words when facing death.

Job's challenge, who will contend with me?, becomes the Servant's and then the Christian's (Rom 8:33-34). The record written against us has been nailed to the cross.
13.examples: Job's pictures of his friends are vivid: plasterers smearing whitewash over cracks, and doctors who leave a sick man worse. His question Will you speak falsely for God? sums up the book's judgment on them. And when he turns to God, his deepest pain is the one the psalms know best: the hidden face.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job would argue his case with God himself (vv. 1-3). The friends whitewash with lies (vv. 4-6). Will they speak falsely for God? He will rebuke them, and their maxims are ashes (vv. 7-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job tells the friends they are lying on God's behalf, and that God will hold them to account for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it. What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you. But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Job knows their theology well, and he is done arguing with them; he wants to argue with God. Argue my case comes from the same Hebrew root as the arbiter of 9:33 and God's own let us reason together (Isa 1:18). Job wants a hearing in the highest court; the friends want to settle his case without one.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all. Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job uses two pictures. The first is plasterers who smear whitewash over a crumbling wall to hide the cracks; Ezekiel used it for false prophets who cried Peace, when there is no peace, and covered a bad wall with whitewash (Ezek 13:10). The second is doctors who came to a sick man and have made him worse.

There is a Physician who does not fail. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick (Mark 2:17). He does not whitewash; he heals.

Proverbs agrees: even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise (Prov 17:28). The friends were wisest in the seven days when they said nothing (2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips. Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him? Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?
verseByVerse.commentary: To defend God, they have to invent guilt in Job. They tell lies on his behalf, pleading his case as if he needed a lawyer. Every attempt to protect God's reputation by bending the truth about a sufferer is this sin. A pastor who says "this must be for something you did" without knowing it, to keep his theology tidy, is speaking falsely for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man? He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality. Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you? Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Job warns them: God searches hearts, and he will not be flattered. You think he is on your side because you are taking his side? He will rebuke you for it. That is exactly what happens. When God has finished speaking to Job, he turns to Eliphaz: My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). Job knew God better than they did. He knew God would not thank anyone for lying in his defence.

Job sits in the ashes, and their sayings are ash too: dry, weightless, blown away; their defences are clay walls that crumble at a touch.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let them be silent while he speaks, whatever comes (vv. 13-14). Though God slay him, he will argue his ways, and he has prepared his case (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Job will go to God though it kills him, sure that the godless could not come before him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may. Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?
verseByVerse.commentary: To put my life in my hand is to risk everything, as Jephthah said going out to battle (Judg 12:3). Bringing his case before God may cost Job his life, and he will do it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are some of the best-loved words in the book, and the Hebrew has a well-known difficulty. The written consonants read "not"; the scribes noted in the margin that it was to be read "in him", two words that sound the same in Hebrew. The ESV's text and the KJV's familiar yet will I trust in him follow the margin. Read the other way (the ESV's note), it says: he will kill me; I have no hope; but I will still argue my ways to his face.

Either way, the second half stands. Job will go to God. Even if it kills him, he will not turn from God to anyone else. That is the answer to Satan's question at its sharpest: a man with nothing left to gain from God, not even his life, who still insists on God. On the ESV's reading it is more than that: it is hope that looks through death to God himself.

The Christian says it with more light. Jesus, dying, said Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46). The Father did let him die, and he hoped in him, and was raised. Because of that, a believer can say Job's words on his own deathbed and mean them fully.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative: “Behold, he will slay me; I have no hope.”

verseByVerse.quote: This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A godless man would never dare to come before God to have his case heard. That Job wants nothing more is itself the sign that he is not godless. His salvation here means his rescue, his vindication.

Paul, writing from prison, not knowing whether he would be executed, borrows its words as the Greek Old Testament gives them: this will turn out for my deliverance, and goes on to Job's hope in the face of death, that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death (Phil 1:19-20). The apostle read himself into Job's place: a righteous man in chains, sure that God would vindicate him, whether he lived or died.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears. Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right. Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has his case ready and is sure of the verdict. It is a bold claim, and Job will learn that being right about his innocence is not the same as being right about God (40:8). But he is not wrong that no charge will stand.

Listen to how these words sound again in Isaiah, on the lips of the Servant of the LORD, beaten and spat upon: He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? ... Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up (Isa 50:8-9). It is the same challenge, with the same moth-eaten garment that ends this chapter (v. 28). And Paul takes the Servant's words and hands them to every Christian: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died (Rom 8:33-34). Job's lonely defiance became the Servant's confidence, and the Servant's confidence became ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Why Do You Hide Your Face?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks God to lift his hand and speak (vv. 20-22), to show him his sin, and to say why he hides his face (vv. 23-24). God pursues a driven leaf and writes bitter things against him (vv. 25-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks to see the charge sheet. The Christian knows where the record against him went.

verseByVerse.quote: Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me. Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Job speaks to God, with the same two requests as at 9:34: take your hand off me, and do not overwhelm me with terror. Then they can talk.

God will take the first option. When he speaks from the whirlwind he says, I will question you, and you make it known to me (38:3). And Job will find that he has nothing to answer. The hearing he longs for will not go the way he imagines; it will be better.

verseByVerse.quote: How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin. Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin. Job asks to be shown the list: if he has sinned, let God name it. It is the prayer of an honest man, and every believer can pray it: Search me, O God, and know my heart (Ps 139:23). Job is not hiding from any sin he might have. He cannot find one that explains this.

Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy? The hidden face is the deepest pain in the psalms: How long will you hide your face from me? (Ps 13:1). And there is a play on words here that a Hebrew reader would hear. Enemy is oyev; Job's name is Iyyov. Why do you treat Job as if he were your enemy?

The gospel turns the question round. God did count us as enemies, and we were: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom 5:10). Job was not God's enemy, and felt treated as one; Christ was not God's enemy, and was treated as one, so that God's real enemies could be made his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff? For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff? Job feels like a dead leaf in the wind, a bit of chaff. Why would the Almighty chase something so small? The picture comes from the covenant curses: the sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight (Lev 26:36). Again Job feels treated as one of the cursed.

God seems to be writing up a charge sheet and adding to it the sins of Job's youth. Job does not deny them; he asks why sins long past should be brought up now. David prayed, Remember not the sins of my youth (Ps 25:7).

There was a written record against us, and it was real. Paul tells us what God did with it: canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross (Col 2:14). The bitter things written against the believer are not being added to. They have been nailed up and cancelled.

verseByVerse.quote: You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet. Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prisoner in the stocks, every step watched, a line drawn round his feet: that is how his illness feels. Paul and Silas once sat with their feet in the stocks in a Philippian jail, and at midnight they were praying and singing hymns to God (Acts 16:24-25). The stocks do not have the last word over God's people.

Job ends rotting like old wood, full of holes like a moth-eaten coat, which leads into chapter 14. It is the image the Servant uses, not of himself, but of his accusers: the moth will eat them up (Isa 50:9).

14.title: If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
14.text: <sup>1</sup>"Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble.<sup>2</sup>He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.<sup>3</sup>And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you?<sup>4</sup>Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one.<sup>5</sup>Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass,<sup>6</sup>look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.<sup>7</sup>"For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease.<sup>8</sup>Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil,<sup>9</sup>yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.<sup>10</sup>But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?<sup>11</sup>As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up,<sup>12</sup>so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.<sup>13</sup>Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!<sup>14</sup>If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.<sup>15</sup>You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands.<sup>16</sup>For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin;<sup>17</sup>my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.<sup>18</sup>"But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place;<sup>19</sup>the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.<sup>20</sup>You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away.<sup>21</sup>His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not.<sup>22</sup>He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
14.overview: Man born of woman is few of days and full of trouble; no one can bring a clean thing out of an unclean; let God look away and give him rest (vv. 1-6). There is hope for a tree, which sprouts again from its stump; but a man dies and does not rise till the heavens are no more (vv. 7-12). Job dares to hope that God would hide him in Sheol, then call him and cover his sin (vv. 13-17). But as water wears stone, God destroys the hope of man (vv. 18-22).
14.theology:
No one born of woman is clean (v. 4), except the one born of woman who was holy. The first flash of resurrection hope in the book (vv. 13-17) is answered in Christ, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, whose voice all in the tombs will hear.

Job hopes to have his sin covered (v. 17), and that is exactly what God does with sin.
14.examples: Job's images stay with the reader: a flower wilting by evening, a stump sprouting at the scent of water, a lake drained in summer, a sentry waiting for his relief. Even his word for never, till the heavens are no more, turns out to have a date.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Few of Days and Full of Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Man is few of days and full of trouble (vv. 1-2). Why bring him into judgment, when no one is clean (vv. 3-4)? His days are numbered; let God give him rest (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job speaks for every human being: short-lived, troubled and unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble. He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job widens his view to every human being. Born of a woman means weak and mortal, and few of days means life is short; full of trouble picks up the last word of chapter 3 (3:26). A flower wilts by evening; a shadow slides across the ground and is gone.

Isaiah heard the same and added what Job could not yet say: The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8), and Peter tells the church that this word is the gospel (1 Pet 1:25). And there is a greater answer in the first phrase. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman (Gal 4:4). The Son of God took on the short, troubled life that Job describes, so that those born of women could be born of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you? Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why would the Almighty fix his eyes on something as brief as a man and haul him into court? It is the complaint of 7:17-19 again: God's attention feels like prosecution.

Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one. Job knows that no one born of a woman is pure. Sin runs in the stock. David said it of himself: in sin did my mother conceive me (Ps 51:5). Job is not claiming to be sinless; he is saying that if God demands perfect cleanness, no human being could ever pass.

And yet once, one clean thing did come out of the unclean. The angel said to Mary, the child to be born will be called holy — the Son of God (Luke 1:35). Job's there is not one was true of every child ever born until that one, the only man who could stand God's scrutiny, and he stood it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass, look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.
verseByVerse.commentary: God has fixed the length of every life. Job does not dispute it; the psalmist rejoiced in it: My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15). His only plea is that, since his days are counted and few, he may have them in peace, with what a hired labourer gets at the end of his shift: a little rest before the day is over (7:1-2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — There Is Hope for a Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A felled tree sprouts again at the scent of water (vv. 7-9). But a man dies and does not rise till the heavens are no more (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job sees more hope for a stump than for a man. God's answer is a risen Messiah, and a day when the heavens will pass away and the sleepers wake.

verseByVerse.quote: "For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease. Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil, yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who has seen green shoots come up from a stump after rain knows the picture. Hope is the word Job said his life had run out of (7:6); a tree has it, but has a man?

Many Christians have set Isaiah's stump beside it: he foresaw the royal line of David cut down to a stump, and promised, There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isa 11:1). That is a promise about a royal house, not about one man's grave. But the Messiah who came from that stump was himself cut down, and came up again from the grave, and his rising answers Job's question about a man. There is hope for a tree; there is more for a man in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he? As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up, so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man is not like the tree. He breathes his last, and where is he? He is like a lake drained in the summer heat.

But look at the phrase he uses: till the heavens are no more. Job means "never". Scripture takes him at his word and gives it a date. The heavens will pass away with a roar (2 Pet 3:10); John saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away (Rev 21:1). There will be a day when the heavens are no more, and on that day the sleepers wake. Jesus called death sleep in the same way, and meant it hopefully: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him (John 11:11).

Does this teach that the dead sleep without awareness until the resurrection? Job speaks of what is seen at the grave: the body lies down and does not rise in this world. The New Testament adds what Job could not yet see clearly: the believer who dies is away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8), with Christ at once (Luke 23:43; Phil 1:23). “Sleep” describes the body; the person is awake with God, waiting for the body’s rising.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job longs for God to hide him in Sheol until his wrath is past and then remember him (vv. 13-14). God would call, long for his handiwork, and cover his sin (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first flash of resurrection hope in the book, and Jesus will make it certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the hope breaks through. Job imagines the grave not as the end but as a hiding place, where God keeps him safe until the storm of wrath has passed, and then sets a day to come and get him. Remember me. Isaiah uses the same picture for God's people: hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by (Isa 26:20).

The Christian knows where that hiding place is: your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:3). And he knows the answer to remember me. A dying thief on a cross said it, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:42), and was told, today you will be with me in paradise.

verseByVerse.quote: If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the great question, asked honestly. It is not a statement of doctrine; it is a man daring to hope. My service is the soldier's hard service of 7:1. There it was hopeless drudgery; here it is a sentry waiting for his relief (the ESV's note), the change of guard. Job imagines the grave as a long watch, waiting to be relieved.

The New Testament answers his question with a person. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20). And Paul describes that relief: we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (1 Cor 15:51-52). The relief Job waited for is coming, and it will come with a trumpet.
verseByVerse.note: “Renewal” may be rendered “relief” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands. For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin; my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the tenderest line Job has spoken. God would call to him out of the grave, and he would answer. And God would long for him, as a craftsman misses the work he made (10:3, 8). Job imagines God missing him, and Jesus said the call would come: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28-29).

God would still number my steps, but as a father watches a child walk, not as a guard watches a prisoner. His sins would be sealed up in a bag, like a legal document tied, sealed and put away, never to be opened again.

And cover over is the verb of 13:4, where Job said the friends whitewash with lies. The friends plaster lies over the truth about Job; Job hopes that God will cover his sin so it is seen no more. That is the gospel's own hope: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered (Ps 32:1). You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (Mic 7:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Destroy the Hope of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As water wears away stone, God destroys man's hope (vv. 18-19); he goes away and never knows what becomes of his sons (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The hope flickers and goes out again, but it will come back stronger.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place; the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the light goes out again. Even mountains crumble; running water grinds stone smooth and carries the soil away. Hope is worn down the same way, slowly and completely.

This is how faith often moves in real suffering. A flash of hope comes, like verses 13-17, and then the old grief rolls back in. The believer should not despise the flash because it did not last. Job's hope will come back, steadier, five chapters on: I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25).

verseByVerse.quote: You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away. His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not. He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death changes a man's face and sends him out of the world. Whatever becomes of his children, honour or disgrace, he will never know; the dead know nothing, as the Preacher says, meaning they have no more share in what is done under the sun (Eccl 9:5-6). Read these lines as the words of a man whose sons are all dead. He would give anything to know anything about them.

The speech ends in pain: the dead feel only their own body, mourn only for themselves. It is the bleakest ending yet. But the reader has already heard, in the middle of the chapter, a man imagining God calling him out of the grave. That call was not imagination. Jesus said, I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), and the voice that will call is his.

15.title: Have You Listened in the Council of God?
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind?<sup>3</sup>Should he argue in unprofitable talk, or in words with which he can do no good?<sup>4</sup>But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God.<sup>5</sup>For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty.<sup>6</sup>Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you.<sup>7</sup>"Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills?<sup>8</sup>Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself?<sup>9</sup>What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us?<sup>10</sup>Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father.<sup>11</sup>Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you?<sup>12</sup>Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash,<sup>13</sup>that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?<sup>14</sup>What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous?<sup>15</sup>Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight;<sup>16</sup>how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!<sup>17</sup>"I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare<sup>18</sup>(what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers,<sup>19</sup>to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).<sup>20</sup>The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless.<sup>21</sup>Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him.<sup>22</sup>He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is marked for the sword.<sup>23</sup>He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand;<sup>24</sup>distress and anguish terrify him; they prevail against him, like a king ready for battle.<sup>25</sup>Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty,<sup>26</sup>running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield;<sup>27</sup>because he has covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his waist<sup>28</sup>and has lived in desolate cities, in houses that none should inhabit, which were ready to become heaps of ruins;<sup>29</sup>he will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure, nor will his possessions spread over the earth;<sup>30</sup>he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots, and by the breath of his mouth he will depart.<sup>31</sup>Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his payment.<sup>32</sup>It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green.<sup>33</sup>He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree.<sup>34</sup>For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery.<sup>35</sup>They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
15.overview: Eliphaz opens the second round without courtesy: Job's words are wind, and he is doing away with the fear of God (vv. 1-6). Has he listened in the council of God? Are the comforts of God too small for him (vv. 7-13)? No man is pure, least of all one who drinks injustice like water (vv. 14-16). Then he describes the fate of the wicked, in dread and ruin (vv. 17-35).
15.theology:
The second round turns to one subject, the fate of the wicked (chs 15, 18, 20), and the portrait of the wicked keeps turning into a portrait of an innocent man. Eliphaz mocks the idea that Job has listened in God's council, but the reader has, and what was said there vindicates Job.

Christ, who is at the Father's side, has made the Father known, and he was numbered with the transgressors.
15.examples: Watch the friends' language harden. Eliphaz has moved from "no one is pure" to "you are foul", yet he calls his own speeches the comforts of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job's words are wind, says Eliphaz, and his own mouth condemns him (vv. 1-6). Has he listened in God's council, or are God's comforts too small for him (vv. 7-13)? No man is pure, much less one who is corrupt (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The second round begins with the courtesy gone, and with a mocking question whose answer the reader already knows.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? Should he argue in unprofitable talk, or in words with which he can do no good? But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God. For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty. Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second round of speeches begins, and it follows the first. The friends' case was set out in chapters 4-5, 8 and 11, and the reader should hold on to the LORD's verdict on it: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7). What is new in round two is the tone, and the subject.

The tone first. Eliphaz began chapter 4 by asking permission to speak. Now Job's words are windy knowledge, the east wind, the scorching desert wind, hot and useless. Job's talk, he says, is destroying piety itself, and yet the fear of God was the very thing God praised in Job (1:1, 8).

Job had said, though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me (9:20), meaning that God would twist his words. Eliphaz takes Job's fear and makes it his verdict. It is common in any quarrel, and cruel in pastoral care, to use what a grieving person says in anguish as evidence against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills? Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself? What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us? Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father. Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you? Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz mocks him as if he thought himself the first man ever made, older than the hills, a member of God's private council. Here is the sharpest irony in the round. The reader has listened in the council of God. Chapters 1 and 2 took us there, and what was said there was that Job was blameless and that his suffering was without reason (2:3). Eliphaz mocks the one source that could settle the argument, and it is against him.

Brought forth before the hills are the words of Wisdom: before the hills, I was brought forth (Prov 8:25). No mere man was there. Many Christians have heard in Wisdom's words the eternal Son, and the New Testament calls Christ the firstborn of all creation (Col 1:15), first in rank over creation, not the first thing made, the only Son who is at the Father's side (John 1:18). He has listened in the council of God, and told us what is in the Father's heart. God himself will use Eliphaz's irony on Job, gently: You know, for you were born then (38:21).

Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you? This is what Eliphaz calls his own speeches: God's comforts, spoken gently. Job's answer will come in the next chapter: miserable comforters are you all (16:2). The test of comfort is not what the comforter calls it.

verseByVerse.quote: What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous? Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight; how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is man, that he can be pure? This is Eliphaz's night vision again, in the same shape and many of the same words (4:17-19); what was said about it there applies here. What is new is where it lands. In chapter 4 the vision spoke of mortals in general. Now the last line is aimed: abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water. Eliphaz has moved from "no one is pure" to "you are foul". That is the whole slide of the friends' argument in one sentence.

The “holy ones” and “heavens” of verse 15 are the angels and heavenly beings: creatures, and so not pure as God is pure. Eliphaz uses this to argue that Job must be corrupt; the reasoning is his, not a revelation that the holy angels are fallen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–35 — The Wicked Man Writhes in Pain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz declares what the wise have handed down (vv. 17-19): the wicked man who defies the Almighty lives in dread, and his wealth will not last (vv. 20-35).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the subject of the whole second round, and Job's own story supplies every detail.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare (what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers, to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).
verseByVerse.commentary: Eliphaz appeals again to what he has seen and to the tradition of the fathers, pure and unmixed, handed down in a land no foreigner entered. Bildad made the same appeal (8:8-10). The trouble is not that tradition is worthless, but that no tradition, however pure, knew what happened in the council of God about this man.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless. Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him. He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is marked for the sword. He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand; distress and anguish terrify him; they prevail against him, like a king ready for battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here begins the new subject of the second round. All three friends will now preach the same sermon: the terrible end of the wicked (15:20-35; 18:5-21; 20:4-29). There are no more promises of restoration, only warning.

Every reader of chapter 1 knows who this describes: a man in prosperity, and the destroyer came. The sword fell on his servants (1:15, 17). He is in pain every day. Eliphaz never names Job; he does not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty, running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield; because he has covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his waist and has lived in desolate cities, in houses that none should inhabit, which were ready to become heaps of ruins; he will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure, nor will his possessions spread over the earth; he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots, and by the breath of his mouth he will depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the reason Eliphaz gives: the wicked man charges at God like a soldier with a studded shield, grown fat and arrogant, like Israel who grew fat, and kicked (Deut 32:15).

But stretched out his hand against God turns the prologue upside down. In chapter 1 it was Satan who asked God to stretch out your hand against Job (1:11). Job has not raised his hand against God. He has kept his hands open to him, even in protest.

The wealth that does not endure and the flame that dries his shoots, like the fire of God that fell on Job's flocks (1:16), are Job's story told as a sinner's fate.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his payment. It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green. He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree. For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery. They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz pictures a vine that drops its grapes before they ripen and an olive that sheds its blossom: children lost before they grew old, a house left barren. Eliphaz has chosen the image of fruit that dies young to describe the wicked, in front of a man whose ten children died young.

They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit. The psalmist says the same of the wicked (Ps 7:14), and it is true of them. It is not true of Job.

There is one man who was treated as everything this chapter describes, and he was wholly innocent. He was counted among the wicked. Jesus said, this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: And he was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37; Isa 53:12). The innocent one was treated as the man Eliphaz describes, so that the guilty could be treated as innocent.

16.title: My Witness Is in Heaven
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all.<sup>3</sup>Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?<sup>4</sup>I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you.<sup>5</sup>I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.<sup>6</sup>"If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me?<sup>7</sup>Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company.<sup>8</sup>And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.<sup>9</sup>He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me.<sup>10</sup>Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me.<sup>11</sup>God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.<sup>12</sup>I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target;<sup>13</sup>his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground.<sup>14</sup>He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.<sup>15</sup>I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust.<sup>16</sup>My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness,<sup>17</sup>although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.<sup>18</sup>"O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.<sup>19</sup>Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.<sup>20</sup>My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God,<sup>21</sup>that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor.<sup>22</sup>For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return.
16.overview: Job calls the friends miserable comforters with windy words; in their place he could mock them, or strengthen them (vv. 1-5). God has worn him out, torn him and handed him over to the wicked; men strike his cheek. He sits in sackcloth, though there is no violence in his hands and his prayer is pure (vv. 6-17). Let the earth not cover his blood: even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, who will plead a man's case with God (vv. 18-22).
16.theology:
Job's description of his suffering (vv. 9-11, 17) anticipates the language of the suffering Servant and of the passion of Christ (Matt 26:67; Acts 2:23): innocent, struck, handed over, though his hands have done no violence.

From no arbiter (9:33) Job climbs to my witness is in heaven (v. 19). Christ is that faithful witness and advocate, and his blood speaks a better word than Abel's (Heb 12:24).
16.examples: Job's phrase miserable comforters has clung to the friends ever since. Yet he knows the mouth that mocks could just as well strengthen, because his own once did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Miserable comforters are you all, says Job (vv. 1-3). In their place he could mock them, or strengthen them (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Job knows what real comfort would sound like, because he used to give it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all. Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz had called his speeches the comforts of God (15:11). Job answers with the description that has clung to the friends ever since: miserable comforters, literally comforters of trouble, the word Job has used for his life since chapter 3. They came to comfort (2:11) and have added to his trouble. And he throws back Eliphaz's opening insult (15:2): whose words are wind now?

Every church needs to hear this: it is possible to arrive with good intentions and the right doctrines and still be a miserable comforter. The friends were not bad men; they talked when they should have listened, and explained when they should have wept. Real comfort is passed on: the God of all comfort comforts us in our affliction so that we can comfort others with the comfort we have received (2 Cor 1:3-4).

verseByVerse.quote: I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you. I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If they swapped places, says Job, he could do what they are doing: string together sermons and shake his head at their misfortune. Or he could strengthen them, comfort them and ease their pain. He had done exactly that for others (4:3-4). The same mouth can do either. Jesus put it in one sentence: whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them (Matt 7:12).

Shake my head is the gesture of scorn. All who see me mock me ... they wag their heads, says the sufferer of Psalm 22 (Ps 22:7), and at the cross those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads (Matt 27:39).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–17 — He Has Torn Me in His Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Speaking or silent, his pain goes on (v. 6). God has worn him out (vv. 7-8), torn him and handed him over to the wicked (vv. 9-11), and run at him like a warrior (vv. 12-14). He sits in sackcloth, though his hands are clean of violence (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's suffering is described in the words the prophets would use for the suffering of the Servant, and the Gospels for the passion of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me? Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company. And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Talking does not help; silence does not help. Anyone in chronic pain knows the trap.

His family is gone, his friends have turned, and his wasted body stands up in court as a witness against me: people see how thin and sick he is and conclude that he must be guilty. That is the false witness; the true one comes at verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me. Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me. God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job believes God has become his enemy, tearing him like a wild beast. By my adversary Job means God, but the reader knows there is another adversary in this story, the one in the council, and God has not become Job's enemy at all. That is a mercy for every sufferer who feels the same. The feeling that God has turned against you is real, and Job is allowed to voice it, but it is not God's verdict. That was spoken in heaven before his trouble began (1:8).

These lines will be heard again. The gaping mouths return in Psalm 22, like a ravening and roaring lion (Ps 22:13), and the blow on the cheek in Micah and Isaiah: with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek (Mic 5:1); I gave ... my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isa 50:6). In the high priest's house they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67). And God gives me up to the ungodly: Peter said of Jesus that he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Job's night is a shadow thrown backwards from Good Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target; his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground. He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.
verseByVerse.commentary: I was at ease: the prosperous life of chapter 1, and then, without warning, everything broken. Job piles up pictures of violence: a man grabbed by the neck and smashed, a target ringed by archers (6:4; 7:20), a wall breached again and again, a soldier charging. The poet of Lamentations felt the same arrows: He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver (Lam 3:13). This is how undeserved suffering feels from the inside. The book lets him say it all, and does not ask the reader to pretend it is anything but agony.

verseByVerse.quote: I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust. My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sackcloth is stitched on, as if grown into his skin; his strength, literally his horn, is in the dirt. The horn is how Scripture pictures strength and honour; Hannah sang, my horn is exalted in the LORD (1 Sam 2:1). And the answer, when it came, came as a horn: God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).

Job is suffering like a criminal, and he has done no violence. Isaiah uses the same words, in the same Hebrew construction, of the Servant of the LORD, who was led like a lamb to the slaughter: they made his grave with the wicked ... although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth (Isa 53:9). What Job could say of himself in part, the Servant could say perfectly. Job's hands were clean of violence; Christ's were clean of every sin, and they were nailed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Witness Is in Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let the earth not cover his blood (v. 18). His witness is in heaven (v. 19). Scorned by his friends, he weeps to God for one who will plead his case (vv. 20-21), for his years are few (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the second step up the ladder of Job's hope: from no arbiter to a witness in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place. Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job expects to die unjustly, and he asks the ground not to soak up his blood and hide it. Let it lie there and cry out, the way Abel's blood cried from the ground after his brother killed him: The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground (Gen 4:10). Innocent blood calls for justice. Hebrews speaks of another blood that cries out, and says something better: the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb 12:24). Abel's blood cried for vengeance; Christ's cries for pardon.

In chapter 9 Job said there was no arbiter (9:33). Now, in a chapter as dark as any he has spoken, he says: even now, someone in heaven knows the truth and will speak for me.

Who? Many readers think Job means God himself: he appeals to God against God, to the God who knows his innocence against the God who seems to be attacking him. Others think he means a heavenly advocate distinct from God. The New Testament shows how both can be true. God the Son, who is God, stands before the Father for us: Jesus Christ the faithful witness (Rev 1:5), who always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25). Job reached into heaven in the dark and found someone there. He was right.

verseByVerse.quote: My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God, that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor. For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends scorn; the tears go to God. The Hebrew word for those who scorn can also mean spokesmen or interpreters, the word Elihu will use for a mediator (33:23). The men who should have spoken for him mock him, so he weeps upward.

He wants his heavenly witness to plead for him before God as one man stands up for his neighbour in court. As a son of man here simply means as one human being for another; the title Jesus would use is not in Job's mind. But the longing is plain: an advocate on God's side of the courtroom who pleads like one of us. Jesus, God the Son made man, is exactly that: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).

He is running out of time and needs the witness to speak soon. The Christian's advocate is speaking now.

17.title: Who Will Put Up Security for Me?
