17.text: <sup>1</sup>"My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me.<sup>2</sup>Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.<sup>3</sup>"Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me?<sup>4</sup>Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph.<sup>5</sup>He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property— the eyes of his children will fail.<sup>6</sup>"He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit.<sup>7</sup>My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.<sup>8</sup>The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless.<sup>9</sup>Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger.<sup>10</sup>But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you.<sup>11</sup>My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart.<sup>12</sup>They make night into day: 'The light,' they say, 'is near to the darkness.'<sup>13</sup>If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness,<sup>14</sup>if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,'<sup>15</sup>where then is my hope? Who will see my hope?<sup>16</sup>Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
17.overview: Job's spirit is broken and the grave is ready. He asks God to lay down a pledge for him with God, for no one else will stand surety for him (vv. 1-5). He has become a byword, yet the righteous holds to his way and grows stronger (vv. 6-10). The friends call night day. If the grave is his home and the worm his mother, where is his hope (vv. 11-16)?
17.theology: Job asks God to stand surety for him with God (v. 3), a request the New Testament sees answered in Christ. The righteous holds to his way even when his spirit is broken (vv. 1, 9), because God holds him. And the bars of Sheol (v. 16) have been opened by the one who holds the keys of Death.
17.examples: The chapter moves between extremes: a man made a byword and spat on, who still says the righteous holds to his way; friends who call night day; and a grave pictured as a family, with the pit for a father and the worm for a mother.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Who Will Put Up Security for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His spirit is broken and mockers surround him (vv. 1-2). He asks God to stand surety for him, for God has closed the friends' minds (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks God to stand surety for him with God, because he can find no one else who will.

verseByVerse.quote: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me. Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.
verseByVerse.commentary: Job speaks in three short, broken clauses: spirit gone, days snuffed out, the cemetery waiting. It is the voice of a man who expects to die soon. And he cannot even die in peace: mockers stand around him, and he cannot stop seeing their taunts. The friends came to sit with him in grief; now he lies awake with their words in front of his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me? Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph. He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property— the eyes of his children will fail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is a startling prayer. In the ancient world, when a man could not pay or could not be trusted to appear in court, someone else could stand surety for him, pledging his own property or person with a handshake. Job finds no one who will do it. So he asks God to stand guarantor for him before God.

The verb is the one Judah used when he offered himself for his brother Benjamin before their father: I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him (Gen 43:9). Judah put his own life on the line for his brother. And the Son of God, of the tribe of Judah, did the same for us. This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant (Heb 7:22). Job asked who would stand surety for him with God. God answered by becoming the surety himself.

God has shut the friends' minds; they will not win this argument. Then Job seems to quote a proverb (the verse is difficult): the man who informs against his friends for gain, his own children pay for it. The friends have informed against Job to God, and the proverb is a warning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Righteous Holds to His Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He has become a byword, spat upon (vv. 6-7); yet the righteous holds to his way, though there is no wise man among the friends (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of his darkest words Job says that the righteous man does not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: "He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit. My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.
verseByVerse.commentary: A byword is a name used as a warning: "you'll end up like Job." It is the covenant curse: you shall become a horror, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples (Deut 28:37). And men spit in his face. The Servant of the LORD would say, I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isa 50:6), and in the high priest's courtyard they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67).

verseByVerse.quote: The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless. Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger. But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly, in the middle of his lowest words, comes a burst of steel. Good people look at what has happened to Job and are horrified. But the righteous man does not give up his road. He holds on, and the one with clean hands gets stronger, not weaker, as the pressure grows.

That is what the Reformed churches have called the perseverance of the saints: not that God's people never stumble or despair, but that the one who truly belongs to God holds to his way, because God holds him and his Spirit is the seal and guarantee he gives them (Eph 1:13-14). The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day (Prov 4:18). Job's spirit is broken (v. 1) and his grip on his way is unbroken, both in one chapter. That is exactly what Satan said could not happen. For the believer who feels he is barely hanging on, the grip that matters most is God's on him, not his on God (John 10:28-29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Where Then Is My Hope?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His days are past (v. 11); the friends call night day (v. 12). If the grave is his home and the worm his mother, where is his hope (vv. 13-16)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job's hope stands at the gate of the grave and asks whether it will go through.

verseByVerse.quote: My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart. They make night into day: 'The light,' they say, 'is near to the darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything he meant to do, everything he hoped for, has been snapped off like thread.

The friends make night into day. Zophar promised that Job's darkness would be like the morning (11:17). It is midnight, and they keep saying dawn is near, if only he will repent. It is the false comfort the prophets condemned: They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jer 6:14). Real comfort does not pretend that night is day; it sits in the night, and waits for the real morning.

verseByVerse.quote: If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness, if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,' where then is my hope? Who will see my hope? Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the grave is the only home left to him, and the only family the pit and the worms, then what has become of his hope? Job has lost his house and his children. Now he pictures the grave adopting him. And he asks whether his hope will go down with him, through the barred gate of the underworld, and lie in the dust beside him.

The Bible answers with a man who went down to those bars. Jonah prayed from the belly of the fish, To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God (Jonah 2:6), and Jesus called his own death and resurrection the sign of Jonah. The risen Christ says, I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades (Rev 1:18). The bars Job feared are locked from the outside, and Christ has the key.

So Job's question has an answer. Where is his hope? Not in the dust. He has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Pet 1:3). A hope that has already been through the grave and come out cannot be buried with us.

18.title: The King of Terrors
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak.<sup>3</sup>Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight?<sup>4</sup>You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place?<sup>5</sup>"Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine.<sup>6</sup>The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out.<sup>7</sup>His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down.<sup>8</sup>For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walks on its mesh.<sup>9</sup>A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him.<sup>10</sup>A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path.<sup>11</sup>Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels.<sup>12</sup>His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling.<sup>13</sup>It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs.<sup>14</sup>He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors.<sup>15</sup>In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation.<sup>16</sup>His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above.<sup>17</sup>His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street.<sup>18</sup>He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world.<sup>19</sup>He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.<sup>20</sup>They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east.<sup>21</sup>Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God."
18.overview: Bildad resents being counted as cattle (vv. 1-4). Then he describes the fate of the wicked: his light goes out, traps seize him, the firstborn of death consumes his skin, he is brought to the king of terrors, and he leaves no descendants. Such is the place of him who does not know God (vv. 5-21).
18.theology:
Bildad's rule that wickedness ends in ruin is true at the last judgment. His error is to read it off one man's suffering in this life, and to conclude that Job does not know God.

Death, the king of terrors, has been dethroned: Christ destroyed the one who has the power of death and freed those enslaved by its fear.
18.examples: Bildad packs six traps into three verses. Then he aims his lines: a disease that eats the skin, said to a man with a skin disease, and no posterity, said to a father of ten dead children.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Why Are We Counted as Cattle?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad resents being counted as cattle (vv. 1-3). Shall the earth be rearranged for Job (v. 4)?
verseByVerse.theology: Bildad's pride is hurt, and he tells Job that the world will not be rearranged to suit him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak. Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight? You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad's case from chapter 8 has not changed. What is new is mostly wounded pride and a sharper picture.

How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak. Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight? Job told them to ask the animals for wisdom (12:7) and said he could not find a wise man among them (17:10). Bildad has taken it personally.

Job said God had torn him (16:9); Bildad says he tears himself. And he throws back Job's own words, the rock is removed from its place (14:18): do you expect the world's moral order to be moved for your sake? Bildad is right that God does not rearrange the world to please a sufferer. He has not considered that God's order might be larger than his account of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–21 — The Light of the Wicked Is Put Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lamp of the wicked goes out (vv. 5-6), and traps seize him (vv. 7-10). Terrors chase him, disease eats his skin, and he is brought to the king of terrors (vv. 11-14). His house is ruined and his memory perishes (vv. 15-19). Such is the place of him who knows not God (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Every line of Bildad's portrait of the wicked describes Job, down to the final verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: "Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine. The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out. His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down. For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walks on its mesh. A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him. A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Proverbs says it too: the lamp of the wicked will be put out (Prov 13:9). Job will remember the days when his lamp shone upon my head (29:3). Bildad says that lamp has gone out because Job is wicked.

Six traps in three verses, and the wicked man walks into them by his own steps. It is true of the wicked: in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught (Ps 9:15). But Job did not set these nets. He is caught in something he cannot see, and the reader knows who laid it.

verseByVerse.quote: Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels. His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling. It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs. He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here Bildad goes further than he has before. The wicked man, he says, dies of a disease that eats his skin: the firstborn of death, probably the deadliest sickness of all, death's eldest son. He says this to a man whose skin is crusting and breaking (2:7; 7:5). It is no longer a general warning but a diagnosis. Christians still do this, reading a friend's cancer or a child's death as the sign of some hidden sin. Jesus refused that reasoning (Luke 13:1-5; John 9:2-3), and so must we. The LORD rebuked exactly that sermon.

Death is pictured as a king, the lord of every fear, and the wicked are marched before him. It is a terrible and true picture of death for those without God. But the New Testament shows the king of terrors dethroned. Christ shared our flesh that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:14-15). The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor 15:26). The believer is not marched before the king of terrors. He is welcomed by the King who conquered him.

verseByVerse.quote: In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation. His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above. His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street. He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world. He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strangers move into his house; burning sulfur falls on it, as on Sodom (Gen 19:24). Root and branch, nothing is left.

The wicked man, says Bildad, leaves no children and no one to carry his name, and he says it to a man whose ten children are in their graves. It is the cruellest turn of his speech. And it is false. Job's name did not perish. Ezekiel named him as a righteous man (Ezek 14:14); James held him up to the church (James 5:11); and his story is read wherever the Bible is read. The righteous ... will be remembered forever (Ps 112:6).

verseByVerse.quote: They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east. Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Bildad's last line is his verdict: Job is a man who does not know God. The LORD will say otherwise, and Bildad will be among the three he rebukes (42:7-9). Job's very next speech will reach its peak with the words Bildad has just denied him: For I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25). The man Bildad says does not know God is about to say one of the best-known sentences of faith in the Old Testament.

19.title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words?<sup>3</sup>These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?<sup>4</sup>And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself.<sup>5</sup>If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me,<sup>6</sup>know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me.<sup>7</sup>Behold, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice.<sup>8</sup>He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths.<sup>9</sup>He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head.<sup>10</sup>He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree.<sup>11</sup>He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary.<sup>12</sup>His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.<sup>13</sup>"He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me.<sup>14</sup>My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.<sup>15</sup>The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes.<sup>16</sup>I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.<sup>17</sup>My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother.<sup>18</sup>Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me.<sup>19</sup>All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.<sup>20</sup>My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.<sup>21</sup>Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me!<sup>22</sup>Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?<sup>23</sup>"Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book!<sup>24</sup>Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!<sup>25</sup>For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.<sup>26</sup>And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God,<sup>27</sup>whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!<sup>28</sup>If you say, 'How we will pursue him!' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,'<sup>29</sup>be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment."
19.overview: Job asks how long the friends will torment him; if they use his disgrace as proof of guilt, let them know God has put him in the wrong (vv. 1-6). He cries Violence! and is not answered; God has walled up his way and uprooted his hope like a tree (vv. 7-12). Everyone has turned from him, and he begs the friends for pity (vv. 13-22). Then, from the bottom, he says, I know that my Redeemer lives, and in his flesh he will see God (vv. 23-29).
19.theology:
The go'el, the kinsman who redeems, is above all God's own name (Isa 41:14), and the risen Christ takes up Job's Redeemer and last as the living one (Rev 1:17-18). This is the summit of the book's longing for a mediator (9:33; 16:19).

After the destruction of his body Job will see God with his own eyes, and not as a stranger: the hope of the resurrection of the body (1 Cor 15:42-44) and of the vision of God.
19.examples: Job's lowest point and his highest stand fifteen verses apart. In between he wishes his words were cut in rock, and they were written somewhere more lasting still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — How Long Will You Torment Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How long will they break him with words (vv. 1-3)? If they use his disgrace against him, let them know that it is God who has put him in the wrong (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job names what the friends have been doing: using his suffering as evidence. He knows the suffering came from God's hand, not from his own feet walking into a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words? These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad has just told Job that he does not know God (18:21). Job's reply begins in exhaustion: how long? Their words have been hammers. Ten times is not a count; the friends have spoken five times so far. It means "over and over again", as Jacob said Laban had changed his wages ten times (Gen 31:7).

Are you not ashamed? The friends came to show him sympathy and comfort him (2:11). They have wronged him, and they do not blush. This chapter goes deeper into the dark than any before it, and then climbs higher than any before it. It begins here, with a man broken by the words of his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself. If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me, know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if he has sinned somewhere, says Job, my error remains with myself: it has not harmed them, and gives them no right to stand over him.

Here is exactly what the friends have done: they have taken his disgrace, his ruined body and his dead children, and made it an argument against me. They have the cause wrong: it was not his sin that did this, but God.

Listen to the two words he chooses. Put me in the wrong is the verb of Bildad's first question, Does God pervert justice? (8:3). And his net answers Bildad's last speech, where the wicked man is cast into a net by his own feet (18:8). No, says Job, I did not walk into this. It was God who spread the net. He is right that God's hand is in it (2:3). He is wrong, and will be told so, to think God has done him wrong (40:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — He Has Walled Up My Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job cries Violence! and is not answered (v. 7). God has walled up his way, stripped his glory and uprooted his hope (vv. 8-10), and besieges him as an enemy (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's picture of God is still of an enemy besieging him. It will not stay that way to the end of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice. He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man attacked in the street shouts for help, and no one comes. Habakkuk would pray almost the same: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you Violence! and you will not save? (Hab 1:2). God did answer Habakkuk, and he will answer Job, but not yet; the waiting is part of the trial.

In chapter 3 God had hedged him in (3:23). Now it is a wall. Lamentations knew it: He has walled me about so that I cannot escape (Lam 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head. He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The honour Job once had, the respect of his city (29:7-11), is gone, as if God had pulled the crown from his head in public.

That is exactly what men did to Christ, in mockery. They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head (Matt 27:28-29). And that is the road by which he came to be crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:9). The glory stripped from Job will be given back. The glory Christ laid down was taken up again, for us.

In chapter 14 Job said there is hope for a tree (14:7). Now even that hope has been torn out by the roots. It is the lowest point his hope has reached, and it comes fifteen verses before the highest.

verseByVerse.quote: He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary. His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.
verseByVerse.commentary: Job pictures God as a general and himself as a besieged town: a whole army against one tent, one sick man. Counts me as his adversary is the complaint of 13:24 again. The reader knows God said the opposite: there is none like him on the earth (1:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Have Mercy on Me, O You My Friends
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Family, friends, servants and his wife treat him as a stranger (vv. 13-19); he has escaped by the skin of his teeth (v. 20). He begs his friends for pity (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the loneliness of the sufferer, described from the inside, and the Son of God knew it.

verseByVerse.quote: "He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me. My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the siege moves inside. Job counts, circle by circle, the people who have abandoned him, and lays even this at God's door: he has put them far from me. When a man is ill and disgraced, people stop coming, some embarrassed, some afraid, some having drawn their own conclusions.

verseByVerse.quote: The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes. I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his own house he is a stranger. The guests he once fed and the maids who served him treat him as a foreigner. The master calls his servant, and the servant does not come; the master has to beg. It is a humiliating inversion of the world of chapter 1.

Keep the word stranger. It will come back at the summit of the chapter, in verse 27.

verseByVerse.quote: My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother. Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me. All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His wife cannot bear his breath. His own brothers find him disgusting. Children jeer when he tries to stand. His closest friends, the ones he loved, have turned their backs. There is no one left.

Set the children beside chapter 29: the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood (29:8). Now children jeer when he struggles to his feet. And his wife, who told him to curse God and die (2:9), cannot come near him. He does not curse her. He grieves that she has gone from him too.

The psalms know this loneliness: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons (Ps 69:8). The New Testament quotes the next verse of that psalm of Jesus (John 2:17), and the whole of it was lived by him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). In Gethsemane, they all left him and fled (Mark 14:50). Whoever reads this chapter alone, abandoned by family and friends, may know that the Son of God has stood exactly there, and does not abandon his own.

verseByVerse.quote: My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary: He is skin and bone, wasted to nothing. By the skin of my teeth has passed into English as the phrase for the narrowest escape. What Job meant is not certain; teeth have no skin, and that may be the point: he has escaped with nothing at all, or he has only his gums left. Either way, he is barely alive, and barely is enough. God said to Satan, only spare his life (2:6), and his life has been spared, just.

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me! Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the only time in the debate, Job begs the friends for pity, twice. He is not arguing now. He is pleading. Touch is the word Satan used (2:5). Job knows nothing of Satan; he knows that the hand on him is God's, and he asks his friends not to add their hands to it.

Here is a man with a skin disease crying for mercy and getting none. Centuries later ten men with a skin disease stood at a distance from Jesus and lifted up their voices, saying, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us (Luke 17:13), and he did. The friends had no mercy for the man whose skin was rotting. The Lord had nothing else for such men.

Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh? They are hunting him as he feels God hunts him. Not satisfied with my flesh is probably an idiom for slander; in the Aramaic of Daniel, to "eat pieces" of a man means to accuse him maliciously (Dan 3:8). They are devouring him with accusations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — I Know That My Redeemer Lives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job wants his words engraved in rock (vv. 23-24): his Redeemer lives, and in his flesh he will see God (vv. 25-27). Let the friends beware of judgment (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: From the bottom of the pit, the summit of the book's faith: a living Redeemer, standing at the last on the dust where Job will lie, and Job seeing God with his own eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns. Job wants what he is about to say cut into rock with an iron chisel and filled with lead, like the royal inscriptions on cliff faces, to outlast him and the friends. He is sure that he will die unvindicated, so he wants his testimony on record.

His wish was granted beyond anything he imagined. His words were written in a book, and that book is Scripture. They have been read in more languages and by more people than any inscription ever cut into a cliff. The man who thought his voice would die with him is still speaking.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad said Job was a man who knows not God (18:21). Job says: I know. Not I hope, not I wish. And what he knows is this: he has a Redeemer, and his Redeemer is alive.

The Hebrew word is go'el, your nearest kinsman, whose duty was to rescue you when you could not rescue yourself. If you sold your land in debt, he bought it back (Lev 25:25). If you were sold as a slave, he redeemed you (Lev 25:48-49). If you were murdered, he avenged your blood (Num 35:19), which is why Job cried, O earth, cover not my blood (16:18). Boaz was Ruth's go'el (Ruth 4:14). But the word belongs above all to God: your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 41:14). Job has no kinsman left who will stand up for him (vv. 13-19). He knows he has one who will.

Who is this Redeemer? Job does not name him, and the question has been asked for as long as the book has been read. Most likely Job means God himself: the God who seems to be his enemy in verses 6-12 is the God he appeals to as his kinsman and defender in verse 25, God against God, the same appeal as in 16:19. But a go'el has to be a kinsman, one of the family. How can God be that? The New Testament answers. The Son of God is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb 2:11); since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things (Heb 2:14). God became our kinsman so that he could be our Redeemer. Job's words reached further than he could see.

This sentence does not come after Job has been healed or answered. Nothing has changed. Fifteen verses ago God had torn up his hope like a tree (v. 10). The harshest things Job says about God and the greatest thing he says about God stand in the same speech. That is how faith often speaks in real suffering. It does not wait for the dark to lift before it says I know. It does not rest on how things look. It rests on who God is. A believer who can only say, today, he has walled up my way, is still allowed to say, in the next breath, my Redeemer lives. Job did.

At the last is acharon, and Isaiah puts Job's two words side by side: Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer ... I am the first and I am the last (Isa 44:6). The Redeemer is the Last. And the risen Christ took that title as his own, with the other word of Job's line: Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore (Rev 1:17-18). My Redeemer lives. And as he said it, John writes, he laid his right hand on me. Job had cried that there was no arbiter who might lay his hand on us both (9:33), and many Christians have heard an echo of that cry in the hand laid on John. The living Redeemer and the Last are one person, and he is not out of reach.

The earth is, in Hebrew, dust (ESV note): the dust of the grave, where Job feared his hope would go down (17:16). His Redeemer will stand up on that very dust, over the place where Job lies, like a kinsman rising in court to speak for the dead. Christ did stand on that dust: he went into the grave and rose from it, and he will stand upon the earth again at the last day.
verseByVerse.note: A go'el was the near relative who stood up for a family member who could not help himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job expects his skin to be destroyed. And yet he will see God. In my flesh can also be read "without my flesh" (ESV note); some take Job to mean he will see God as a spirit after death. These are among the hardest verses in the book. The King James Version's though after my skin worms destroy this body supplies worms and body (printed in italics), and the Greek Old Testament reads the line as God raising up Job's skin. In every version Job will see God for himself. And my eyes shall behold: eyes belong to a body. The Christian reads here the resurrection of the body: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory (1 Cor 15:43). The wasted flesh on the ash heap will be raised, and with those eyes Job will see his God.

Not another means not as a stranger. His own household counts him a stranger (v. 15), but he will look at God, and it will not be as a stranger. He will see God for himself, face to face, as one who belongs to him. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). They will see his face (Rev 22:4).

My heart faints within me! This is not calm doctrine. It is a man overwhelmed by what he has just said. Every believer who has stood by a grave and said these words knows the feeling. And Job will taste the first of it before he dies: now my eye sees you (42:5).
verseByVerse.note: “In my flesh” may be rendered “without my flesh” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: If you say, 'How we will pursue him!' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,' be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job turns back to the friends with a warning. If there is a Redeemer who will stand up at the last, there is also a judgment, and it may fall on you. It did: My anger burns against you and against your two friends (42:7). The man they condemned would pray for them (42:8).

That is the shape of the gospel. We who condemned Christ were saved by the prayers of the one we condemned: Father, forgive them. Job's Redeemer lives, and he lives to intercede.

20.title: The Wicked Man's Portion
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me.<sup>3</sup>I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.<sup>4</sup>Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth,<sup>5</sup>that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment?<sup>6</sup>Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds,<sup>7</sup>he will perish forever like his own dung; those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?'<sup>8</sup>He will fly away like a dream and not be found; he will be chased away like a vision of the night.<sup>9</sup>The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him.<sup>10</sup>His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth.<sup>11</sup>His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.<sup>12</sup>"Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue,<sup>13</sup>though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth,<sup>14</sup>yet his food is turned in his stomach; it is the venom of cobras within him.<sup>15</sup>He swallows down riches and vomits them up again; God casts them out of his belly.<sup>16</sup>He will suck the poison of cobras; the tongue of a viper will kill him.<sup>17</sup>He will not look upon the rivers, the streams flowing with honey and curds.<sup>18</sup>He will give back the fruit of his toil and will not swallow it down; from the profit of his trading he will get no enjoyment.<sup>19</sup>For he has crushed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house that he did not build.<sup>20</sup>"Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not let anything in which he delights escape him.<sup>21</sup>There was nothing left after he had eaten; therefore his prosperity will not endure.<sup>22</sup>In the fullness of his sufficiency he will be in distress; the hand of everyone in misery will come against him.<sup>23</sup>To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body.<sup>24</sup>He will flee from an iron weapon; a bronze arrow will strike him through.<sup>25</sup>It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him.<sup>26</sup>Utter darkness is laid up for his treasures; a fire not fanned will devour him; what is left in his tent will be consumed.<sup>27</sup>The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.<sup>28</sup>The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath.<sup>29</sup>This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God."
20.overview: Zophar, stung by what he hears as an insult, says the triumph of the wicked has always been short: though he reach the clouds, he perishes like dung (vv. 1-11). Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to venom; God rains anger on him, and heaven and earth rise against him: this is the wicked man's portion from God (vv. 12-29).
20.theology:
Zophar's last speech ignores Job's confession of a living Redeemer and turns Job's own hope against him. Its one new picture is a true warning: sin is sweet in the mouth and deadly in the stomach (vv. 12-16; James 1:14-15).

Christ received the wicked man's portion though he knew no sin, and so the believer's portion is God himself.
20.examples: Zophar never speaks again after this, and his parting line, the wicked man's portion, is one Job will quote back at him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Exulting of the Wicked Is Short
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar is stung (vv. 1-3). The joy of the godless is brief (vv. 4-5): though he reach the clouds, he will vanish like a dream (vv. 6-9), and his children will beg from the poor (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar has heard only the warning aimed at him, not the hope that came just before it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me. I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Zophar's last speech. As the text stands, he will say nothing at all in the third round (some scholars think part of chapter 27 was once his). His case was set out in chapter 11 and the round's subject, the end of the wicked, in chapter 15; what follows repeats both. What is new is what he does not say.

Job has just said, I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25), the highest confession of faith in the book so far. Zophar does not mention it. What he heard was the warning that judgment might fall on the friends (19:28-29), censure that insults me. It is a very human failure: people in an argument often hear only the sentence that stings them, and miss the one that could have changed everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth, that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment? Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds, he will perish forever like his own dung; those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?' He will fly away like a dream and not be found; he will be chased away like a vision of the night. The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him. His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth. His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man's triumph is brief. That is true in the end, and the psalms say it: until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end ... How they are destroyed in a moment (Ps 73:17-19). But Zophar means that it is always short in this life, and Job will spend the next chapter showing that it often is not.

The proud man who climbs to the clouds, like the king of Babylon who said I will ascend to heaven (Isa 14:13), ends on the dung heap and vanishes like a dream. Job said the same of every man (7:8-10); Zophar says it only of the wicked.

The children begging from the poor, the wealth handed back and the strong body in the dust are, once more, drawn from Job's own life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–29 — The Wicked Man's Portion from God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to venom (vv. 12-19). God rains anger on him (vv. 20-26), and heaven and earth rise against him: this is his portion from God (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar turns Job's hope into his doom, and God will turn the verdict back on Zophar.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth, yet his food is turned in his stomach; it is the venom of cobras within him. He swallows down riches and vomits them up again; God casts them out of his belly. He will suck the poison of cobras; the tongue of a viper will kill him. He will not look upon the rivers, the streams flowing with honey and curds. He will give back the fruit of his toil and will not swallow it down; from the profit of his trading he will get no enjoyment. For he has crushed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house that he did not build.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the one new picture in the speech, and it is a true one. Sin is like a sweet in the mouth: the sinner rolls it round his tongue, cannot bear to let it go, and swallows it, and in the stomach it turns to snake venom. Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel (Prov 20:17). James traces the same course: desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death (James 1:15). Every believer should hear the warning, and run from the sweet poison to the mercy that forgives and the Spirit who gives new desires (Gal 5:16).

God makes the greedy man bring his riches back up, like the rich fool who heard, This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:20). And here, for the first time, a friend hints at a specific charge: Job crushed and abandoned the poor. Eliphaz will say it outright (22:6-9). It is false. Job was the man who delivered the poor who cried for help (29:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not let anything in which he delights escape him. There was nothing left after he had eaten; therefore his prosperity will not endure. In the fullness of his sufficiency he will be in distress; the hand of everyone in misery will come against him. To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body. He will flee from an iron weapon; a bronze arrow will strike him through. It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him. Utter darkness is laid up for his treasures; a fire not fanned will devour him; what is left in his tent will be consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man always hungry for more will be filled at last, with God's wrath. Zophar pictures sickness in the body as anger rained down from heaven, and he is looking at Job's body when he says it.

Job had described his suffering in exactly these terms: God's archers, and he pours out my gall on the ground (16:13). Zophar makes Job's picture of his own pain the death of the wicked. A fire not fanned is one no human hand lit, as none lit the fire of God that fell on Job's flocks (1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here Zophar answers Job directly, and it is cleverly done. Job had cried, O earth, cover not my blood, and my witness is in heaven (16:18-19); and just now, that his Redeemer will stand upon the earth (19:25). Zophar turns all three round: heaven will witness against you, and the earth will rise up, the same verb as stand, not for you but against you. Job's hope is thrown back at him as his doom.

Zophar's last words are a verdict, the wicked man's portion from God. Job will quote the line back almost word for word (27:13).

The heavens did reveal the truth in the end, and it was not Job's iniquity. God spoke from heaven and said that Job had spoken rightly and Zophar had not (42:7). There was one man who received the wicked man's portion from God though he was not wicked: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). Because he took that portion, the believer's portion is God himself: God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps 73:26).

21.title: Why Do the Wicked Live?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort.<sup>3</sup>Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.<sup>4</sup>As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient?<sup>5</sup>Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth.<sup>6</sup>When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.<sup>7</sup>Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?<sup>8</sup>Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes.<sup>9</sup>Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.<sup>10</sup>Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry.<sup>11</sup>They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance.<sup>12</sup>They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe.<sup>13</sup>They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.<sup>14</sup>They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.<sup>15</sup>What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'<sup>16</sup>Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me.<sup>17</sup>"How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger?<sup>18</sup>That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?<sup>19</sup>You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it.<sup>20</sup>Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty.<sup>21</sup>For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?<sup>22</sup>Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high?<sup>23</sup>One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure,<sup>24</sup>his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist.<sup>25</sup>Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity.<sup>26</sup>They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.<sup>27</sup>"Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me.<sup>28</sup>For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?'<sup>29</sup>Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony<sup>30</sup>that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath?<sup>31</sup>Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done?<sup>32</sup>When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb.<sup>33</sup>The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable.<sup>34</sup>How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
21.overview: Job asks the friends simply to listen; his complaint is with God (vv. 1-6). Why do the wicked live to old age in power, their children dancing, dying in peace, though they tell God to depart (vv. 7-16)? How often is the lamp of the wicked actually put out? One dies at ease and another in bitterness, and the worms cover both (vv. 17-26). Any traveller knows the evil man is often spared and buried with honour, so the friends' comfort is empty (vv. 27-34).
21.theology:
Job answers the second round with the facts: the wicked often prosper and die in peace. Scripture agrees (Jer 12:1; Ps 73) and places the reckoning beyond death: after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27; Luke 16:25). The friends' neat system is empty nothings, and God will say so (42:7).

The wicked reject God because prayer brings no profit (v. 15). Satan accused Job of serving God for profit (1:9), yet Job goes on serving God when it has cost him everything.
21.examples: Some of the chapter's phrases are worth carrying away. Let this be your comfort tells every visitor to the sick and the grieving that listening is itself a gift. What profit do we get if we pray? is Satan's premise from chapter 1 turned inside out. And How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? takes Bildad's own picture and asks how often anyone has actually seen it happen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Lay Your Hand over Your Mouth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks to be heard (vv. 1-3); his complaint is with God, and what he is about to say makes him shudder (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The best comfort the friends could have given was to listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort. Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar has made his last speech. Job answers with something new: not a lament, but a sustained argument from the facts. And he begins with a request that every comforter should hear. Let this be your comfort: the comfort you could give me is simply to listen. Hear me out, and then mock if you must.

The friends came to comfort (2:11) and have done everything but listen. The ministry Job asks for is the cheapest there is and the rarest.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient? Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth. When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is my complaint against man? His quarrel is with God, not with any man. That is why he cannot simply calm down: a man can ignore a human critic, but not the Almighty.

Lay your hand over your mouth: look at me and be silent. When God has spoken from the whirlwind, Job himself will say, I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4). The silence he asks of the friends before his suffering, he will give to God before his glory.

When I remember, I am dismayed: he is going to describe the world as it actually is, and it does not fit what anyone has been taught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — Why Do the Wicked Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked flourish and die in peace (vv. 7-13), though they tell God to depart (vv. 14-15). Job still refuses their counsel (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Job answers the whole second round with plain facts. And he refuses the wicked's creed even though it seems to work.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes. Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? Zophar said the exulting of the wicked is short (20:5). Then why do so many of them live to a ripe old age, with their grandchildren around them? Their houses are safe; God's rod never falls on them. Job knows the rod; it is on him (9:34).

Jeremiah asked the same: Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? (Jer 12:1). Both men hold that God is righteous and bring the question to him. Faith does not require pretending otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry. They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance. They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe. They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herds that breed; little boys let out to play like lambs; children dancing to tambourine and pipe. Every line hurts, because Job's own children once feasted together in their brother's house (1:4). The wicked's children dance; his are in the ground.

And the wicked die in peace: no long illness, no ash heap. Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus answers this line: remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish (Luke 16:25). The peaceful death is not the end of the story.

verseByVerse.quote: They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?' Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prosperous wicked tell God to go away, and give their reason: religion does not pay.

The first chapter is turned inside out. Satan accused Job of serving God for profit: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). The wicked reject God because serving him brings no profit; Job serves him when it has brought him nothing but loss. And their Depart from us will be answered in their own words at the last: I never knew you; depart from me (Matt 7:23).

The counsel of the wicked is far from me. Job wants no part of their philosophy, however well it seems to work. It is the first line of the Psalter (Ps 1:1), and Eliphaz will quote Job's line back at him word for word (22:18).

That refusal matters for anyone who watches the wicked do well, where the temptation is not only to doubt God but to envy them. Asaph nearly slipped on exactly this, and found his footing only when he saw that what he had was God himself: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Ps 73:25). Job has lost everything the wicked still have, and he would rather have God with nothing than their prosperity without him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — How Often Is the Lamp of the Wicked Put Out?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks how often the wicked are really punished (vv. 17-21), and sets two deaths side by side under the same dust (vv. 22-26).
verseByVerse.theology: In this life the lamp of the wicked often burns to the end. The book's answer, and the gospel's, lies beyond the grave.

verseByVerse.quote: "How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger? That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?
verseByVerse.commentary: How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? Bildad said, the light of the wicked is put out ... his lamp above him is put out (18:5-6). Job takes his words and asks: how often do you actually see it? The psalm says the wicked are like chaff that the wind drives away (Ps 1:4). But in this life, how often do we watch it happen? Not often. Job is not denying that God judges. He is denying that you can see the judgment on schedule, in time for your argument.

verseByVerse.quote: You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it. Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty. For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?
verseByVerse.commentary: Job anticipates the reply: God punishes the children instead. But what does the wicked man care, once he is dead? If justice means anything, it must reach the man himself, as Ezekiel would later say in God's own word: The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek 18:20). And Job has heard where that argument leads, for Bildad said his own children died for their sins (8:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high? One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure, his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist. Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high? The friends are trying to tell God how his justice must work, as if he were bound to run the world by their tidy system. Who taught him the path of justice? asks Isaiah (Isa 40:14), and Paul, who has been his counselor? (Rom 11:34). No one teaches God. That cuts against the friends' neat system, and it will cut against Job's demands too when God speaks.

Two deaths: one well fed and comfortable to the last, the other bitter all his days. And the grave makes no distinction; the worms take both. If this life were all, there would be no justice at all. The New Testament answers where Job's argument points: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27). The dust is not the verdict.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job knows the friends mean his own house (vv. 27-28). Common experience says the evil man is often spared and buried with honour (vv. 29-33), so their comfort is empty (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Job sums up the friends' comfort as vapour and treachery.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me. For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?' Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived? Job knows exactly whose house they mean. His own lies in ruins. They have been describing it for three chapters.

Have you not asked those who travel the roads? Ask anyone who has travelled and seen the world. They will tell you that disaster often passes the evil man by. Job appeals to common experience against a theory that ignores it.

verseByVerse.quote: Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done? When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb. The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable. How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who declares his way to his face? The powerful wicked man is never confronted; no one dares tell him the truth.

Watch is kept over his tomb: a grand funeral, a guard of honour at the grave, the earth lying lightly on him, crowds in the procession. Christians may remember another guarded tomb, watched for a very different reason. The authorities made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard (Matt 27:66), to keep the Righteous One in. It could not.

Verse 34 is Job's verdict on the friends' whole case. Empty nothings is hevel, vapour, the word of Ecclesiastes; falsehood is the word Chronicles uses again and again for unfaithfulness to God. Their comfort is vapour, and their answers a kind of betrayal. God will give the same verdict at the end: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7).

22.title: Is Not Your Evil Abundant?
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself.<sup>3</sup>Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless?<sup>4</sup>Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?<sup>5</sup>Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities.<sup>6</sup>For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing.<sup>7</sup>You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.<sup>8</sup>The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it.<sup>9</sup>You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.<sup>10</sup>Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you,<sup>11</sup>or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.<sup>12</sup>"Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are!<sup>13</sup>But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness?<sup>14</sup>Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.'<sup>15</sup>Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod?<sup>16</sup>They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away.<sup>17</sup>They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?'<sup>18</sup>Yet he filled their houses with good things— but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.<sup>19</sup>The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent one mocks at them,<sup>20</sup>saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'<sup>21</sup>"Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you.<sup>22</sup>Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.<sup>23</sup>If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents,<sup>24</sup>if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed,<sup>25</sup>then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.<sup>26</sup>For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.<sup>27</sup>You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows.<sup>28</sup>You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways.<sup>29</sup>For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'; but he saves the lowly.<sup>30</sup>He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
22.overview: Eliphaz says God gains nothing from man's righteousness, so Job's suffering must mean great evil, and he lists sins Job never committed (vv. 1-11). He puts the words of the wicked in Job's mouth and Job's own words in his (vv. 12-20). Let Job agree with God, return, and have the Almighty as his gold; then God will deliver even the one who is not innocent through the cleanness of Job's hands (vv. 21-30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Is Not Your Evil Abundant?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gains nothing from a man's righteousness (vv. 1-4), so Job's suffering must mean great sins against the poor (vv. 5-11).
verseByVerse.theology: With no evidence, Eliphaz invents Job's crimes. They are the opposite of what the narrator and God have said of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless? Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third round begins, and Eliphaz speaks for the last time. What is new in this speech is that he stops hinting and starts inventing, and that his last words say more than he knows.

Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless? God gains nothing from us. Half of that is true: God needs nothing, and Paul asks, who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? (Rom 11:35), quoting this very book (41:11). But the other half is false. God does take pleasure in the righteous. He said so in heaven: Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). He will rejoice over you with gladness (Zeph 3:17). Eliphaz's God is too remote to care.

Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you? Eliphaz means it as sarcasm: surely God is not punishing you for being godly! The reader, who has been in the council, knows the answer. Yes. It was precisely because of Job's fear of God that the trial came: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). Eliphaz has asked the question the whole book turns on, and got the answer backwards.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities. For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing. You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry. The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it. You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed. Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you, or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not your evil abundant? Eliphaz has no evidence, so he supplies it. Job must have taken the cloak of a poor man as security for a debt and left him naked; refused water to a traveller and bread to the hungry; turned widows away and trampled orphans. None of it is true. Job will answer every item: I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him (29:12); if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing ... if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep (31:19-20). And the orphans are Job's own charge against the friends turned round (6:27).

For nothing is chinnam, Satan's word: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). God said Job's suffering was without reason (2:3). The word that marks Job's innocence is now used to accuse him. And the list is the very list by which Christ will judge the nations: I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink ... naked and you did not clothe me (Matt 25:42-43). Eliphaz has charged Job with the sins of the goats. Job was a sheep.

Therefore snares are all around you. When the facts will not fit the friends' theology, the facts are invented. A counsellor who "knows" what a sufferer must have done, without evidence, is doing what Eliphaz did, and God will call it what he called it (42:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz charges Job with doubting that God sees (vv. 12-14) and with walking the old path of the wicked (vv. 15-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Eliphaz puts the words of the wicked in Job's mouth, and borrows Job's own words to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are! But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness? Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.' Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod? They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away. They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?' Yet he filled their houses with good things— but the counsel of the wicked is far from me. The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent one mocks at them, saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz now puts words in Job's mouth, and they are the wicked man's words: How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High? (Ps 73:11). Job has said the opposite all along. His complaint is that God sees too much: he said God would watch all my paths (13:27) and test him every moment (7:18). Eliphaz is not listening; he is answering the man his theory needs Job to be.

Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod? Probably the generation of the flood, swept away with their foundations (2 Pet 2:5). Their Depart from us is Job's own description of the wicked (21:14), and the counsel of the wicked is far from me is Job's own sentence, word for word (21:16). Eliphaz takes Job's words and sets them in his own mouth: I, Eliphaz, am the one far from the wicked. He has turned Job's confession into his accusation. The righteous see it and are glad when the wicked fall; the fire consumes what they left, as it consumed Job's flocks (1:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–30 — Agree with God, and Be at Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz calls Job to return to God (vv. 21-25) and promises that his prayers will be heard (vv. 26-30).
verseByVerse.theology: These are the loveliest words Eliphaz ever speaks, and his last. Their final line comes true in a way he never meant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents, if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed, then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are lovely words, and in another setting they would be the gospel's own invitation: be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:20). But in Eliphaz's mouth the order is reversed: return, and then you will be built up. The gospel's invitation stands on what God has already done: in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them (2 Cor 5:19). And Job has not been disagreeing with God, only with Eliphaz about God. He has already done what Eliphaz demands: I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food (23:12). In the end God will say which of them agreed with him (42:7).

The Almighty will be your gold. It is true, and beautiful, and Paul lived it: I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8). Job has already lost all his gold. He is about to prove that God is his treasure without it.

verseByVerse.quote: For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows. You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways. For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'; but he saves the lowly. He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will hear you. Every word of this comes true. Job will pray and God will hear, but the prayer God hears will be Job's prayer for Eliphaz.

These are Eliphaz's last words in the book, and a prophecy he does not understand. He means that a repentant Job will be able to rescue other sinners by his prayers. In chapter 42 God, angry with Eliphaz, sends him with seven bulls and seven rams to Job and says, my servant Job shall pray for you ... not to deal with you according to your folly (42:8). The one who was not innocent was Eliphaz. The clean hands were Job's. Eliphaz was delivered through the prayers of the man he had accused.

That is the gospel in a sentence Eliphaz spoke without knowing it. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet 3:18). The guilty are delivered through the clean hands of another, hands that were pierced for them.

22.theology:
When the facts do not fit the friends' system, Eliphaz invents them (vv. 5-9), and God judged the speech false (42:7). Yet his sarcastic question, whether God reproves Job for his fear of God (v. 4), is answered yes by the prologue (1:8-9).

Eliphaz's last words (v. 30) are fulfilled on himself: the one who was not innocent is delivered through Job's intercession (42:8), as the guilty are saved through the clean hands of Christ.
22.examples: Eliphaz is a warning to every comforter. He answers the man his theory needs rather than the man in front of him, and even borrows Job's own words to accuse him. Yet he also speaks the chapter's loveliest line, the Almighty will be your gold, which is true whatever the speaker's motives: God is the treasure that remains when everything else has gone.

23.title: He Knows the Way That I Take
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.<sup>3</sup>Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat!<sup>4</sup>I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments.<sup>5</sup>I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.<sup>6</sup>Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me.<sup>7</sup>There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.<sup>8</sup>"Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him;<sup>9</sup>on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.<sup>10</sup>But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.<sup>11</sup>My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside.<sup>12</sup>I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.<sup>13</sup>But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does.<sup>14</sup>For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.<sup>15</sup>Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him.<sup>16</sup>God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me;<sup>17</sup>yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.
23.overview: If only Job knew where to find God, he would lay out his case, and God would listen and acquit him (vv. 1-7). He cannot find God anywhere, but he knows the way that I take; tried, Job will come out as gold, for he has kept God's way and treasured his words (vv. 8-12). Yet God's unchangeable purpose terrifies him, and still the darkness has not silenced him (vv. 13-17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh, That I Knew Where I Might Find Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job longs to find God and lay out his case, sure now that God would listen (vv. 1-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Job now longs to stand in the court he once feared.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.
verseByVerse.commentary: Today also: nothing has changed. Eliphaz has just accused him of crimes he never committed (22:5-9), and Job does not answer the charges yet. He turns away from Eliphaz altogether. The rest of this chapter is about God: where he is, and what he knows.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat! I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Few prayers in the Bible are more honest. Job does not doubt that God exists. He does not know where to find him. It is what every believer in the dark has longed for: not an explanation from a friend but a hearing from God himself.
