The Christian knows the way Job did not. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us (Heb 10:19-20). I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). There is a road to the seat Job longed for, and it has been opened.

verseByVerse.quote: Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me. There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In chapter 9 Job was sure that God would simply overpower him: How then can I answer him? (9:14). Now he says: no, God would not crush me with his strength. He would listen. Something has changed in Job since chapter 9, and it is not his circumstances. Somewhere between the arbiter, the witness and the Redeemer, he has come to believe that God, if he could only reach him, would be fair.

Acquitted forever by my judge. That is the verdict every believer has in Christ: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). Job hoped for it through his own innocence. We receive it through another's.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — He Knows the Way That I Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job cannot find God in any direction, but God knows Job's way, and Job has kept God's (vv. 8-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job cannot find God, and God has never lost sight of Job. The fire is a refiner's, and he will come out as gold.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
East, west, north, south, and God is nowhere to be found. Job knows God is at work, when he is working, but he cannot see him. This is the hiddenness of God in suffering, and many of God's people have lived through seasons exactly like it.

Set it beside Psalm 139. There the psalmist tries every direction too, and cannot get away from God: If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! (Ps 139:8). Job said he would make my bed in darkness in the grave (17:13); the psalm answers that God is there too. The God Job cannot find is the God no one can get away from. Hidden is not the same as absent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I cannot find him, but he knows the way that I take. Job has lost sight of God; God has not lost sight of Job. It is the first psalm's promise: the LORD knows the way of the righteous (Ps 1:6). The believer who cannot find God in the dark is still completely known.

When he has tried me, I shall come out as gold. Job has spoken of testing before: God would test him every moment (7:18), and there it was a complaint. Now he sees that it is a refiner's fire, not an executioner's. Gold is put into the furnace to take out what is not gold; what comes out is purer than what went in. Eliphaz had promised that the Almighty will be your gold (22:25) if Job repented; Job answers that he will come out as gold because God is testing him, not punishing him. Malachi pictures the Lord who will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (Mal 3:3), and Peter writes to suffering Christians of the tested genuineness of your faith — more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Pet 1:7). Job came out as gold. So will every believer whose faith is in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside. I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is not boasting. It is the testimony God himself gave of Job (1:8). And the last line answers Eliphaz, who told him to receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart (22:22): Job already has, more than his daily bread.

That is exactly the answer Jesus gave when he was tested, hungry, in the wilderness: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4). My food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34). Job held on to God's word when he had nothing else. Christ held on to it when he could have had everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — What He Desires, That He Does
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will complete what he has appointed, and Job is terrified (vv. 13-16), yet he goes on speaking in the dark (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereignty frightens Job, and it is also the ground of his hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does. For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the fear returns: what God has decided, he will do. The psalm says it as praise: Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (Ps 115:3). Job says it with a shiver. Whatever God has appointed for him, God will carry through to the end, and Job does not know what that is.

The Christian hears the same truth and is steadied by it, because he knows what God has appointed: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil 1:6). The God who will complete what he appoints is exactly the God you want if what he has appointed is your salvation. Job could not yet see that it was his gold, not his ruin, that God was completing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him. God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me; yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trust in verse 10 and terror in verse 15, in the same man and the same speech: real faith under pressure is not a steady glow but swings between confidence and dread.

Yet I am not silenced because of the darkness. He goes on praying, arguing, hoping, into the dark. Isaiah gives the word for such a person: Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isa 50:10). That is what Job is doing, and it is what anyone in his darkness may do. A believer who can only keep talking to God, without feeling anything, is still walking by faith. Christ himself prayed in the dark of Gethsemane and on the cross, and the Father heard him (Heb 5:7).

23.theology: God may be hidden from the sufferer but is never absent (vv. 8-10), and trials are a refiner's fire from which faith comes out as gold (v. 10). The same unchangeable will that terrifies Job (vv. 13-16) is the believer's assurance, for what God has appointed he will complete. And the way to the seat Job longed for has been opened in Christ (Heb 10:19-22).
23.examples: This chapter has been a lifeline for believers who feel God has gone silent. It gives them words for the longing (Oh, that I knew where I might find him), a reason to hold on when they cannot see him (he knows the way that I take), and permission to keep praying when they feel nothing (yet I am not silenced because of the darkness).

24.title: Why Are Not Times of Judgment Kept?
24.text: <sup>1</sup>"Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?<sup>2</sup>Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them.<sup>3</sup>They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge.<sup>4</sup>They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.<sup>5</sup>Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children.<sup>6</sup>They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man.<sup>7</sup>They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.<sup>8</sup>They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.<sup>9</sup>(There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor.)<sup>10</sup>They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves;<sup>11</sup>among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst.<sup>12</sup>From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.<sup>13</sup>"There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths.<sup>14</sup>The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief.<sup>15</sup>The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me'; and he veils his face.<sup>16</sup>In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light.<sup>17</sup>For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.<sup>18</sup>"You say, 'Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards.<sup>19</sup>Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned.<sup>20</sup>The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.'<sup>21</sup>"They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow.<sup>22</sup>Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life.<sup>23</sup>He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways.<sup>24</sup>They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain.<sup>25</sup>If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say?"
24.overview: Job asks why the Almighty does not keep times of judgment. The strong rob orphans and widows, and the poor go naked and hungry, yet God charges no one with wrong (vv. 1-12). Murderers, adulterers and burglars love the dark (vv. 13-17). The ESV takes vv. 18-20 as the friends' view that the wicked are swept away; Job answers that God lets the mighty stand a while and then cuts them off like heads of grain, and challenges anyone to prove him a liar (vv. 18-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Why Are Not Times of Judgment Kept?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job asks why God does not hold court (v. 1), and sets out what the strong do to the poor while God seems to charge no one with wrong (vv. 2-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's question widens from his own suffering to the suffering of the poor. He is asking what the prophets and James will ask: when will God judge?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 23 was about Job's own case. Now he looks beyond himself. Why does God not hold court on fixed days, like a king, and put things right? Why do the people who know God live and die without ever seeing him act? It is not only a sufferer's question; it is the question of every believer who reads the news. Where is the day of the Lord?

The New Testament gives two answers, and holds them together. The delay is mercy: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Pet 3:9). And the day is fixed: he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed (Acts 17:31). The times of judgment are kept. They are kept on God's calendar, and the Judge has already been named and raised from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them. They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge. They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary: Job lists the crimes of the strong against the weak. They shift the boundary stone to steal a neighbour's land, which the law cursed (Deut 27:17). They drive off an orphan's only donkey, and take a widow's ox as security for a debt when the law forbade even taking her cloak (Deut 24:17). They shove the poor off the road until they hide. These are the very sins Eliphaz accused Job of (22:6-9). Job has not done them. He has seen them done, and he is asking why God lets them go on.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children. They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man. They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold. They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the answer to Eliphaz. He said Job had stripped the naked of their clothing (22:6). Here is Job describing the naked poor: scavenging in the wilderness like wild animals to feed their children, picking over the leftovers in a rich man's vineyard, lying all night without a blanket, soaked by mountain storms, pressing themselves against a rock for shelter. No man who had done this to them could describe them like this. It is written with compassion, from a heart that has looked at them.

Hebrews describes God's faithful people in almost the same terms: destitute, afflicted, mistreated — of whom the world was not worthy — wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth (Heb 11:37-38). The poor on the mountainside are not forgotten by God, even when they seem to be.

verseByVerse.quote: (There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor.) They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves; among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst. From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A baby taken from its mother's arms as security for a debt; men carrying armfuls of grain while they starve, pressing olive oil they will never taste, treading grapes with parched throats. Even an ox was not to be muzzled while it threshed (1 Cor 9:9). James, the New Testament writer who holds Job up to the church, writes in the same chapter: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts (James 5:4). Job heard those cries. So does God.

Charges no one with wrong uses the very word of the prologue: In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong (1:22). Now he complains that God does not charge the oppressors with wrong. It is the complaint of a man who still believes God is just, and cannot see the justice being done. God will answer it, not with a timetable, but with himself (chs 38-41).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Those Who Rebel Against the Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some rebel against the light: the murderer, the adulterer and the burglar all work in the dark (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Evil loves the dark because it thinks the dark hides it. It does not (Ps 139:12; John 3:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: "There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths. The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief. The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me'; and he veils his face. In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light. For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job turns from the oppressor in daylight to the criminal who rebels against the light (v. 13).

The killer is out before dawn; the adulterer waits for dusk, as in Proverbs, in the twilight, in the evening (Prov 7:9); the burglar tunnels through a mud-brick wall at night, the picture Jesus used for thieves who break in (Matt 6:19).

For them the night is the working day. Jesus said it exactly: people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19). And they are wrong that no eye will see: even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day (Ps 139:12).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked are swept away (vv. 18-20), but only when God's harvest comes (vv. 21-24). Job dares the friends to prove him wrong (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The wicked do fall at last, but on God's schedule and not the friends'.

verseByVerse.quote: "You say, 'Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards. Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned. The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.'
verseByVerse.commentary: These verses are one of the hard places in the book, and the reader should know why. They sound like the friends: the wicked swept away like debris on a flood, their fields cursed, swallowed by the grave as melting snow is swallowed by the heat, forgotten, broken like a tree. The Hebrew has no You say; the ESV has added it, taking these lines as Job quoting the friends' view before he answers it. Other readers think Job himself is saying that the wicked do come to a bad end in the end, which he never denied. Others think a piece of one of the friends' speeches has been misplaced here. The first two readings come to the same place: the wicked do perish, but not on the friends' timetable, and not in a way that lets anyone read a man's guilt from his troubles.

verseByVerse.quote: "They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow. Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life. He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways. They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain. If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The powerful who prey on the childless and the widow are kept alive by God's power; when they seem to be dying, they recover. His eyes are upon their ways: God is watching them, as he is watching Job (23:10). He is not blind. He is patient.

Cut off like the heads of grain: in the end they die like everyone else, like ears of wheat at harvest. That is Job's real answer to his own question in verse 1. Judgment comes; it comes at harvest.

Jesus told a parable that fits this chapter exactly. A man's field was sown with weeds by an enemy, and his servants wanted to pull them up at once. No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest (Matt 13:29-30). That is why the times of judgment seem not to be kept. God is protecting the wheat. The harvest is certain.

If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say? Job's challenge to the friends: prove me wrong. They cannot. Bildad will try, with six verses (ch 25), and then the friends fall silent for good.

24.theology: The delay of judgment is God's patience, and the day is fixed and the Judge named (2 Pet 3:9; Acts 17:31). Until then God lets the wheat and the weeds grow together (Matt 13:30). Job's complaint is the complaint of a man who still believes God is just and cannot yet see the justice being done.
24.examples: Job's portrait of the poor clinging to the rock in the rain is the best answer to Eliphaz's charge: no one who had stripped them could describe them with such compassion. It also gives every believer who reads the news a prayer to pray, Why are not times of judgment kept?, and the parable of the wheat and weeds to hold on to while waiting for the answer.

25.title: How Can Man Be in the Right Before God?
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven.<sup>3</sup>Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?<sup>4</sup>How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?<sup>5</sup>Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes;<sup>6</sup>how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!"
25.overview: In his last and shortest speech Bildad praises God's dominion, then asks how man, a mere maggot, can be right before God. The friends never speak again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Man, Who Is a Maggot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad praises God's dominion (vv. 1-3) and asks how man, a mere maggot, can be right before him (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The friends' last words ask the right question, but ask it to crush, and offer no answer. God gives the answer, and calls his people worms in order to call himself their Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven. Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the last time any of the friends speaks. Bildad manages six verses, Zophar none, and the cycle that began so confidently in chapter 4 has run out of breath. Some scholars think the third round was disturbed in copying and parts of chapters 26-27 were once Bildad's and Zophar's; possibly, but as the text stands the friends simply run out of words. The LORD's verdict on everything they said still stands: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7).

What Bildad does say is true. He makes peace in his high heaven: Bildad means he keeps the heavenly powers in order. The New Testament hears a deeper peace in those words. God was pleased through Christ to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross (Col 1:20). The God who makes peace in heaven made it on earth, at a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz's night visitor asked the great question (4:17), Job asked it (9:2), and now it is the friends' last question. It is the right question, the question every human being must face before a holy God. And Bildad has no answer. He asks it to shut Job's mouth, and leaves it hanging.

The book of Job does not answer it either, not in so many words. The answer came later, and it came in a person. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom 3:23-24). Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Rom 5:1). The question Bildad used as a club, the gospel answers as good news.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes; how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the moon and stars look dim beside God's holiness, what is a human being? A maggot. A worm. Bildad's last word on man is contempt, and he says it to a man whose sores are full of worms (7:5).

But Scripture uses the same word in two places that change everything. God himself calls his people worms, and says it tenderly: Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 41:14). The same God who sees how small we are calls himself our Redeemer, the word of Job's great confession (19:25). And in the psalm the cross fulfilled, the sufferer says of himself, But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people (Ps 22:6). Bildad called man a worm to crush him. The Son of Man became the worm, scorned and despised, to lift us. God's last word is redemption.

25.theology: The friends' debate collapses. Their last question, how man can be right before God (v. 4), is the right one, and they cannot answer it; the gospel does (Rom 3:23-24; 5:1). Bildad calls man a worm in contempt (v. 6), but God uses the same word tenderly of his people, and the sufferer of Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, takes it on himself.
25.examples: Bildad shows how a true doctrine can be used as a club. Human smallness before a holy God is real, but he says it with contempt, to a man whose sores are full of worms. Scripture says the same truth with tenderness, and anyone who speaks to sufferers should learn to say it that way.

26.title: The Outskirts of His Ways
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength!<sup>3</sup>How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge!<sup>4</sup>With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?<sup>5</sup>The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants.<sup>6</sup>Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.<sup>7</sup>He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing.<sup>8</sup>He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them.<sup>9</sup>He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud.<sup>10</sup>He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.<sup>11</sup>The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke.<sup>12</sup>By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab.<sup>13</sup>By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.<sup>14</sup>Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?"
26.overview: Job mocks Bildad's help (vv. 1-4), then praises God's power over the dead, the earth, the clouds and the sea, and ends: these are but the outskirts of his ways (vv. 5-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — How You Have Helped Him Who Has No Power!
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job mocks the help Bildad has given him (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Job answers the friends' last speech with sarcasm. Six verses about worms have helped no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength! How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge! With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad's six verses told Job he was a maggot. Job's reply drips with sarcasm: what a help you have been to the weak! He is the man with no power and, in their eyes, no wisdom; they came to strengthen him and have told him he is a worm.

Whose breath has come out from you? Not God's; perhaps the spirit that glided past Eliphaz's face in the night (4:15). A counsellor should ask himself Job's question before he speaks: whose breath is this? Am I speaking God's word, or only my own certainty?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — He Hangs the Earth on Nothing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job praises God's power over the dead, the earth, the clouds and the sea (vv. 5-13), and calls it all only the outskirts of his ways (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Job outdoes the friends in praising God's power, and ends where all theology must: we have heard only a whisper.

verseByVerse.quote: The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants. Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dead, the shades below the waters, tremble before God. Sheol is the grave; Abaddon means destruction, the place of ruin. Neither is hidden from him. Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! (Prov 15:11).

Hebrews says the same of every one of us: no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13). For the friends that is a threat. For Job it is a hope. If even the grave is naked before God, then Job's innocence is not hidden from him either.

verseByVerse.quote: He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing. He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them. He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud. He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ancient world usually pictured the earth resting on pillars or on the back of something. Job says God hangs it on nothing. It is poetry, not a science lesson, but the point is exact: nothing holds the world up except God. The New Testament names the one who does it: the Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Heb 1:3); in him all things hold together (Col 1:17). The same hands that hold up the earth hold up the believer who has nothing left under him.

The cloud is not split open under them: tons of water carried in a cloud that does not burst; the moon veiled; the horizon drawn like a compass line where sea meets sky, the edge of day and night. Wisdom says it too: when he drew a circle on the face of the deep (Prov 8:27). Everything Job points to is ordinary and astonishing at once.

verseByVerse.quote: The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke. By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab. By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mountains that seem to hold up the sky shake when he rebukes them. He calmed the raging sea. Rahab is the sea monster of 9:13, and the fleeing serpent is Leviathan, whom Isaiah calls Leviathan the fleeing serpent (Isa 27:1), the monster Job once wanted roused against his birthday (3:8). The powers of chaos are nothing to God. His wind clears the sky after the storm.

Then read the Gospel. A storm on the lake, the boat filling with water, and Jesus asleep. And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm (Mark 4:39). The disciples asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41). Job has told us. Only God stills the sea. The man in the boat was God.

Does the Bible endorse pagan myths of sea monsters? Job borrows the imagery of the nations’ stories, in which the gods fought chaos monsters, to say that the true God rules what the nations feared; there is no battle and no rival. Rahab is also a poetic name for Egypt (Ps 87:4; Isa 30:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all that, Job says: this is only the edge. The underworld, the sky, the sea, the stars: all of it is the fringe of God's garment, the outskirts of his ways, a faint whisper of who he is. If this is the whisper, who could stand the thunder?

This verse judges every neat explanation of suffering, the friends' and ours. They thought they had God's ways mapped: sin brings trouble, righteousness brings blessing, and Job's case can be read off the chart. Job says: we have heard a whisper. Paul says the same of the Christian's knowledge now: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Cor 13:12). Humility is not a lack of faith; it is faith that knows how big God is.

And the thunder is coming. In twelve chapters the LORD will answer Job out of the whirlwind (38:1), and Job will hear more than a whisper. It will not explain his suffering. It will show him God.

26.theology: The God who holds up the world with nothing beneath it and stills the sea by his rebuke is the God made known in the Son, who upholds the universe and calmed the storm on the lake. Yet all that can be seen of him is the outskirts of his ways (v. 14), and no theology, the friends' or ours, has him mapped.
26.examples: Job's question to Bildad, Whose breath has come out from you?, is one every preacher and counsellor can ask before speaking. And the picture of the earth hung on nothing comforts anyone who feels there is nothing left under them: the same hands hold them up.

27.title: I Will Not Put Away My Integrity
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And Job again took up his discourse, and said:<sup>2</sup>"As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter,<sup>3</sup>as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,<sup>4</sup>my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.<sup>5</sup>Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me.<sup>6</sup>I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.<sup>7</sup>"Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous.<sup>8</sup>For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?<sup>9</sup>Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?<sup>10</sup>Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?<sup>11</sup>I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal.<sup>12</sup>Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?<sup>13</sup>"This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty:<sup>14</sup>If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread.<sup>15</sup>Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep.<sup>16</sup>Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay,<sup>17</sup>he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver.<sup>18</sup>He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes.<sup>19</sup>He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone.<sup>20</sup>Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off.<sup>21</sup>The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place.<sup>22</sup>It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight.<sup>23</sup>It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.
27.overview: With the friends silent, Job swears by the God who has taken away his right that he will not speak falsehood or put away his integrity (vv. 1-6). Let his accusers be as the wicked, who have no hope when God takes their life (vv. 7-12). This is the portion of the wicked: children for the sword, wealth gone overnight, swept away by the east wind (vv. 13-23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — I Will Not Put Away My Integrity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job swears that he will not put away his integrity (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job swears by the God he is protesting to.

verseByVerse.quote: And Job again took up his discourse, and said:
verseByVerse.commentary: It would be Zophar's turn, and Zophar says nothing. So Job speaks again, and a new heading marks the change: he took up his discourse. From here to chapter 31, with the great poem on wisdom in the middle, Job speaks alone. What follows is his closing statement.

verseByVerse.quote: "As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter, as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swears an oath, and he swears it by God. As God lives was the most solemn oath there was. And he swears by the God who has taken away my right, who has made my soul bitter. Job is protesting against God and swearing by him in the same breath. That is the way for every sufferer: bring the complaint to God, not away from him.

Those words have been heard before, in the mouth of a widow who came home from Moab with nothing: call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me (Ruth 1:20). And Naomi's story ends with a kinsman-redeemer, a go'el, the very word of Job's great confession (19:25). Both were being led, without knowing it, to a redeemer.

As long as my breath is in me: every breath he uses to speak is God's gift (12:10), and he will not use it to lie. As at the beginning, Job did not sin with his lips (2:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me. I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the answer to a question asked in chapter 2. God said, He still holds fast his integrity (2:3). Job's wife said, Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die (2:9). Now Job answers, on oath, with the same word and the same verb: I will not put away my integrity ... I hold fast my righteousness. A false confession would end the argument, and he will not tell that lie. That is what God saw in him from the start.

My heart does not reproach me. John writes, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God (1 John 3:21). But Paul adds a caution every believer needs: I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me (1 Cor 4:4). A clear conscience is a gift; it is not the final verdict. The believer's confidence before the Judge rests on another's record: not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ (Phil 3:9). Job's defence of his innocence is true, and it will be vindicated (42:7). But Elihu will accuse him of justifying himself rather than God (32:2), and God will ask him, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8). Holding fast to one's integrity is right. Using it to put God in the wrong is not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Let My Enemy Be as the Wicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job turns the friends' doctrine on his accusers and offers to teach them (vv. 7-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job does not deny that God judges the wicked. He denies that he is one.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous. For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life? Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let my enemy be as the wicked: Job turns the friends' doctrine on them. They have risen up against him like false witnesses, and the law said a false witness should receive what he meant for his brother (Deut 19:18-19).

What is the hope of the godless? Every one of these questions is a quiet claim about Job. He has hope (19:25); he cries to God and expects to be heard (23:3-7); Eliphaz told him to delight yourself in the Almighty (22:26), and he has never stopped calling on God. That is not how a godless man behaves.

verseByVerse.quote: I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal. Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?
verseByVerse.commentary: Job will teach the teachers. They have seen the same world he has, the wicked prospering and the righteous suffering. Why then have they filled the air with vapour, empty talk (21:34)? Their answers do not fit what their own eyes have seen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Portion of a Wicked Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job describes the portion of the wicked man at God's hands (vv. 13-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Job holds the same truth about the wicked as the friends; he refuses their use of it against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty: If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread. Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These words are almost exactly Zophar's last line (20:29), and the paragraph that follows sounds like the friends: the wicked man's children fall by the sword, his survivors die of plague, his widows do not mourn him. Some readers think this is Zophar's missing third speech, misplaced in the copying of the book. Others think Job is quoting the friends' doctrine back to them. But the text gives it to Job, and it fits what he has just said: let my enemy be as the wicked (v. 7). Job has never denied that God judges the wicked. He has denied that everyone who suffers is wicked. He believes this portion is real, and he warns the men who have falsely accused him that it is theirs to fear.

If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword. It is hard to read these words from a man whose children are dead. Job does not turn them round and apply them to himself. That was the friends' mistake: reading the harvest back into the seed.

Is Job now contradicting chapter 21, where he said the wicked often prosper and die in peace? In chapter 21 he spoke of this life; here he speaks of their end, when God settles accounts. Both are true, and Psalm 73 holds them together: the wicked prosper, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay, he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver. He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes. He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The innocent will divide the silver. The sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22). Job himself will one day be given money and gold by those who come to him (42:11).

Like a moth's cocoon, a watchman's shelter of branches in a vineyard: flimsy things that vanish in a season. The rich man goes to sleep secure and wakes up with nothing, like the man in Jesus' parable who heard, This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off. The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place. It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight. It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of the wicked is a storm in the night: the hot east wind from the desert picks him up and throws him away, and then claps its hands and hisses at him, the gesture of derision passers-by made at ruined Jerusalem (Lam 2:15). A great wind took Job's children (1:19), and the friends drew their conclusion. Job says: the storm that sweeps away the wicked is real, and it is God's; but not every man a storm has struck is wicked.

The difference between Job and the wicked man is not what has happened to them. It is where their hope is. The wicked man's hope ends when God takes his life (v. 8). Job's does not: I know that my Redeemer lives.

27.theology: Job holds fast his integrity and will not buy peace with a false confession. Yet a clear conscience is a gift, not the final verdict: God will vindicate Job's honesty and also correct his self-justification. Job affirms the judgment of the wicked while denying that suffering proves wickedness, and the difference between him and the wicked lies in where their hope is when God takes a man's life.
27.examples: Job shows a sufferer how to complain rightly: he protests to God and swears by him in the same breath, bringing the bitterness to God rather than away from him, as Naomi did. And he shows a costly honesty: he would rather go on suffering than make a false confession to end the argument.

28.title: Where Shall Wisdom Be Found?
28.text: <sup>1</sup>"Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine.<sup>2</sup>Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.<sup>3</sup>Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness.<sup>4</sup>He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro.<sup>5</sup>As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire.<sup>6</sup>Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.<sup>7</sup>"That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it.<sup>8</sup>The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.<sup>9</sup>"Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots.<sup>10</sup>He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing.<sup>11</sup>He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.<sup>12</sup>"But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?<sup>13</sup>Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.<sup>14</sup>The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'<sup>15</sup>It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price.<sup>16</sup>It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.<sup>17</sup>Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold.<sup>18</sup>No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls.<sup>19</sup>The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.<sup>20</sup>"From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding?<sup>21</sup>It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air.<sup>22</sup>Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.'<sup>23</sup>"God understands the way to it, and he knows its place.<sup>24</sup>For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.<sup>25</sup>When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure,<sup>26</sup>when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder,<sup>27</sup>then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.<sup>28</sup>And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'"
28.overview: Men know where to mine silver and gold; they sink shafts into darkness where no hawk or lion has been, and bring hidden things to light (vv. 1-11). But where shall wisdom be found? Not in the deep or the sea; no jewel can buy it; even Death has only heard a rumour of it (vv. 12-22). God alone knows its place, and he said to man, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom (vv. 23-28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men know how to get silver and gold out of the dark heart of a mountain (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Human beings can get treasure out of the heart of a mountain. The poem admires it, and is about to ask what they cannot get.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine. Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After twenty-five chapters of argument, the voice changes. There is no accusation in this chapter, no complaint, no raised voice. It is a quiet poem, and it asks the question underneath the whole debate: where is wisdom?

Who speaks it? The chapter runs straight on from Job's discourse (27:1), and the ESV sets it as his. But its calm is so unlike the speeches around it, and chapter 29 begins again with And Job again took up his discourse (29:1), that many readers take it as the author's own interlude, a pause between the debate and Job's last defence. Either way, it stands in the middle of the book like a hinge. Everything before it has been men claiming wisdom. Everything after it will lead to God speaking.

It begins underground. Men know where treasure is, and how to get it out.
verseByVerse.note: The poem pictures ancient mining: men tunnelling for silver, gold and gems.

verseByVerse.quote: Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness. He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The miner carries his lamp into gloom and deep darkness, the very words Job called down on his birthday (3:5). Here men go into that darkness on purpose, looking for something precious. The verb matters: he searches out the ore. It is the word the poem will use at the end, where God searched ... out wisdom (v. 27). Man can search out silver to the end of the seam. Only God can search out wisdom.

They hang in the air: shafts sunk in lonely valleys, and the miners let down on ropes, swinging in the dark, far from anyone. Human beings will risk their lives for silver.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire. Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary: On the surface, a quiet wheat field. Underneath, men are breaking the rock with fire, splitting it open to reach the sapphire and the gold dust. The same ground feeds us on top and hides treasure below, and man has learned to get at both. Job once said the suffering dig for death more than for hidden treasures (3:21). This poem goes down into the same mines, and asks what is more precious than any of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it. The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hawk sees a mouse from the sky and has never seen a mine. The lion goes anywhere it likes and has never walked these tunnels. Man goes where the sharpest-eyed bird and the boldest beast cannot. Wisdom will be concealed from the birds of the air too (v. 21), and it will be hidden from the miner.

The proud beasts is literally "the sons of pride", a phrase found only once more, where God ends his description of Leviathan: he is king over all the sons of pride (41:34). The proud creatures that never found the miner's path are the creatures God will parade before Job, and he is their Master.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots. He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing. He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flint, mountains, channels cut through stone, underground streams dammed so the miners can work: there seems to be nothing man cannot do with the earth. The thing that is hidden he brings out to light. Job said that about God: He uncovers the deeps out of darkness (12:22). Man can do something like it with rock and ore.

The eyes in this poem tell the story. Man's eye sees every precious thing in the rock (v. 10). Wisdom is hidden from the eyes of all living (v. 21). And God sees everything under the heavens (v. 24). Human sight reaches the sapphire and stops. Only God's reaches wisdom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — Where Shall Wisdom Be Found?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom cannot be found anywhere in creation, or bought at any price (vv. 12-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing that matters most cannot be dug up or bought. It has to be given.

verseByVerse.quote: "But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the question, and the whole book has been asking it. The friends thought they had found wisdom: in visions (4:12), in the fathers (8:8), in their own long experience (15:10). Job has searched for it too, and for God. Men can find silver in a mountain. Where can they find the wisdom to understand God's ways with a suffering man?

Not found in the land of the living: we do not even know what it would cost. The question will be asked again in almost the same words (v. 20), like a refrain.

verseByVerse.quote: The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The poem sends the question to the deepest places the ancient world knew, the places no miner could reach, and they answer: not here. Wisdom is not a matter of digging deeper.

verseByVerse.quote: It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price. It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If it cannot be dug up, can it be bought? No. Silver was weighed out on scales in a sale; there is not enough silver in the world for this. The gold of Ophir was the finest gold there was. Onyx and sapphire, the treasures the miners risked their lives for (v. 6), are worthless as payment.

Eliphaz had told Job to throw his gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed, and God would be his gold (22:24-25). He was right that God is more precious than Ophir's gold. The poem adds what Eliphaz forgot: so is wisdom, and Eliphaz did not have it either.
verseByVerse.note: “Sapphire” may be lapis lazuli (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls. The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glass was a luxury in that world, as precious as jewellery. Coral from the sea, rock crystal, pearls, topaz from far-off Cush: the poem piles up the whole jeweller's window and says, do not even mention them. Proverbs says the same: She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her (Prov 3:15).

Jesus told of a man who found something more precious than everything he had: on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it (Matt 13:46). The parable is about the kingdom, not this poem, but it prizes the same way: what matters most is worth more than everything else. The friends had plenty of learning. They did not have this.

verseByVerse.quote: "From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air. Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From where, then, does wisdom come? The refrain again: hidden from every living eye, even the falcon's (v. 7).

We have heard a rumor of it. The poem goes below the sea, to Destruction and Death themselves, the places Job said lie naked before God (26:6). Death knows many secrets, and not this one. Not the living, not the dead, not the deep, not the sky: no one in all creation holds it. There is only one place left to look.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — The Fear of the Lord, That Is Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God alone knows wisdom's place, and he has told man what wisdom is for him (vv. 23-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom belongs to God, and man's share in it is to fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "God understands the way to it, and he knows its place. For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is not lost; it is with God. He knows the road to it and where it lives, because he sees everything, to the ends of the earth. What man cannot find by digging, God has always known.

This is the book's turning point. The friends spoke as if they had wisdom and could apply it to Job's case. Job spoke as if he could summon God and argue it. Both were looking for wisdom in the wrong place, in themselves. It belongs to God. Any wisdom a human being will ever have must come from him, as a gift. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him (James 1:5), written by the apostle who holds Job up to the church.

verseByVerse.quote: When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure, when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder, then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God made the world he weighed the wind, measured out the seas, gave the rain its law and the lightning its path. And at that moment, the poem says, he looked at wisdom, spoke it, set it in place. Wisdom is the pattern God built into creation. Proverbs pictures Wisdom present at the making of the world, a poetic figure rather than a second person beside God: The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old (Prov 8:22). Yet the New Testament gives the wisdom by which God made the world a name and a face: In the beginning was the Word ... All things were made through him (John 1:1, 3). The wisdom by which God made the world is the Son by whom he made it.

God's wisdom is measuring. He gives weight even to the wind, which seems to weigh nothing: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand ... and weighed the mountains in scales? (Isa 40:12). A God who weighs the wind has weighed Job's trouble too, to the ounce. Job asked for his calamity to be laid in the balances (6:2). It had been, by the only one who could.

Two words here reach across the book. A way for the lightning of the thunder is the same Hebrew phrase God himself will use when he speaks from the whirlwind, a way for the thunderbolt (38:25). The poem is pointing ahead: when God speaks, he will speak about exactly this. And searched it out is Eliphaz's proud word, this we have searched out; it is true (5:27), and Bildad's, what the fathers have searched out (8:8). They claimed to have searched it out. Only God has.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the mines, the jewels, the deep and death itself, the answer is short. Man cannot possess God's wisdom. But God has told man what wisdom looks like for him: to fear the Lord, and to turn from evil. Not to understand everything, but to reverence the one who does, and to live accordingly. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Ps 111:10; cf. Prov 1:7). It is the only place in the book where God is called the Lord in the sense of Master, and it is fitting: wisdom begins with knowing who is Master.

Turn back to the first verse of the book. That man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil (1:1). By the definition God gives here, Job was the wise man all along: not the three wise men from Teman, Shuah and Naamah with their visions and traditions, but the man on the ash heap who feared God and would not let go of him. Jesus thanked his Father that he had hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children (Matt 11:25).

And the New Testament tells us where the hidden treasure finally is. The miners dig for treasure and cannot find wisdom; Paul points to Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3). Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). The wisdom no one could dig out of the earth came down to it, in a person. To fear the Lord now is to trust the Son in whom God has given that wisdom, and who is himself our righteousness and redemption; and the Spirit who rested on him, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD (Isa 11:2), now works that fear in his people.

What does this mean for someone in Job's place? The fear of the Lord is not terror; it is the reverent trust of a creature who knows God is God. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence (Prov 14:26). It is not an explanation of suffering, and the poem does not pretend it is. It is a way of living when there is no explanation: hold God in awe, keep turning from evil, and leave the understanding with him. That is exactly what Job did on the first day of his troubles, before any friend had spoken, when he fell on the ground and worshiped (1:20). He did not understand then either. He was wise.

28.theology: Wisdom belongs to God alone: man cannot dig it out or buy it, and only God has searched it out (v. 27). Man's share in it is to fear the Lord and turn from evil (v. 28), which makes the man on the ash heap the wise man of the book. Its hidden treasures are in Christ, and God gives wisdom to those who ask.
28.examples: The poem's pictures stay in the mind: miners swinging on ropes in the dark where no hawk has looked, a wheat field on the surface and fire in the rock beneath, and Death admitting it has only heard a rumour of wisdom. Each says the same thing. Our cleverness reaches a long way, but the wisdom to live well before God is something we receive, not something we dig out.

29.title: Oh, That I Were as in the Months of Old
29.text: <sup>1</sup>And Job again took up his discourse, and said:<sup>2</sup>"Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me,<sup>3</sup>when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,<sup>4</sup>as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent,<sup>5</sup>when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me,<sup>6</sup>when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!<sup>7</sup>When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square,<sup>8</sup>the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood;<sup>9</sup>the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth;<sup>10</sup>the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.<sup>11</sup>When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved,<sup>12</sup>because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him.<sup>13</sup>The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.<sup>14</sup>I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban.<sup>15</sup>I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.<sup>16</sup>I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know.<sup>17</sup>I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.<sup>18</sup>Then I thought, 'I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand,<sup>19</sup>my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches,<sup>20</sup>my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.'<sup>21</sup>"Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel.<sup>22</sup>After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them.<sup>23</sup>They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain.<sup>24</sup>I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down.<sup>25</sup>I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.
29.overview: Job longs for the months when God watched over him and his children were around him (vv. 1-6). At the city gate all honoured him, because he delivered the poor and the fatherless, wore righteousness like a robe and was eyes to the blind (vv. 7-17). He expected to die old in his nest; men waited for his words like rain, and he comforted mourners (vv. 18-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Days When God Watched Over Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job longs for the months when God watched over him (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: What Job misses most is not his wealth but God's nearness, and his children.

verseByVerse.quote: And Job again took up his discourse, and said: "Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job's closing defence runs through three chapters. In this one he looks back, in the next he looks at the present, and in chapter 31 he swears his innocence before God. It begins with longing: if only it were like it used to be.

What he misses first is not his flocks. The days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head. The words sound like the blessing Israel's priests pronounced: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Num 6:24-25). Job had lived under that blessing: kept, and shone upon. And with God's lamp over him he could walk through dark places unafraid. For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness (Ps 18:28).

Many believers know this ache: the memory of a season when God seemed close, set against a present in which he seems far. Job does not pretend the memory is not there. But the reader knows something Job does not: God has not stopped watching over him. The limit set in heaven, only spare his life (2:6), is God's watch still being kept.

verseByVerse.quote: as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent, when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me, when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friendship of God is a striking phrase, and the Hebrew is exactly the phrase Eliphaz used when he mocked Job for thinking he had listened in the council of God (15:8). Job says: I had God's friendship once, over my own tent. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him (Ps 25:14). Jesus gives it to his disciples: I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15).

When my children were all around me. It is the line that hurts most. Your children will be like olive shoots around your table (Ps 128:3), and his were, and they are gone. Then the abundance: paths so rich they seemed washed in butter, oil flowing from the rock (Deut 32:13). His life overflowed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — I Was Eyes to the Blind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole city honoured him (vv. 7-10), because he was a champion of the poor (vv. 11-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Every charge Eliphaz invented is answered by the life Job actually lived. It is a portrait of the King the psalms long for, and Christ is.

verseByVerse.quote: When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square, the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood; the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth; the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city gate was the court, the council chamber and the town square of an ancient city, where the elders sat to judge and decide. When Job came, the young men stepped back respectfully, the old men got to their feet, and even princes stopped talking. Compare 19:18: now children jeer when he tries to stand.

Laid their hand on their mouth. The great men of the city did before Job what Job will do before God. When the LORD has spoken from the whirlwind, Job will say, I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4). Respect for a man silences the princes. The glory of God silences the man.
verseByVerse.note: Elders sat in the city gate to judge cases.

verseByVerse.quote: When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved, because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him. The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why did they honour him? Not for his money. Because he rescued the poor who cried out and the orphan who had no one. Dying men blessed him; widows sang because of him. This is the answer to Eliphaz, who said Job sent widows away empty and crushed the fatherless (22:9). Job does not argue the charge. He describes his life, and the life answers it.

Is this boasting? Job is answering false charges with the truth, as Paul answers his critics (2 Cor 11). His good deeds are not his ground of acceptance with God; the danger lies in the use he will make of them, to put God in the wrong (40:8).

verseByVerse.quote: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban. I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know. I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness was what he wore every day, as a judge wears his robe. He was the eyes of the blind man, the feet of the lame; he was a father to the destitute. And I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know: when a stranger's case came before him, he investigated it properly. Searched out is the verb Eliphaz used for his confident conclusions (5:27). Job used it for the hard work of finding out the truth about a stranger, which is exactly what the friends never did for him.

This is the picture of the king Israel longed for: he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper ... From oppression and violence he redeems their life (Ps 72:12, 14). It is the picture of God himself, who put on righteousness as a breastplate (Isa 59:17). And it is Christ. When John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one, Jesus answered, the blind receive their sight and the lame walk (Matt 11:5). Job was eyes to the blind. Christ gave the blind their own.

I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth. The oppressor is pictured as a wild beast with a victim in its jaws, and Job as the man who wrenched the victim out. It is what the psalmist asks God to do: you break the teeth of the wicked (Ps 3:7). Job's justice was God's justice at work through a human judge. That is what earthly authority is for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Like One Who Comforts Mourners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He expected to die old in his nest, a counsellor and comforter to the end (vv. 18-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Job had been the comforter the friends failed to be. The comforter of all who mourn is the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I thought, 'I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand, my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches, my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He expected to die at home, old and surrounded by his family, like a bird in its nest. He pictured himself as a tree with roots in the water and dew on its leaves every night: the blessed man of the first psalm, like a tree planted by streams of water (Ps 1:3). He is not proud to have expected it. Any godly man might have.

And the strange thing is that it came true. After this Job lived 140 years ... And Job died, an old man, and full of days (42:16-17). The tree he thought uprooted (19:10) put down its roots again. But not before he had been through the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel. After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them. They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain. I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down. I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People waited for his advice the way a dry field waits for rain, and when he spoke there was no more to be said. Moses prayed, May my teaching drop as the rain (Deut 32:2). Job's counsel was like that.

When others lost heart, his smile gave them courage. He led like a king, and he was one who comforts mourners.

Then the light of my face. At the start of the chapter God's lamp shone on Job (v. 3). Here Job's face shines on others, the discouraged and frightened. He passed on what he received. That is the believer's calling still: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16).

That is the last line of the chapter, and it is pointed. The friends came to comfort him (2:11). Job had been, for years, the man who comforted mourners, and they could not do for him what he had done for others. The Messiah's mission is described in the same words: the Spirit of the Lord is upon him to bind up the brokenhearted ... to comfort all who mourn (Isa 61:1-2), and Jesus read the opening of that passage in Nazareth and said it was fulfilled in him (Luke 4:18-21). The comforter Job was, Christ is, to everyone who mourns.

29.theology: What Job misses most is God's watching care and friendship (vv. 2-4), though in fact God had not stopped watching (2:6). His past life answers Eliphaz's invented charges and sketches the righteous King who delivers the needy (Ps 72:12-14), the King whom Christ fulfils as the comforter of all who mourn.
29.examples: This chapter gives words to anyone who remembers a better season: a time when God seemed close, the family was whole, and their work did good. Job neither pretends the memory away nor lets it be the last word. And his picture of a life spent as eyes to the blind and feet to the lame is still a pattern for anyone with influence over others.

30.title: But Now They Laugh at Me
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock.<sup>2</sup>What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?<sup>3</sup>Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation;<sup>4</sup>they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food.<sup>5</sup>They are driven out from human company; I stand, and you only look at me.<sup>21</sup>You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me.<sup>22</sup>You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm.<sup>23</sup>For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.<sup>24</sup>"Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help?<sup>25</sup>Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? 30.overview: But now Job is laughed at by young outcasts, driven from society to live in gullies (vv. 1-8). He has become their byword; they spit at him, because God has loosed his cord (vv. 9-15). His soul is poured out; he cries and God does not answer (vv. 16-23). He wept for others, but when he hoped for good evil came, and his lyre is turned to mourning (vv. 24-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — But Now They Laugh at Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Job is laughed at by outcasts (vv. 1-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The man before whom princes fell silent is mocked by outcasts. And the bitterness of it shows in how he speaks of them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock. What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 29 was then. This chapter answers it three times: but now (v. 1), and now (v. 9), and now (v. 16). The man who once sat at the city gate while princes fell silent is laughed at by young men of the lowest kind, men whose fathers he would not have trusted to guard his sheepdogs.

Something has to be said honestly here. These are harsh words, and they do not sit well beside the Job of chapter 29, a father to the needy (29:16), or the Job who described the homeless poor with such compassion (24:5-8). Suffering has done what suffering often does: it has brought pride to the surface. The mockers are cruel, and Job is right that they are. But the contempt in his reply is not the best of him. The one who was mocked by the lowest of men and answered differently is Christ: When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23). Job is a real man, not a plaster saint, and the book lets us see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation; they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food. They are driven out from human company; they shout after them as after a thief. In the gullies of the torrents they must dwell, in holes of the earth and of the rocks. Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together. A senseless, a nameless brood, they have been whipped out of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are outcasts: men driven out of the towns, living in dry wadis and caves, eating salty desert plants and bitter roots, chased off like thieves, huddling in the scrub like animals. They have nothing and no name. And even they look down on Job now. He has fallen below the bottom of society.

Compare the picture with 24:5. There Job described the homeless poor as wild donkeys in the desert, scavenging for their children, and he wrote with tenderness. Here the same kind of men bray among the bushes, and he writes with scorn. The picture is the same; the heart has changed, because now they are mocking him. Every reader should hold that mirror up to himself: how we speak of the poor can change the moment they turn on us.

It is the depth of social disgrace, and the Son of God went there too. The men who spat on him, the passers-by who shook their heads at the cross, the criminal who mocked him as he hung there: he was despised by the despised. He came down further than Job, and he came down on purpose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — I Have Become Their Song
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He has become their byword, because God has loosed his cord (vv. 9-15).
verseByVerse.theology: He is a joke and a song among the lowest of men, as the sufferer of Psalm 69 was, and as Christ was.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them. They abhor me; they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me. Because God has loosed my cord and humbled me, they have cast off restraint in my presence.
