verseByVerse.commentary:
They make up songs about him. The psalm of innocent suffering the New Testament applies to Christ says the same: I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me (Ps 69:12). A byword, a joke, a face spat on (17:6). The spitting will come again at the trial of Jesus.

God has loosed my cord. God has cut his tent-rope, or unstrung his bow; either way, his strength and standing are gone, and people who once feared him feel free to do as they like. Job traces even their insolence back to God's hand. He is right that God's hand is in it (2:3), and still does not know why.

verseByVerse.quote: On my right hand the rabble rise; they push away my feet; they cast up against me their ways of destruction. They break up my path; they promote my calamity; they need no one to help them. As through a wide breach they come; amid the crash they roll on. Terrors are turned upon me; my honor is pursued as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed away like a cloud.
verseByVerse.commentary: The siege of 19:12 again, but now it is a mob, not an army: rabble pushing him off the path, pouring through the breach in his defences. My honor is pursued as by the wind, and his wealth is gone like a cloud that crosses the sky and is not there any more.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — I Cry to You and You Do Not Answer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job's life drains away, and God does not answer his cries (vv. 16-23).
verseByVerse.theology: These are the words of Psalm 22, and of the cross. God did not answer yet, but he would.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction have taken hold of me. The night racks my bones, and the pain that gnaws me takes no rest. With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic. God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third now, and the deepest. His life drains out of him like water from a jar. At night the pain is in his bones, gnawing, never resting. It is the language of Psalm 22, the psalm of the cross: I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint (Ps 22:14).

With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic. God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes. His clothes cling to his sores; he is thrown in the mud. Dust and ashes: Abraham used the words of himself before God, I who am but dust and ashes (Gen 18:27), and Job will use them once more, at the very end, when he has seen God: I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes (42:6). Here they are the words of humiliation. There they will be the words of worship.

Anyone living with chronic pain, or with depression that will not lift, may find their own nights in these verses. Scripture gives such words to pray, and praying them is not unbelief. The God who let Job say all this, and then came to him, does not turn away from the same prayer now.

verseByVerse.quote: I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me. You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me. You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm. For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the loneliest lines in Job's prayers. He cries, and there is no answer. He stands up, and God just looks at him. Many believers have prayed into that silence. The psalm of the cross prays it: O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer (Ps 22:2). And on the cross Jesus cried My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). The Son of God entered the silence Job describes, so that for those who belong to him it would never be the last word.

You only look at me. Job feels God's gaze as cold, a spectator watching him suffer. But he said himself, in a better hour, he knows the way that I take (23:10). God's eyes on Job were never the eyes of indifference. They were the eyes that had looked at him in the council and said, there is none like him on the earth (1:8).

This is Job's hardest charge: God has become cruel. It is not true, and the reader must not take it as true; God will ask Job, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8). But Job says it to God, and God does not strike him for it. God can bear his children's worst words spoken to his face. And God will speak to him out of a storm (38:1). The grave, the house appointed for all living, is coming for everyone (Heb 9:27). Job expects to go there unanswered. He will not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — My Lyre Is Turned to Mourning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job wept for others, but no one weeps for him, and his music has turned to mourning (vv. 24-31).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Job's closing lament. The God who turns mourning into dancing has not finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help? Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy? But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surely a man buried in the rubble may reach out his hand and shout for help. And Job had always helped others who cried: he wept for people having a hard day, he grieved for the poor. Weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). He did it for others. Why will no one do it for him?

But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came. The prophet confessed the same for a whole people: we hope for light, and behold, darkness (Isa 59:9). It is the experience of disappointed hope, and Scripture does not pretend it never happens to the faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: My inward parts are in turmoil and never still; days of affliction come to meet me. I go about darkened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help. I am a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches. My skin turns black and falls from me, and my bones burn with heat. My lyre is turned to mourning, and my pipe to the voice of those who weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His skin is blackened, but not by sunburn; it is the disease. He stands up in public and cries for help and gets none. His only kin now are jackals and ostriches, the creatures of the ruined places whose wailing cries in the night were proverbial; Micah would say, I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches (Mic 1:8). And when God speaks, he will talk about the ostrich (39:13-18), with something like a smile. The creature Job named as his companion in misery, God describes as his own handiwork.

The last lines of his lament. Fever in his bones, skin peeling off. And his music has changed: the lyre and pipe that should play at feasts play funeral songs. The wicked still rejoice to the sound of the pipe (21:12). Job's pipe weeps.

But the book is not over, and neither is God. You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness (Ps 30:11). Job has stitched sackcloth to his skin (16:15). God will loose it.

30.theology: Job's lament uses the words of Psalms 22 and 69, the psalms Christ fulfilled in his suffering. His charge that God is cruel (v. 21) is false and God will correct it, yet God receives it without striking him. And suffering exposes pride even in the godly (vv. 1-8), where Christ, reviled, did not revile in return.
30.examples: This is a chapter for the long nights of pain and the prayers that seem to meet only silence. Job gives the sufferer honest words, and the book does not rebuke him for using them. It also shows, gently, how suffering can sour the way we speak of others, and it ends with a lyre turned to mourning that God has promised to turn back to dancing.

31.title: Here Is My Signature
31.text: <sup>1</sup>"I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?<sup>2</sup>What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high?<sup>3</sup>Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity?<sup>4</sup>Does not he see my ways and number all my steps?<sup>5</sup>"If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit;<sup>6</sup>(Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!)<sup>7</sup>if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands,<sup>8</sup>then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.<sup>9</sup>"If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door,<sup>10</sup>then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her.<sup>11</sup>For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges;<sup>12</sup>for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.<sup>13</sup>"If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me,<sup>14</sup>what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him?<sup>15</sup>Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?<sup>16</sup>"If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail,<sup>17</sup>or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it<sup>18</sup>(for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow),<sup>19</sup>if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering,<sup>20</sup>if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,<sup>21</sup>if I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate,<sup>22</sup>then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket.<sup>23</sup>For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.<sup>24</sup>"If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence,<sup>25</sup>if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much,<sup>26</sup>if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor,<sup>27</sup>and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand,<sup>28</sup>this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.<sup>29</sup>"If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him<sup>30</sup>(I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse),<sup>31</sup>if the men of my tent have not said, 'Who is there that has not been filled with his meat?'<sup>32</sup>(the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler),<sup>33</sup>if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart,<sup>34</sup>because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors—<sup>35</sup>Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary!<sup>36</sup>Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown;<sup>37</sup>I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him.<sup>38</sup>"If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together,<sup>39</sup>if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last,<sup>40</sup>let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley." The words of Job are ended.
31.overview: Job swears his innocence in a series of oaths. He made a covenant with his eyes, dealt honestly and did not lust after his neighbour's wife (vv. 1-12). He heard his servants, for the same God made them, and fed the orphan and clothed the naked (vv. 13-23). He did not trust gold, worship the heavens, curse his enemy or hide his sins (vv. 24-34). Here is his signature: let the Almighty answer. The words of Job are ended (vv. 35-40).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Covenant with My Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job swears to purity of eye, hand and heart (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's innocence begins where Jesus' teaching begins: not only with the deed, but with the look.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin? What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high? Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity? Does not he see my ways and number all my steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Job's last speech, and it takes a form every reader in the ancient world would have recognised: the oath of clearance. "If I have done this, then let that happen to me." A man who swore it was calling God's judgment down on himself if he lied. Job goes through the whole of life, sin by sin, and swears to each. It answers Eliphaz's invented charges more thoroughly than any argument could.

And he starts with the eyes. Not with adultery but with the look that comes before it. He made a solemn agreement with his own eyes that they would not linger on a young woman with desire. Jesus would teach the same: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28). Job's righteousness was not only a matter of what people saw him do. It went down to where he let his eyes go.

What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high? Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity? Does not he see my ways and number all my steps? Job kept his covenant because he knew God was watching every step. That is not fear of being caught. It is the fear of the Lord, which is wisdom (28:28).

What does a covenant with the eyes mean today? It is a decision made beforehand, not in the moment, not to look at another person, or an image on a screen, in order to desire them. A passing glance is not the sin; the second look, kept and fed, is. Keeping the covenant means guarding what you allow before your eyes, removing what you know will draw you in (Matt 5:29), and bringing every failure to Christ, who forgives and cleanses. Nor is it kept by willpower alone: the Spirit who lives in believers is the one who makes it keepable, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh (Gal 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit; (Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!) if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands, then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.
verseByVerse.commentary: Deceit in business, dishonest gain, the heart following wherever the eyes lead (Num 15:39), a stain on his hands. If so, let someone else eat his harvest. And in the middle, a cry: let me be weighed in a just balance. He asked the same at the start (6:2). A king of Babylon was once weighed by God and found wanting (Dan 5:27). Job asks to be weighed, because he believes the scales will show his integrity, the word God used of him (2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door, then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her. For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.
verseByVerse.commentary: If he had waited at his neighbour's door for the husband to go out, then let his own wife become another man's servant and worse. It is one of the harshest curses in the chapter, and it measures how seriously he takes the sin. To a modern reader it seems unjust to his wife, and the reader is right to feel it. Job is not asking for it to happen to her; he uses the shame-language of a world where a man's household shared his disgrace, to say how unthinkable the sin is to him. Scripture elsewhere insists that each bears his own guilt (Ezek 18:20). Adultery is more than a crime for the courts: it is a fire that burns everything a man has. Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? ... So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife (Prov 6:27, 29). Job knew it, and did not touch the fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Did Not He Who Made Me Make Him?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He swears to justice for his servants (vv. 13-15) and generosity to the poor (vv. 16-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Master and servant were made by the same God in the same way. Job lived as if that were true.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me, what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him? Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Job's world a servant had no rights against his master. Job listened to his servants' complaints anyway, because he knew he had a Master too, who would one day ask him how he had treated them.

Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb? Here is the reason. The same God made master and slave, in the same way, in their mothers' wombs. Neither is more human than the other. Has not one God created us? asks Malachi (Mal 2:10). Paul tells Christian masters to treat their servants well, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him (Eph 6:9). The dignity of every human being rests here: not on what he can do, or what he owns, but on the fact that God made him.

Does this mean the Bible approves of slavery? Job had servants, as every household of means did in his world, and Scripture regulates that world's institutions before it overturns them. But this verse lays an axe at the root of treating any person as property or as less than human, and the law put to death anyone who kidnapped a man to sell him (Exod 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10). In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Gal 3:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow), if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering, if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job answers on oath every item of Eliphaz's charge (22:6-9). He never ate alone while an orphan went without; orphans grew up in his house as if he were their father; he never let a poor man freeze while his own sheep had wool. The poor man's body blessed him, warm under Job's fleece.

It is the religion James describes: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27). And it is the religion of the sheep in Jesus' judgment, who fed the hungry and clothed the naked (Matt 25:35-36). The list Eliphaz threw at Job is the list of the last judgment, and Job's life stands on the right side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: if I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate, then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket. For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.
verseByVerse.commentary: It would have been easy. An orphan had no one to speak for him at the city gate, where the elders were Job's friends and Job himself sat as judge (29:7). Job could have raised his hand against the helpless and won. If he had, let that arm be torn off. He did not, because he feared God more than he feared any man, and loved justice more than advantage. Power over the defenceless is the real test of a man, and Job passed it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–34 — If I Have Made Gold My Trust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He turns to the sins no one could see: greed, idolatry, spite and concealment (vv. 24-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The inward sins, greed, idolatry, spite, secrecy, are the ones a man could hide. Job swears he did not hide them.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence, if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much, if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sins no one could see. Trusting in money: Job was the richest man in the east, and he swears his confidence was never in his gold. That is why he could lose it and still bless God (1:21). Paul calls greed what it is, covetousness, which is idolatry (Col 3:5), and tells the rich not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God (1 Tim 6:17).

And the worship of the sun and moon, the religion of most of the ancient world, which Moses warned Israel against (Deut 4:19). To "kiss the hand" was to blow a kiss of worship toward the sky. Job never did it, even secretly. Either sin, trusting in gold or bowing to the heavens, would have been false to God above. Idolatry is unfaithfulness to the one true God, and Job was faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him (I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse), if the men of my tent have not said, 'Who is there that has not been filled with his meat?' (the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler),
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not gloat when an enemy fell, and he never cursed an enemy's life. Do not rejoice when your enemy falls (Prov 24:17). Jesus went further: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt 5:44). In 27:7 Job said of his accusers, Let my enemy be as the wicked; that was an appeal for justice against false witnesses, not a curse on a man's life, and here he holds to the same standard.

If the men of my tent have not said, Who is there that has not been filled with his meat? (the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler). His servants could say there was no one who had not eaten at his table. No traveller ever had to sleep in the square. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers (Heb 13:2). Job's door was always open.

verseByVerse.quote: if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart, because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has never claimed to be sinless. What he swears here is that he did not hide the sins he had. As others do can also be read, as the ESV's note says, "as Adam did". The first man, when he sinned, hid himself (Gen 3:10). Job did not hide. He did not keep quiet about his faults out of fear of what the neighbours would think.

That is the way of the gospel. Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov 28:13). If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). The fear of people is what makes us hide, and the fear of man lays a snare (Prov 29:25). Job feared God, and so he did not need to hide from anyone.

No one but Christ could swear this whole chapter without a flaw. He kept it perfectly, in our place, and by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19). So the failures this chapter exposes in us are not the end: the way back is the confession Job did not hide from, and the mercy God has promised.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job signs his defence and calls on the Almighty to answer (vv. 35-40).
verseByVerse.theology: Job signs his defence and rests his case. The next voice he hears will be God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary! Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown; I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job ends his defence like a man in court signing his statement. Here is my signature is, in Hebrew, "here is my mark": the name of the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script was written as a simple cross-mark. Now let God answer.

And he asks for the charge sheet: let my accuser write out the case against me. I would bind it on me as a crown: he would wear the indictment proudly, because he knows it would prove nothing, and he would walk into God's presence with his head up.

Read those words beside the cross. Christ was crowned, with thorns, and over his head they put the charge against him, which read, This is Jesus, the King of the Jews (Matt 27:37). He carried a written charge that was no crime, and he carried ours, which were real: the record of debt that stood against us, which God set aside, nailing it to the cross (Col 2:14). Job wanted to wear his indictment as a crown because he was innocent. Christ wore ours because we were not. And because he did, we can do what Job longed to do, and approach God with confidence (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together, if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last, let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley." The words of Job are ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A last oath, about the land itself. If he had got his fields by fraud, eaten their yield without paying, and brought their owners to their death, the soil would cry out against him, as Abel's blood cried from the ground (Gen 4:10) and as the unpaid wages of the harvesters are crying out against you (James 5:4). If so, let the curse of Eden fall on his fields: thorns and thistles instead of grain (Gen 3:18).

The words of Job are ended. He has nothing more to say to the friends, and he has made his last appeal to God. The next time Job opens his mouth it will be to God, and it will be short: Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4). Between here and there, a young man will speak, and then the LORD himself.

31.theology: Job's oath describes righteousness from the heart outward: the eye, the servant made by the same God, the orphan and widow, the heart that does not trust in gold, the enemy not cursed, sin confessed and not hidden. Only Christ kept it all, and he wore the charge and the crown because we were guilty.
31.examples: Read slowly, this chapter is a searching examination of conscience: what we let our eyes rest on, how we treat those who work for us, whether our money has quietly become our trust, whether we hide our faults. No reader passes it as Job did, and the chapter itself points to the confession and mercy that meet us where we fail.

32.title: I Am Young in Years
32.text: <sup>1</sup>So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.<sup>2</sup>Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God.<sup>3</sup>He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong.<sup>4</sup>Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he.<sup>5</sup>And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger.<sup>6</sup>And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: "I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you.<sup>7</sup>I said, 'Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.'<sup>8</sup>But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand.<sup>9</sup>It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right.<sup>10</sup>Therefore I say, 'Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion.'<sup>11</sup>"Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say.<sup>12</sup>I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words.<sup>13</sup>Beware lest you say, 'We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man.'<sup>14</sup>He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches.<sup>15</sup>"They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say.<sup>16</sup>And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more?<sup>17</sup>I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion.<sup>18</sup>For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me.<sup>19</sup>Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst.<sup>20</sup>I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.<sup>21</sup>I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person.<sup>22</sup>For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.
32.overview: The three friends stop answering Job because he is righteous in his own eyes. Elihu the Buzite, who had waited because he was younger, burns with anger at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without an answer (vv. 1-5). Wisdom, he says, comes not from age but from the Spirit of the Almighty, and he is full of words, ready to burst (vv. 6-22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The friends fall silent, and a new speaker, Elihu, is angry with both Job and the friends (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator does not tell us whether Elihu is right; the end of the book will, by what it does not say.

verseByVerse.quote: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary: The debate is over, and the narrator tells us why, from the friends' point of view: Job was righteous in his own eyes. They could not move him. The reader knows that Job was righteous in God's eyes too (1:8). But the phrase is a warning as well. There is a way of holding on to one's innocence that begins to look like self-righteousness, and the next speaker will say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God. He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong. Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he. And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new voice, and one the reader has not been told was there. Elihu is the only speaker in the book given a family tree. Buz was the brother of Uz in the family of Abraham's brother Nahor (Gen 22:21), so Elihu's clan and Job's homeland carry the names of two brothers.

And he is angry. The narrator says it four times in four verses. He is angry at Job because he justified himself rather than God. That is a real charge, and it is not the friends' charge. The friends said Job had sinned before his suffering. Elihu says Job is going wrong in how he speaks now: defending himself at God's expense. God himself will put the same question to Job: Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8).

The friends condemned Job and could not prove it. Elihu sees that too.

The phrase burned with anger returns. At the end of the book the LORD will say to Eliphaz, My anger burns against you and against your two friends (42:7), the same expression. Elihu's anger burns against Job and the friends. God's burns against the friends alone. Elihu is half right.
verseByVerse.note: Elihu was from Buz, a name linked with Abraham’s family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–22 — I Am Young in Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu says he is young, but understanding comes from God (vv. 6-10); the friends have failed (vv. 11-14), and he is bursting to speak (vv. 15-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu is right that wisdom is God's gift and not the property of the old. Whether he has it is what the next five chapters will show.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: "I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you. I said, 'Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.' But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand. It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right. Therefore I say, 'Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has kept quiet out of respect, expecting the old men to show their wisdom. They did not.

The breath of the Almighty makes a man understand: not grey hair but God's Spirit, the breath God breathed into man at the beginning. Job had quoted the friends' proverb, Wisdom is with the aged (12:12), and answered it: With God are wisdom and might. Elihu agrees.

That is a true word for the church. Paul told a young pastor, Let no one despise you for your youth (1 Tim 4:12), and he taught that God's things are known not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit (1 Cor 2:13). Age deserves respect. It does not guarantee wisdom, and youth does not rule it out.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say. I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words. Beware lest you say, 'We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man.' He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Searched out: the friends' favourite verb once more (5:27; 8:8). They searched and searched for what to say, and none of them actually answered Job. Elihu has been listening carefully, and he has noticed what the friends never admitted: they lost the argument.

Beware lest you say, We have found wisdom: do not retreat into saying "only God can deal with him". Elihu promises a fresh approach: he will not recycle their arguments. How far he keeps that promise is the question of the next chapters. At times he says new and true things. At times he sounds exactly like them.

verseByVerse.quote: "They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say. And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more? I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion. For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is bursting to speak, like new wine fermenting in a sealed skin. Jesus used the picture: new wine is put into fresh wineskins (Matt 9:17). A prophet described the same compulsion: there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jer 20:9).

Readers have heard this preface two ways. Some hear a true messenger, pressed by God's Spirit to speak, preparing for the voice from the whirlwind. Others hear a young man in love with his own words: seventeen verses about how much he has to say before he says any of it. Both readings have something in the text to stand on. The end of the book gives the clue: the LORD rebukes the three friends and commends Job, and says nothing about Elihu at all (42:7-9).

Why does God neither rebuke nor commend Elihu? The best reading is that Elihu speaks partly truly and partly not. He rightly says that God can use suffering to teach and that God cannot be unjust, and his speech of the storm prepares for God’s answer out of the whirlwind. But he still assumes that Job’s suffering must have a cause in Job. God passes over him because God himself now speaks; Elihu’s words are neither a rival to his nor the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person. For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.
verseByVerse.commentary: He will not take sides for anyone's sake, and he will not flatter. That is the right spirit for anyone who speaks about God: God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34), and his servants should not either. Job had accused the friends of showing partiality to God, lying in his defence (13:8). Elihu promises to tell the truth to Job and friends alike. The best test of it will be whether he can tell the difference between Job's words, which were sometimes wrong, and Job's life, which was not.

32.theology: Elihu is right that understanding is the Spirit's gift and not the property of the old (vv. 8-9; 1 Cor 2:12-13), and right that Job has begun to justify himself at God's expense (v. 2). But his anger burns against Job and the friends, while God's burns against the friends alone: he says true things and is not the last word.
32.examples: Elihu is an encouragement to the young believer who hesitates to speak among older Christians: wisdom is God's gift, not the reward of grey hair. He is also a caution, since he burns with anger four times in four verses, and zeal that is half right can still wound. It is wise to listen as long as he did before speaking, and then to speak with less heat.

33.title: I Have Found a Ransom
33.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words.<sup>2</sup>Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks.<sup>3</sup>My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely.<sup>4</sup>The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.<sup>5</sup>Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay.<sup>7</sup>Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.<sup>8</sup>"Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words.<sup>9</sup>You say, 'I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me.<sup>10</sup>Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy,<sup>11</sup>he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.'<sup>12</sup>"Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man.<sup>13</sup>Why do you contend against him, saying, 'He will answer none of man's words'?<sup>14</sup>For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it.<sup>15</sup>In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds,<sup>16</sup>then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings,<sup>17</sup>that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man;<sup>18</sup>he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.<sup>19</sup>"Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones,<sup>20</sup>so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food.<sup>21</sup>His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out.<sup>22</sup>His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.<sup>23</sup>If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him,<sup>24</sup>and he is merciful to him, and says, 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom;<sup>25</sup>let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor';<sup>26</sup>then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.<sup>27</sup>He sings before men and says: 'I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me.<sup>28</sup>He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.'<sup>29</sup>"Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man,<sup>30</sup>to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life.<sup>31</sup>Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak.<sup>32</sup>If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you.<sup>33</sup>If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
33.overview: Elihu addresses Job as one made by God's Spirit and clay like him (vv. 1-7). Job is wrong to say God does not answer, for God is greater than man (vv. 8-13). God speaks in warning dreams and in pain that brings a man near death (vv. 14-22). If a mediator says, I have found a ransom, the man is restored, sees God's face with joy and confesses his sin; Elihu wants to justify Job (vv. 23-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Too Was Pinched Off from Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu addresses Job as a fellow creature of clay (vv. 1-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu offers to meet Job as an equal. It is a kinder start than the friends', and a faint picture of the Mediator Job wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words. Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks. My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely. The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
verseByVerse.commentary: Elihu turns to Job and addresses him by name, O Job, which the three friends never once did in all their speeches. He promises honesty, and grounds it where he grounded his right to speak: the Spirit of God made him, the breath of the Almighty keeps him alive (32:8; Gen 2:7). Whatever else is true of Elihu, he knows where his life comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand. Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay. Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job had asked God, let not dread of you terrify me (13:21), and longed for an arbiter who was a man, as I am (9:32). Elihu steps forward almost as if to be that: I am clay too, pinched off the same lump as you; you need not be afraid of me. It is gracious, and it is a kinder beginning than the friends made.

But Elihu cannot be what Job needs, because he is only clay. The arbiter Job longed for had to be able to lay his hand on God as well as on man (9:33). Only one person has ever been both. Elihu's gentleness is a faint outline; Christ is the portrait.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — In This You Are Not Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu quotes Job's complaints (vv. 8-11) and says he is wrong to claim that God does not answer (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: God has not been silent, Elihu says; Job has not been hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words. You say, 'I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me. Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy, he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Elihu has been listening, and most of this is Job's own words: count me as your enemy (13:24), you put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths (13:27). He quotes Job fairly there. The first line overstates him. Job never claimed to be without any sin; he asked God to pardon his transgression (7:21) and spoke of the iniquities of his youth (13:26). What Job denied was sin that could explain this suffering. Elihu, like the friends, has flattened that distinction a little. But he has heard far more than they did.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. Why do you contend against him, saying, 'He will answer none of man's words'?
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is Elihu's charge. Not that Job sinned before his trouble, but that he is wrong now in how he speaks of God: as if God owed him an answer and had refused to give it. Job had said, I cry to you for help and you do not answer me (30:20). Elihu replies: God is greater than man; he is not bound to answer on our terms. And God has not been silent. You have not been hearing him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — God Speaks in One Way, and in Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks in warning dreams (vv. 14-18) and in pain that brings a man near death (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Elihu's real contribution, true in itself though it does not explain Job's case.

verseByVerse.quote: For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it. In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds, then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the heart of what Elihu adds. God speaks, and more than one way. First, at night: dreams that frighten a man away from what he was about to do, that cut his pride short before it ruins him, that keep him from the grave. Eliphaz's night vision gave him a doctrine to use against Job (4:13). Elihu's night warnings are rescues.

Hebrews begins with the same thought and brings it to its end: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:1-2). God speaks in one way and in two, says Elihu. In the end he spoke in a Son, and everything he has to say to us is in him.

Does God still speak in dreams? In Elihu’s day, before the Scriptures were complete, God did. Now he has spoken finally in his Son (Heb 1:1–2), and a dream may stir the conscience or prompt prayer, but no believer should treat one as a message from God. Faithful Christians differ on whether God still gives such dreams, and many who think he may still agree that any dream must be tested by Scripture; this commentary holds, with the historic Reformed churches, that Scripture is now sufficient for all we need to know and do (2 Tim 3:16-17).

verseByVerse.quote: "Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones, so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food. His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out. His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second way God speaks is pain. Illness on the bed, aching bones, no appetite, flesh wasting until the bones show, death coming near. Elihu is describing Job, and he says: this too can be God speaking.

That is a real step beyond the friends. They asked what Job had done to deserve it. Elihu asks what God might be saying through it. Suffering, he says, can be God's warning and his discipline, meant to rescue a man, not to repay him. Scripture agrees: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (Ps 119:67). It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes (Ps 119:71). God disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10). A believer in pain may ask God what he is teaching, and should. He need not find the answer to be faithful; Job never learned the reason for his trial, and he was God's servant all through it.

But hold the limit. This is not why Job suffered; the prologue said his suffering was without reason in him (2:3). Elihu has found a true word about suffering. He is still applying it to a man whose case it does not fit. Pain can be discipline. Not all pain is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — I Have Found a Ransom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A mediator finds a ransom, and the dying man is restored and confesses his sin (vv. 23-30). Elihu wants to justify Job (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the clearest picture in the book of a mediator who pays a ransom. The New Testament names him: one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.

verseByVerse.quote: If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him, and he is merciful to him, and says, 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom;
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the high point of Elihu's speeches, and one of the brightest gleams of the gospel in the book. A man is dying, near the pit. Then a messenger from God, a mediator, one in a thousand, speaks up for him and says, Do not send him down to the grave; I have found a ransom.

Two words here carry the whole Bible's hope. Mediator: one who stands between and speaks for another, what Job's friends should have been and were not (16:20). Ransom is the price paid to set a condemned life free. The psalmist knew that no human being can pay it: Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly (Ps 49:7-8).

Elihu speaks of a heavenly messenger who finds a ransom. The New Testament speaks of a Mediator who is the ransom. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim 2:5-6). Both of Elihu's words, in one sentence. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The price that no man could pay, God paid.
verseByVerse.note: Elihu imagines a mediator who finds “a ransom”, a hope fulfilled in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor'; then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary: The dying man is restored: his skin fresh as a child's, as Naaman's was when his skin disease was cleansed in the Jordan: his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (2 Kgs 5:14). He prays, God accepts him, he sees God's face and shouts for joy, and God gives him back his righteousness. Every part of this will happen to Job: the LORD will accept his prayer (42:9), he will see God (42:5), and he will be restored. It happens to every believer in Christ, whose ransom has been paid: accepted, righteous, and one day raised with a body that will never wear out.

verseByVerse.quote: He sings before men and says: 'I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescued man sings, and his song is a confession. I sinned; I twisted what was right; and I did not get what I deserved. That is the song of grace. I acknowledged my sin to you ... and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Ps 32:5). It is the prodigal's Father, I have sinned (Luke 15:21), met by a father running down the road. He has redeemed my soul: God redeems your life from the pit (Ps 103:4).

The restored man confesses sin. Elihu's gospel is not "you were innocent all along" but "you were not, and you were ransomed." That is closer to the truth about every human being than anything the friends said, and it is the truth Job will come to when he sees God (42:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life. Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak. If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you. If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not give up after one warning. Again and again he works to bring a man back from the edge. And the goal is the light of life, the very phrase Jesus used of himself: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12). The man brought back from the pit lives in the light of Christ.

I desire to justify you: Elihu, unlike the friends, wants Job to come out in the right. His manner is lecturing, and he will go on for four more chapters. But his heart, at least here, is for Job.

33.theology: Suffering can be God's speech, a warning and discipline meant to rescue (vv. 14-22; Heb 12:10-11). That is Elihu's real advance on the friends, though it is not the reason for Job's suffering (2:3). And the mediator who finds a ransom (vv. 23-24) is fulfilled in Christ: no man can ransom another, and God did.
33.examples: Elihu models some good habits for anyone who comes alongside a sufferer: he uses Job's name, meets him as one creature of clay to another, and quotes him fairly. His best word is that pain may be God speaking to rescue us, and his ransom points to the one Mediator who gave himself (1 Timothy 2:5-6). Held with its limit, that can help a sufferer ask what God is teaching without concluding that the pain is a punishment.

34.title: Far Be It from God to Do Wickedness
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Elihu answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know;<sup>3</sup>for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food.<sup>4</sup>Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good.<sup>5</sup>For Job has said, 'I am in the right, and God has taken away my right;<sup>6</sup>in spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.'<sup>7</sup>What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water,<sup>8</sup>who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men?<sup>9</sup>For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God.'<sup>10</sup>"Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong.<sup>11</sup>For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him.<sup>12</sup>Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice.<sup>13</sup>Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world?<sup>14</sup>If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath,<sup>15</sup>all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.<sup>16</sup>"If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say.<sup>17</sup>Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty,<sup>18</sup>who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked man,'<sup>19</sup>who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands?<sup>20</sup>In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand.<sup>21</sup>"For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps.<sup>22</sup>There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves.<sup>23</sup>For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.<sup>24</sup>He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place.<sup>25</sup>Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed.<sup>26</sup>He strikes them for their wickedness in a place for all to see,<sup>27</sup>because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways,<sup>28</sup>so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted—<sup>29</sup>When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him, whether it be a nation or a man?—<sup>30</sup>that a godless man should not reign, that he should not ensnare the people.<sup>31</sup>"For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more;<sup>32</sup>teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'?<sup>33</sup>Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know.<sup>34</sup>Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say:<sup>35</sup>'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.'<sup>36</sup>Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men.<sup>37</sup>For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."
34.overview: Elihu appeals to the wise against Job, who he says drinks scoffing like water (vv. 1-9). God cannot do wickedness; every breath is his, and he shows no partiality (vv. 10-20). He sees every step and hears the poor; when he is silent, who can condemn him? Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin (vv. 21-37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — What Man Is Like Job?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu calls the wise to test Job's words, and accuses him of scoffing (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Here Elihu starts to sound like the friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elihu answered and said: "Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know; for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good. For Job has said, 'I am in the right, and God has taken away my right; in spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.' What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men? For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his second speech Elihu begins to slide.

Hear my words, you wise men ... for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. That is Job's own line (12:11), almost word for word. For Job has said, I am in the right, and God has taken away my right; that is fair, Job said it (27:2). And let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good is a sound instinct: test the arguments and keep what is true, as Paul says, test everything; hold fast what is good (1 Thess 5:21). The trouble is what Elihu does next.

What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men? For he has said, It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God. Now Elihu sounds like the friends. Drinks ... like water is Eliphaz's picture of a man who drinks injustice like water (15:16). In company with evildoers is the friends' charge. And the last sentence is not Job's at all. Job described the wicked saying, what profit do we get if we pray to him? (21:15), and said their counsel was far from him. Elihu has put the wicked's words into Job's mouth, exactly as Eliphaz did (22:13, 17). The young man who promised not to answer Job with your speeches (32:14) is doing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — Far Be It from God to Do Wickedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God cannot do wickedness; every breath is his, and he shows no partiality (vv. 10-20).
verseByVerse.theology: This is true, and Job needed it: the God who gives every breath is just and owes no one an explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong. For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him. Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice. Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world? If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad said it (8:3), and it is true. Paul says it: Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! (Rom 9:14). And Job needed to hear it, because he had said God put me in the wrong (19:6) and turned cruel to me (30:21). God is not unjust, however things look from the ash heap.

The fullest proof came at the cross. How can a just God let the guilty go? Paul answers that God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, a sacrifice that turns away God's wrath, to show his righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). Sin was not overlooked. It was punished, in the Son. Far be it from God to do wickedness: at Calvary he forgave without doing any.

Who gave him charge over the earth? God answers to no one; no one handed him the world to run. Every breath in every creature is his, lent moment by moment. When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created (Ps 104:29-30). A God like that is not a debtor to anyone.

Then according to the work of a man he will repay him (v. 11). That is true, and the New Testament says it as plainly: He will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6); we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10). The question has never been whether God repays. It is when. The friends, and Elihu here, expected the repayment to be visible now, in each man's health and wealth. Scripture places the full reckoning at the last day. Put the truth at the wrong time and it becomes a lie about the sufferer in front of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say. Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty, who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked man,' who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands? In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: Could a God who hated justice rule the world? He tells kings to their face what they are; he treats rich and poor alike, for they are all the work of his hands. That was Job's own argument about his servants: Did not he who made me in the womb make him? (31:15). Elihu turns it on Job: if God is impartial with kings, will he be unjust to you? In a moment they die ... and the mighty are taken away by no human hand. The great fall overnight at his word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees all and needs no trial (vv. 21-28); his silence is not injustice (vv. 29-33); and Job speaks without knowledge (vv. 34-37).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu is right about Job's words and wrong about Job's heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps. There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves. For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment. He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place. Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed. He strikes them for their wickedness in a place for all to see, because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways, so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted— When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him, whether it be a nation or a man?— that a godless man should not reign, that he should not ensnare the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has no need to consider a man further: he sees every step, and no deep darkness hides anyone (v. 22). Here is a new point, aimed straight at Job's great demand. Job has wanted a hearing, a day in court (13:18; 23:4; 31:35). Elihu says: God does not need one. He knows everything already; he does not have to hold an inquiry. That is true. And yet in a few chapters God will grant Job the audience he asked for (38:1). He did not owe it. He gave it. That is grace.

He heard the cry of the afflicted: God hears the poor; that answers Job's complaint that the dying groan and God does nothing (24:12). When he is quiet, who can condemn? God's silence is not injustice. Job took God's silence as proof that God was against him (30:20). Elihu is right that silence proves nothing of the kind.

And the mighty whom God shatters, he replaces: sets others in their place (v. 24). Daniel praised the same God: he removes kings and sets up kings (Dan 2:21). History is not a machine running on its own. Every throne is held at his pleasure, and he takes it back when he chooses, often suddenly, in the night (v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: "For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more; teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'? Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know. Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say: 'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.' Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men. For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach me what I do not see: Elihu wants Job to say this. Job had said something very like it long ago: Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray (6:24).

Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? God does not adjust his justice to our preferences. That is a fair word to Job, who had wanted God's ways to fit his expectations. It is a fair word to the friends too, who wanted them to fit theirs.

Job speaks without knowledge. Here Elihu is right, and God will say the same thing in almost the same words: Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? (38:2). Job had spoken about things he did not understand.

He adds rebellion to his sin. And here Elihu is wrong. He wishes Job more suffering, calls his answers those of the wicked, and assumes a sin to which Job has added rebellion. That is the friends' verdict, and God will overturn it: you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). In two verses Elihu is right about Job's words and wrong about Job's heart. It is a warning to every critic, however sound his doctrine: it is possible to be right about what a sufferer said and wrong about who he is.

34.theology: God cannot do wrong, every breath is his, and his silence is not injustice (v. 29). He owes no one a hearing (v. 23), and grants Job one as grace. Elihu, sliding into the friends' voice, is half right: Job spoke without knowledge, but he did not add rebellion to sin.
34.examples: Elihu's slide is easy to recognise in ourselves. He begins by fairly quoting Job, then puts words in his mouth that Job never said. Anyone arguing with a hurting person needs the discipline to answer what was actually said, and to remember that sound doctrine about God does not license a harsh verdict on the person in front of us.

35.title: Songs in the Night
35.text: <sup>1</sup>And Elihu answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Do you think this to be just? Do you say, 'It is my right before God,'<sup>3</sup>that you ask, 'What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?'<sup>4</sup>I will answer you and your friends with you.<sup>5</sup>Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you.<sup>6</sup>If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him?<sup>7</sup>If you are righteous, what do you give to him? Or what does he receive from your hand?<sup>8</sup>Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.<sup>9</sup>"Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty.<sup>10</sup>But none says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,<sup>11</sup>who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'<sup>12</sup>There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men.<sup>13</sup>Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it.<sup>14</sup>How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him!<sup>15</sup>And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression,<sup>16</sup>Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge."
35.overview: Elihu asks what Job gains by not sinning: his sin does not harm God and his righteousness gives God nothing (vv. 1-8). People cry out under oppression but none asks, Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night? Job, he says, multiplies words without knowledge (vv. 9-16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu asks what Job gains by not sinning, since neither his sin nor his righteousness touches God (vv. 1-8).
verseByVerse.theology: God is not harmed by us and needs nothing from us, but that does not mean he does not care.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu answered and said: "Do you think this to be just? Do you say, 'It is my right before God,' that you ask, 'What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?' I will answer you and your friends with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his third and shortest speech Elihu puts a question in Job's mouth: what good has my righteousness done me? Job never said it in those words. He said God destroys both the blameless and the wicked (9:22), and he quoted the wicked asking what profit do we get if we pray to him? (21:15). Satan said Job served God for profit (1:9). If Job now asked what profit his goodness had brought him, Satan would have won. The whole point of Job's faith is that it is not a bargain.

I will answer you and your friends with you. Elihu will correct all four of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you. If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him? If you are righteous, what do you give to him? Or what does he receive from your hand? Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.
verseByVerse.commentary: Look up: God is higher than the clouds, and your sin cannot damage him nor your goodness add to him; what you do affects other people. Eliphaz said the same (22:2-3), and half of it is true. God needs nothing and cannot be harmed. But he is not indifferent. He can be grieved by his people's sin, do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God (Eph 4:30), and he delights in his servants, Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). A God who could not be harmed and did not care would not be the God of this book.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oppressed cry out but do not seek their Maker (vv. 9-11), and God does not answer the empty cry (vv. 12-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God himself, and Job, for all his faults, has been seeking God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty. But none says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night, who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the one new thing in the chapter. People who are crushed cry out, of course. But crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God. How many call for help, and never ask, Where is God my Maker? They want the pain gone. They do not want him.

Who gives songs in the night: the God who, in the dark, gives his people something to sing. At night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life (Ps 42:8). Let me remember my song in the night (Ps 77:6). In a Philippian prison, about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God (Acts 16:25). A person who seeks God himself in suffering, not only rescue, may find a song in the night before he finds the morning.

On the night he was betrayed, Jesus sang a hymn with his disciples (Matt 26:30), probably the Passover psalms. He sang on the darkest night any man has faced, and walked into it for us; because he did, his people are never left in theirs without a song.

Elihu means this as a rebuke to Job, and it does not fit him. Job has not only cried out for relief. He has cried for God: Oh, that I knew where I might find him (23:3). But the sentence is true, and every sufferer should ask it of himself: am I seeking relief, or am I seeking him?

verseByVerse.quote: There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it. How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. God does not answer the proud, who want his gifts without him. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly (James 4:3). This is not about the weak, stumbling prayer of a believer in pain; God hears that (Rom 8:26).

You are waiting for him! Elihu faults Job for saying he cannot see God and is waiting for his case to be heard. But waiting for God is not sin; it is faith. Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD! (Ps 27:14). And Job's case was before God, and God was about to answer it (38:1). Here Elihu is simply wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression, Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge."
verseByVerse.commentary: Because God has not struck Job down for his words, Elihu says, Job has taken advantage of God's patience and piled up empty talk, hevel, vapour. And words without knowledge is exactly the phrase God will use: Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? (38:2). On that, Elihu and God agree. What Elihu missed, God will not: that the man who said it was still his servant, and had spoken to him, and of him, rightly (42:7).

35.theology: God cannot be harmed by our sin nor enriched by our goodness (vv. 6-7), yet he is grieved and delighted by his people. Crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God, who gives songs in the night (v. 10). Elihu faults Job for waiting on God (v. 14), but waiting on God is faith, and God will answer.
35.examples: The question Elihu leaves with every sufferer is worth asking honestly: am I seeking relief, or am I seeking God himself? Many believers have found that when they seek him, he gives songs in the night before the morning comes. And anyone who is still waiting for God to answer may take heart: waiting is faith, not sin.

36.title: He Delivers the Afflicted by Their Affliction
36.text: <sup>1</sup>And Elihu continued, and said:<sup>2</sup>"Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf.<sup>3</sup>I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker.<sup>4</sup>For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding.<sup>6</sup>He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right.<sup>7</sup>He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne he sets them forever, and they are exalted.<sup>8</sup>And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction,<sup>9</sup>then he declares to them their work and their transgressions, that they are behaving arrogantly.<sup>10</sup>He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity.<sup>11</sup>If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness.<sup>12</sup>But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.<sup>13</sup>"The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them.<sup>14</sup>They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes.<sup>15</sup>He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity.<sup>16</sup>He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness.<sup>17</sup>"But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside.<sup>19</sup>Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress, or all the force of your strength?<sup>20</sup>Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place.<sup>21</sup>Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction.<sup>22</sup>Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him?<sup>23</sup>Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, 'You have done wrong'?<sup>24</sup>"Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung.<sup>25</sup>All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar.<sup>26</sup>Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable.<sup>27</sup>For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain,<sup>28</sup>which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly.<sup>29</sup>Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion?<sup>30</sup>Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea.<sup>31</sup>For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance.<sup>32</sup>He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark.<sup>33</sup>Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.
36.overview: Elihu speaks for God, claiming to be perfect in knowledge. God despises no one; when his people are bound in affliction he shows them their sin and calls them back (vv. 1-14). He delivers the afflicted by their affliction; let Job not be turned aside by anger or choose iniquity over affliction (vv. 15-21). God is great beyond knowing, and the crash of the gathering storm declares his presence (vv. 22-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — God Is Mighty, and Does Not Despise Any
