verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu speaks for God (vv. 1-4), who despises no one and uses affliction to call his people back (vv. 5-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu restates his teaching that affliction is God's instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu continued, and said: "Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf. I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker. For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: In his last speech, two chapters long, Elihu will defend God, ascribe righteousness to my Maker, and that is a good aim. But the last line gives pause: one who is perfect in knowledge is with you. He means himself. In the next chapter he will use exactly this phrase of God: the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge (37:16). Elihu has claimed for himself, without noticing, the title that belongs to God alone. Every preacher who speaks on God's behalf should feel the warning.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding. He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right. He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne he sets them forever, and they are exalted. And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction, then he declares to them their work and their transgressions, that they are behaving arrogantly. He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity. If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness. But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding. A lovely line. The mighty God despises no one, however small. A bruised reed he will not break (Isa 42:3), said of the Servant who is Christ.

This is Elihu's teaching of chapter 33 again: affliction as God's instruction, opening the ear, calling a man back from pride (33:14-30). What was said there stands, including its limit. It is true of how God often deals with his people, and it is not the explanation of Job's suffering (2:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — He Delivers the Afflicted by Their Affliction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God delivers the afflicted through their affliction (vv. 13-15), and Elihu warns Job not to be turned aside (vv. 16-21).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Elihu's best sentence: God rescues his people not only from affliction but through it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them. They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes. He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity. He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the one truly new thought in Elihu's last speeches, and one of the weightiest sentences in the book. God does not only rescue his people from affliction. He rescues them by it. The suffering itself becomes the means of their deliverance: it opens their ears, loosens their grip on the world, drives them to God. In Hebrew the words for afflicted and affliction are almost the same, as if to say: the thing that crushes is the thing that saves.

Paul knew it: suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope (Rom 5:3-4); this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17). And it is the pattern of Christ himself: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8). God delivered the world by the affliction of his Son. The believer may trust that his own affliction is not wasted.

Into a broad place: God wants to bring Job out into open country, with a full table. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me (Ps 18:19). Elihu does not know how true that last phrase is of Job (1:8).

The godless nurse their resentment and never turn to God, even in chains. The cult prostitutes of verse 14 were the men and women of pagan fertility worship (Deut 23:17; 1 Kgs 14:24). Elihu says the godless die young, in the shameful company of the vice they chose.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you. Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside. Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress, or all the force of your strength? Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place. Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu warns Job: you are so taken up with the judgment you think the wicked deserve, and with your own case, that you may be tempted to scoff at God. The greatness of the ransom is the same word as 33:24's ransom: perhaps, do not let the price of your suffering turn you away from God; perhaps, do not think a great payment could buy you out. Either way, the one ransom that could was still to come.

Do not long for the night, the death that swallows whole nations; Job had longed for it since chapter 3 (7:15). Anyone who longs for death today should tell someone at once: a pastor, a friend, a doctor. Job's longing was heard by God, not punished, and he lived to see good days again (42:12). And do not choose sin as a way out of suffering. That is a real temptation for every sufferer, and Elihu is right to name it, though he is wrong to say Job had chosen it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–33 — God Is Great, and We Know Him Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu turns to praise of God's greatness in the rain and the storm (vv. 22-33).
verseByVerse.theology: As Elihu praises, a storm begins to gather, and God will speak from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him? Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, 'You have done wrong'? "Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung. All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar. Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Elihu turns from argument to praise, and his voice changes. God is the great Teacher, and no one teaches him: what man shows him his counsel? (Isa 40:13). No one can tell God he has done wrong. That is the answer to Job's worst charges (19:6; 30:21), and God will make it himself (40:8).

Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung. The right response to God is not argument but praise. Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! (Rev 15:3). We know him not: he is greater than all our understanding. And his years are unsearchable, the word Eliphaz used at the start (5:9) and the psalmist sings: his greatness is unsearchable (Ps 145:3). The friends claimed to have searched God out. The book keeps saying that no one can.

verseByVerse.quote: For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain, which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly. Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion? Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea. For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance. He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark. Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He draws up the drops of water into the clouds and sends them down as rain. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full (Eccl 1:7). Ordinary weather is God at work.

Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion? Clouds spreading like a tent over the sky, thunder, lightning thrown like a spear at its target. The same rain can destroy a nation's harvest or fill its barns; God did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons (Acts 14:17). And its crashing declares his presence: the thunder announces that God is near.

Many readers have noticed that Elihu seems to be describing a storm that is actually coming up as he speaks. The cattle sense it; the thunder rolls. Keep watching the sky. In a few verses the storm will break, and the LORD will speak out of it (38:1).

36.theology: God delivers the afflicted by their affliction (v. 15): suffering can be the means of rescue (Rom 5:3-5), as it was for Christ, who learned obedience through what he suffered. God is great beyond our knowing (v. 26), and those who speak for him must not claim the knowledge that is his alone.
36.examples: For a believer in a long trial, he delivers the afflicted by their affliction is a word to hold on to: the suffering is not wasted. It does not explain any particular pain, and it does not make pain good in itself, but it says God can bring rescue through the very thing that hurts.

37.title: The Almighty: We Cannot Find Him
37.text: <sup>1</sup>"At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place.<sup>2</sup>Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth.<sup>3</sup>Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth.<sup>4</sup>After it his voice roars; he thunders with his majestic voice, and he does not restrain the lightnings when his voice is heard.<sup>5</sup>God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.<sup>6</sup>For to the snow he says, 'Fall on the earth,' likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour.<sup>7</sup>He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it.<sup>8</sup>Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens.<sup>9</sup>From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds.<sup>10</sup>By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast.<sup>11</sup>He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning.<sup>12</sup>They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world.<sup>13</sup>Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.<sup>14</sup>"Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God.<sup>15</sup>Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine?<sup>16</sup>Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge,<sup>17</sup>you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind?<sup>18</sup>Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror?<sup>19</sup>Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness.<sup>20</sup>Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up?<sup>21</sup>"And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them.<sup>22</sup>Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty.<sup>23</sup>The Almighty—we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate.<sup>24</sup>Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit."
37.overview: Elihu trembles at the thunder of God's voice. God commands snow, rain, whirlwind and ice, and turns the clouds whether for correction, for his land, or for love (vv. 1-13). Let Job stop and consider God's works: does he know how the lightning shines or the clouds balance? No one can argue a case with God (vv. 14-20). Golden splendour comes from the north; the Almighty we cannot find, and he does not regard the wise in their own conceit (vv. 21-24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Thunder of His Voice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu trembles at the thunder, and sees all weather doing God's bidding (vv. 1-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu hears the storm as God's voice.

verseByVerse.quote: "At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place. Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth. Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth. After it his voice roars; he thunders with his majestic voice, and he does not restrain the lightnings when his voice is heard. God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The storm that began to gather at the end of chapter 36 is breaking, and Elihu's heart is pounding. He hears the thunder as God's voice, rolling across the sky; the lightning flashes to the ends of the earth. God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.

Scripture often hears God in the thunder: The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders (Ps 29:3). And once, when the Father spoke from heaven about his Son, the crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered (John 12:29). God's voice is too great for human ears to take in. Elihu is right to tremble. In a few moments God will speak from this storm in words.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the snow he says, 'Fall on the earth,' likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour. He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it. Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens. From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds. By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast. He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning. They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world. Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Snow and heavy rain come at his word. When they do, work in the fields stops; every man's hand is sealed up, forced to rest, so that people may see who is really in charge. The animals take shelter. From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds. By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast. Winter itself is his breath.

Here is the wisest thing Elihu says: God sends the storm for different reasons. Sometimes for correction: judgment on sin. Sometimes for his land: the earth needs rain. Sometimes for love: the word is chesed, God's covenant love, the steadfast love Job spoke of in God's care for him (10:12). The friends knew only the first reason, and read every storm as punishment. Elihu, at his best, knows better. The same weather that judges one man waters another's field and is a gift of love to a third. A believer caught in a storm cannot tell from the storm itself which it is. He can know the God who sends it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — God Is Clothed with Awesome Majesty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu tells Job to stop and consider God's works (vv. 14-20), and ends with God's splendour coming from the north (vv. 21-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu ends by saying no one can find God. In the next verse, God finds Job.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God. Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine? Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge, you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind? Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror? Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness. Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God. Stop talking; look. Be still, and know that I am God (Ps 46:10). It is the right advice, and God is about to give Job the fullest possible opportunity to take it.

Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine? Elihu starts to ask Job questions: do you know how clouds float, how lightning is made? It is a foretaste of how God will speak in the next chapter, question after question. And him who is perfect in knowledge is now said of God, where Elihu had said it of himself (36:4). He has found its right owner.

We cannot draw up our case because of darkness. No one can draw up a legal case against God; we are in the dark. Who would ask to be summoned before him, when it would be like being swallowed alive? Job had asked exactly that (31:35). He is about to get it, and he will not be swallowed up.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them. Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty. The Almighty—we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate. Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wind sweeps the clouds away and the sky blazes, too bright to look at, and from the north comes a golden glory. God is dressed in terrifying majesty. Ezekiel saw God come the same way: behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually (Ezek 1:4). Elihu may be describing, without knowing it, the approach of God himself.

These are Elihu's last words. We cannot find him: it is what Job said, Oh, that I knew where I might find him (23:3). Elihu is right. No one can find God by searching. And the very next line of the book is, Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (38:1). Job could not find God, so God came and found Job. That is the whole shape of the gospel: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10).

And the last line is a warning to everyone in the book: God does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit. Not the friends, sure they had searched him out; not Elihu, who called himself perfect in knowledge; not Job, who demanded that God answer him. Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil (Prov 3:7), the two things that were said of Job on the first page (1:1) and called wisdom in the poem (28:28). Now God speaks.

37.theology: God sends storms, and sufferings, for different ends (v. 13), so no one can read his purpose off the weather, and the friends' single explanation fails. Thunder is his voice, and his coming is glory (v. 22). And though man cannot find God (v. 23), God at once comes to Job: the shape of the gospel, in which God seeks the lost.
37.examples: Verse 13 is a steadying word for anyone in a hard season: the storm may be correction, or provision, or love, and from inside it we often cannot tell which. What we can know is the God who sends it, and the chapter ends with him coming near.

38.title: Where Were You?
38.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:<sup>2</sup>"Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?<sup>3</sup>Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.<sup>4</sup>"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.<sup>5</sup>Who determined its measurements—surely you know! Or who stretched the line upon it?<sup>6</sup>On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone,<sup>7</sup>when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?<sup>8</sup>"Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb,<sup>9</sup>when I made clouds its garment and thick darkness its swaddling band,<sup>10</sup>and prescribed limits for it and set bars and doors,<sup>11</sup>and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed'?<sup>12</sup>"Have you commanded the morning since your days began, and caused the dawn to know its place,<sup>13</sup>that it might take hold of the skirts of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it?<sup>14</sup>It is changed like clay under the seal, and its features stand out like a garment.<sup>15</sup>From the wicked their light is withheld, and their uplifted arm is broken.<sup>16</sup>"Have you entered into the springs of the sea, or walked in the recesses of the deep?<sup>17</sup>Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?<sup>18</sup>Have you comprehended the expanse of the earth? Declare, if you know all this.<sup>19</sup>"Where is the way to the dwelling of light, and where is the place of darkness,<sup>20</sup>that you may take it to its territory and that you may discern the paths to its home?<sup>21</sup>You know, for you were born then, and the number of your days is great!<sup>22</sup>"Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or have you seen the storehouses of the hail,<sup>23</sup>which I have reserved for the time of trouble, for the day of battle and war?<sup>24</sup>What is the way to the place where the light is distributed, or where the east wind is scattered upon the earth?<sup>25</sup>"Who has cleft a channel for the torrents of rain and a way for the thunderbolt,<sup>26</sup>to bring rain on a land where no man is, on the desert in which there is no man,<sup>27</sup>to satisfy the waste and desolate land, and to make the ground sprout with grass?<sup>28</sup>"Has the rain a father, or who has begotten the drops of dew?<sup>29</sup>From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who has given birth to the frost of heaven?<sup>30</sup>The waters become hard like stone, and the face of the deep is frozen.<sup>31</sup>"Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion?<sup>32</sup>Can you lead forth the Mazzaroth in their season, or can you guide the Bear with its children?<sup>33</sup>Do you know the ordinances of the heavens? Can you establish their rule on the earth?<sup>34</sup>"Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that a flood of waters may cover you?<sup>35</sup>Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go and say to you, 'Here we are'?<sup>36</sup>Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind?<sup>37</sup>Who can number the clouds by wisdom? Or who can tilt the waterskins of the heavens,<sup>38</sup>when the dust runs into a mass and the clods stick fast together?<sup>39</sup>"Can you hunt the prey for the lion, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions,<sup>40</sup>when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in their thicket?<sup>41</sup>Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God for help, and wander about for lack of food?
38.overview: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind: who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge (vv. 1-3)? Where was Job when God laid the earth's foundation while the morning stars sang, set limits to the sea, commanded the dawn, or saw the gates of death (vv. 4-21)? Has he seen the storehouses of snow, watered empty deserts, bound the Pleiades or numbered the clouds (vv. 22-38)? Can he feed the lion, or the young ravens that cry to God (vv. 39-41)?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asked for a hearing, and God comes. He does not come to explain; he comes to question, and in coming he gives Job what he most needed: himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
After thirty-five chapters of human voices, God speaks. Elihu has just said, The Almighty — we cannot find him (37:23). And the next words are, Then the LORD answered Job. Job could not find God. God found Job.

Notice the name: the LORD, God's covenant name, which the narrator has not used since the prologue. The God of the council in chapters 1 and 2, who called Job my servant, is the God who now speaks. And God answered Job. In chapters 1 and 2 God spoke only to Satan; these are the first words God speaks to Job in the whole book. He speaks out of the whirlwind, the storm Elihu watched gathering. God comes in storm, as he came at Sinai; his way is in whirlwind and storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet (Nah 1:3).

Job had asked again and again for a hearing (13:22; 23:3; 31:35), and that God comes at all is grace. Elihu was right that God owes no one a trial (34:23). He came anyway.

And he came in a storm. It was a great wind out of the wilderness that brought the house down on Job's children (1:19). The kind of thing that broke his life is where God meets him. Many believers have found the same: the place of their deepest loss became the place where God spoke.
verseByVerse.note: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, not with an explanation but with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's first sentence is a rebuke, and a precise one. Counsel is God's plan, his purpose. Job has been speaking about God's purposes as if he understood them, calling God cruel, an enemy, unjust, and in doing so he has put a shadow over God's plan. Without knowledge: he did not know about the council, the challenge Satan made, the delight God had in him. Job will take these words on his own lips at the end (42:3). And God does not say Job is wicked, or that his suffering was punishment. The friends' whole theory falls without a word.

Dress for action like a man means tuck up your robe for hard work or a fight. Like a man is the word from the night Job cursed, A man is conceived (3:3). God treats him as a man fit to be questioned. And he takes Job at his word: Job had said, call, and I will answer (13:22). Now God calls.
verseByVerse.note: “Dress for action like a man” is literally “gird up your loins” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where was Job when God founded the earth (vv. 4-7), set limits to the sea (vv. 8-11) and first commanded the dawn (vv. 12-21)?
verseByVerse.theology: God answers Job's questions with his own, and every one of them is about God. The Maker of the world has not lost control of it, and he still sets limits to the sea.

verseByVerse.quote: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who determined its measurements—surely you know! Or who stretched the line upon it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has been judging how God runs the world. Where was he when it was built? God pictures himself as the builder who drew the plan and stretched the measuring line, and Job was not there. And if you have understanding is pointed. The wisdom poem said what understanding is for a man: to turn away from evil is understanding (28:28). Job has that. What he does not have is the architect's understanding, and he has been speaking as if he did.

The point is not to humiliate Job but to put him in the place of every creature: he came late to a world already made, and he does not have the plans. We see a few feet of a building whose architect saw the whole.

And who is speaking? Hebrews takes the words of a psalm about God laying the earth's foundation and applies them to the Son: You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands (Heb 1:10). The voice from the whirlwind asking Where were you? is the voice of the one through whom all things were made, who would one day stand on that earth in flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone, when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth is a building with foundations sunk and a cornerstone laid. And when the cornerstone went in, there was music: the morning stars singing, all the sons of God shouting for joy. The sons of God are the heavenly council of chapter 1 (1:6). God gives him a glimpse of it, not as a courtroom, but at a celebration. Creation began in joy.

That matters for a man in pain. The world was not made in anger. It was made to shouts of delight, and the God who made it that way has not changed. The New Testament uses the same builder's picture for God's new building, with Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Eph 2:20): the Son through whom the first world was founded (Heb 1:10) is the foundation of the second.

The morning stars and sons of God are angels, joined to the stars in poetry, as in Psalm 148:2–3. They were there, singing, when the earth was founded, so the poem implies they were made before it, though it does not say when.

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb, when I made clouds its garment and thick darkness its swaddling band, and prescribed limits for it and set bars and doors, and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea, the ancient symbol of chaos, is pictured as a newborn baby bursting out of the womb, and God wraps it in swaddling clothes of cloud and darkness, as a mother wraps her infant. The chaos that terrifies men is, to God, a baby he dressed.

And he set it limits. Bars and doors; a line in the sand: Thus far shall you come, and no farther. Jeremiah heard the same: I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea ... though they roar, they cannot pass over it (Jer 5:22). Job had asked, Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me? (7:12). God answers: I do set a guard over the sea.

And the reader has seen those words before in another form. Only against him do not stretch out your hand (1:12); only spare his life (2:6). God set the same kind of limit on Satan that he sets on the waves. The chaos that broke over Job came so far and no farther, because God said so. That is what God was doing all along, while Job thought God had lost control.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you commanded the morning since your days began, and caused the dawn to know its place, that it might take hold of the skirts of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it? It is changed like clay under the seal, and its features stand out like a garment. From the wicked their light is withheld, and their uplifted arm is broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every morning the dawn takes hold of the edges of the earth like a blanket, and shakes it, and the wicked who have been working in the dark fall out. Job complained that the murderer, the adulterer and the thief love the night and are never caught (24:13-17). God answers: I send the dawn every day, and every day it exposes them. From the wicked their light is withheld, and their uplifted arm is broken. Job swore that if he had ever raised my hand against the fatherless, his own arm should be broken from its socket (31:21-22). God answers that he breaks the arm raised against the weak, every day, and the dawn is his witness.

Job tried to curse one day out of existence: let that day be darkness, let it not come into the number of the months (3:4, 6). God asks whether Job has commanded even one morning since your days began. Job tried to unmake a single day. God makes every one.

God has commanded the dawn every morning of Job's life, including the mornings on the ash heap. And the Bible's great dawn is still coming: the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1:78-79), words Zechariah sang over the birth of the forerunner of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you entered into the springs of the sea, or walked in the recesses of the deep? Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness? Have you comprehended the expanse of the earth? Declare, if you know all this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Down to the bottom of the ocean, where the springs rise. Down further, to the gates of death. Deep darkness is what Job called down on his birthday (3:5), and the deep shadow of the grave he dreaded (10:21). Has he seen its gates? God has.

Jesus spoke of those gates too: on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt 16:18). And the risen Christ says, I have the keys of Death and Hades (Rev 1:18). The gates God asks Job about, Christ has opened from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: "Where is the way to the dwelling of light, and where is the place of darkness, that you may take it to its territory and that you may discern the paths to its home? You know, for you were born then, and the number of your days is great!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light and darkness are pictured as living in houses, going out and coming home each day. Does Job know the road to their homes? God knows where darkness lives, and keeps it there.

You know, for you were born then, and the number of your days is great! Gentle irony. Eliphaz once mocked Job, Are you the first man who was born? (15:7). God uses the same irony, but the tone is different. Eliphaz wanted to shut Job up. God is bringing him to see.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — The Storehouses of the Snow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns to the snow, the rain, the stars and the clouds (vv. 22-38).
verseByVerse.theology: Weather and stars are all under God's hand, and his care reaches places no human eye will see.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or have you seen the storehouses of the hail, which I have reserved for the time of trouble, for the day of battle and war? What is the way to the place where the light is distributed, or where the east wind is scattered upon the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps snow and hail in storerooms, like weapons in an armoury, ready for the day he needs them. He used them: hail on Egypt (Exod 9:23), and at Beth-horon there were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword (Josh 10:11). It is kept, and used, for God's purposes.

What is the way to the place where the light is distributed, or where the east wind is scattered upon the earth? The east wind was the hot desert wind; the great wind that killed Job's children came across the wilderness (1:19). God knows where every wind comes from, and where it is going.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who has cleft a channel for the torrents of rain and a way for the thunderbolt, to bring rain on a land where no man is, on the desert in which there is no man, to satisfy the waste and desolate land, and to make the ground sprout with grass?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A way for the thunderbolt echoes the wisdom poem (28:26), which pointed ahead to this moment. Then something striking: God sends rain on a desert where no one lives. No farmer will ever harvest that grass; no human eye will see it grow. God waters it anyway, because he delights in his world for its own sake.

Job has thought of the world as if everything in it must be about him and his case. God's care is much wider than that. He tends places no one will ever visit. If his care reaches the empty desert, it reaches Job, even where Job cannot see it. And it reaches the lonely places in every believer's life that no one else knows about.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has the rain a father, or who has begotten the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who has given birth to the frost of heaven? The waters become hard like stone, and the face of the deep is frozen.
verseByVerse.commentary: Father and mother pictures again: who fathered the rain? Out of whose womb came the ice? No one's but God's. Every drop of dew has a Father. James calls God the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes down (James 1:17). The same Father who begets the dew and brings the frost is the Father of every believer, and he gives good gifts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion? Can you lead forth the Mazzaroth in their season, or can you guide the Bear with its children? Do you know the ordinances of the heavens? Can you establish their rule on the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion? These are the constellations Job himself named when he praised God's power (9:9). The Pleiades, the cluster of stars that seems held together by a chain; Orion, the hunter with his belt; the Mazzaroth, probably another constellation, as the ESV's note says; the Bear with her cubs. Can Job lead them out night by night across the sky? God does.

The ordinances of the heavens: the stars keep God's laws without fail. God once pointed to exactly that to assure his people of his faithfulness: If this fixed order departs from before me ... then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation (Jer 31:36). His promises are as fixed as the stars.
verseByVerse.note: “Mazzaroth” is probably the name of a constellation (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that a flood of waters may cover you? Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go and say to you, 'Here we are'? Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind? Who can number the clouds by wisdom? Or who can tilt the waterskins of the heavens, when the dust runs into a mass and the clods stick fast together?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can Job shout at the clouds and make it rain? Can he dispatch the lightning like a messenger, and have it report back, Here we are? The lightnings are pictured as God's servants reporting for duty, as the heavenly beings came to present themselves before the LORD (1:6). Everything in the sky answers to him.

Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind? Who can number the clouds by wisdom? Or who can tilt the waterskins of the heavens, when the dust runs into a mass and the clods stick fast together? The ESV's note offers another reading for the first line, "the ibis" and "the rooster", birds that seem to know the weather is changing. Either way, whatever wisdom any creature has, God gave it. And the rain clouds are waterskins God tips over, so that the dusty ground turns to mud. Job has been asking where wisdom is (28:12). It is with the one who counts the clouds. And the God who puts wisdom in a bird puts it in a heart: you teach me wisdom in the secret heart (Ps 51:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 39–41 — Who Provides for the Raven?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Can Job feed the lion or the young ravens (vv. 39-41)?
verseByVerse.theology: The first speech ends with God feeding baby birds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you hunt the prey for the lion, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions, when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in their thicket? Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God for help, and wander about for lack of food?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now God turns to the animals. The lion is the king of beasts, and God, not Job, feeds him every day.

And the first speech ends with baby ravens. Their parents are out looking for food; the chicks are squawking in the nest, and God says: that noise is a prayer, and I answer it. He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry (Ps 147:9).

Jesus took this very picture and drew the conclusion Job needed. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! (Luke 12:24). The God who hears raven chicks crying has heard every word Job has cried, and the world Job thought had no one in charge has a Father.

Step back and see what this speech has done. It has not explained Job's suffering; Job never hears about the council, and never will. It has not accused him of any sin; the friends' theory is not even mentioned. It has asked questions, dozens of them, and every question has turned Job's eyes away from himself to the Maker: his wisdom in the foundations, his power over the sea and the stars, his care for deserts and lions and raven chicks. There is humour in it, and tenderness: the sea in swaddling clothes, the baby birds. It is not the voice of a tyrant. It is the voice of a Father showing his son the world he made. The answer to Job's suffering is not a reason. It is a Person, and Job will say so: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you (42:5). For the sufferer who reads this chapter, that is the offer still: not an explanation, but God himself, the God who made everything, rules everything and feeds the ravens. That is not a smaller gift than an explanation. It is the gift Christ gave at Bethany: he did not tell the grieving sisters why, but wept with them and told them who he was, the resurrection and the life (John 11:25, 35).

38.theology: God answers Job not with an explanation but with himself. He brings no charge of sin, so the friends' theory falls without a word, and he shows Job the Maker and ruler of all things, who set limits to the sea as he set limits to Satan (1:12; 2:6). The one who laid the earth's foundation is the Son, the cornerstone of God's new building, the sunrise who visits those in the shadow of death, who holds the keys of death.
38.examples: Many sufferers have found that this chapter helps when explanations do not. Its pictures are tender as well as vast: the sea wrapped like a newborn and told thus far, rain on a desert no one will ever see, raven chicks whose squawking God counts as prayer. A God who cares for all that has not forgotten you.

39.title: Who Has Let the Wild Donkey Go Free?
39.text: <sup>1</sup>"Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does?<sup>2</sup>Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth,<sup>3</sup>when they crouch, bring forth their offspring, and are delivered of their young?<sup>4</sup>Their young ones become strong; they grow up in the open; they go out and do not return to them.<sup>5</sup>"Who has let the wild donkey go free? Who has loosed the bonds of the swift donkey,<sup>6</sup>to whom I have given the arid plain for his home and the salt land for his dwelling place?<sup>7</sup>He scorns the tumult of the city; he hears not the shouts of the driver.<sup>8</sup>He ranges the mountains as his pasture, and he searches after every green thing.<sup>9</sup>"Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?<sup>10</sup>Can you bind him in the furrow with ropes, or will he harrow the valleys after you?<sup>11</sup>Will you depend on him because his strength is great, and will you leave to him your labor?<sup>12</sup>Do you have faith in him that he will return your grain and gather it to your threshing floor?<sup>13</sup>"The wings of the ostrich wave proudly, but are they the pinions and plumage of love?<sup>14</sup>For she leaves her eggs to the earth and lets them be warmed on the ground,<sup>15</sup>forgetting that a foot may crush them and that the wild beast may trample them.<sup>16</sup>She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers; though her labor be in vain, yet she has no fear,<sup>17</sup>because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding.<sup>18</sup>When she rouses herself to flee, she laughs at the horse and his rider.<sup>19</sup>"Do you give the horse his might? Do you clothe his neck with a mane?<sup>20</sup>Do you make him leap like the locust? His majestic snorting is terrifying.<sup>21</sup>He paws in the valley and exults in his strength; he goes out to meet the weapons.<sup>22</sup>He laughs at fear and is not dismayed; he does not turn back from the sword.<sup>23</sup>Upon him rattle the quiver, the flashing spear, and the javelin.<sup>24</sup>With fierceness and rage he swallows the ground; he cannot stand still at the sound of the trumpet.<sup>25</sup>When the trumpet sounds, he says 'Aha!' He smells the battle from afar, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.<sup>26</sup>"Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads his wings toward the south?<sup>27</sup>Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up and makes his nest on high?<sup>28</sup>On the rock he dwells and makes his home, on the rocky crag and stronghold.<sup>29</sup>From there he spies out the prey; his eyes behold it from far away.<sup>30</sup>His young ones suck up blood, and where the slain are, there is he."
39.overview: God shows Job the wild creatures: the mountain goats and deer giving birth unseen, the wild donkey he set free, the wild ox no one can yoke (vv. 1-12). The foolish ostrich outruns the horse, and the war horse laughs at fear (vv. 13-25). The hawk and the eagle find their way and their food by the wisdom God gave them, not Job (vv. 26-30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Who Has Let the Wild Donkey Go Free?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God points to wild creatures that no one tends but him (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Creatures no one feeds, tames or even sees: God knows each one. The world is larger than man, and all of it is his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does? Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth, when they crouch, bring forth their offspring, and are delivered of their young? Their young ones become strong; they grow up in the open; they go out and do not return to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? God turns from the sky to the animals, and the first thing he points to is a birth. High on the mountains, where no shepherd goes, the wild goats give birth, and the deer in the thickets. No human being counts their months or sits with them in labour. God does. The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth (Ps 29:9). Jesus said the same of the smallest bird: not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father (Matt 10:29).

Look at the animals God chooses in this chapter. Nearly every one is wild: goats, deer, donkey, ox, ostrich, hawk, eagle. Most never meet man, and even the war horse, the one tame creature here, has a courage no rider gave it. God tends them all, for their own sake. Job has spoken as if the whole world should be arranged around his case. God shows him a world full of creatures God cares for that have nothing to do with Job at all.

And there is a line here that a bereaved father would feel: they go out and do not return to them. The young grow up and leave, and do not come back. God knew every one of those births and every one of those leavings. He knew the births of Job's ten children, and their going.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who has let the wild donkey go free? Who has loosed the bonds of the swift donkey, to whom I have given the arid plain for his home and the salt land for his dwelling place? He scorns the tumult of the city; he hears not the shouts of the driver. He ranges the mountains as his pasture, and he searches after every green thing.
verseByVerse.commentary: Who has let the wild donkey go free? The wild donkey has run all through this book. Job compared his cry to its bray (6:5); Zophar used it as an insult (11:12); Job likened the homeless poor to wild donkeys in the desert (24:5). Now God speaks of it, and with obvious pleasure. He set it free. He gave it the salt flats for a home. It roams the hills looking for every green shoot. God made it free, and he enjoys its freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger? Can you bind him in the furrow with ropes, or will he harrow the valleys after you? Will you depend on him because his strength is great, and will you leave to him your labor? Do you have faith in him that he will return your grain and gather it to your threshing floor?
verseByVerse.commentary: Is the wild ox willing to serve you? The wild ox, the great aurochs, is stronger than any farm animal. Try to yoke it to a plough, and see what happens. It will not sleep in Job's stable or bring in his harvest. Job once owned five hundred yoke of oxen (1:3), all tame. He cannot command this one. Christian readers may also remember the wild oxen of Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross: Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen! (Ps 22:21). The link is only a shared picture, not this chapter's meaning, but it is a true one: brute strength no man can yoke closed in on the Son of God in his suffering, and God rescued him by raising him from the dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Ostrich and the War Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows Job the foolish ostrich and the fearless war horse, both his work and both beyond Job's control (vv. 13-25).
verseByVerse.theology: A silly bird and a fearless horse, both God's work and both beyond Job's control. God speaks of them with something like a smile.

verseByVerse.quote: "The wings of the ostrich wave proudly, but are they the pinions and plumage of love? For she leaves her eggs to the earth and lets them be warmed on the ground, forgetting that a foot may crush them and that the wild beast may trample them. She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers; though her labor be in vain, yet she has no fear, because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding. When she rouses herself to flee, she laughs at the horse and his rider.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone becomes almost comic. The ostrich flaps her great wings as if she were proud of them, but she cannot fly. Plumage of love is a difficult phrase; the ESV's note says the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. It is probably a play on the Hebrew name of the stork, a bird thought of as caring for its young, whose name sounds like the word for steadfast love, chesed. The ostrich has the feathers and not the love. She lays her eggs in the sand and wanders off, as if they were not hers. Even jackals ... nurse their young; but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness (Lam 4:3).

Because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding. When she rouses herself to flee, she laughs at the horse and his rider. God made a bird without much sense, on purpose, and she survives by the gift he did give her: speed. She can outrun a horse. Job called himself a companion of ostriches in his misery (30:29). God describes the ostrich with a smile. Even the foolish creatures are part of his wise design, and he is not embarrassed by them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you give the horse his might? Do you clothe his neck with a mane? Do you make him leap like the locust? His majestic snorting is terrifying. He paws in the valley and exults in his strength; he goes out to meet the weapons. He laughs at fear and is not dismayed; he does not turn back from the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary: Do you give the horse his might? From the ostrich that laughs at the horse to the horse that laughs at fear. The war horse is one of the great portraits in the Bible: the arched neck, the flowing mane, the leap, the snort, the stamping hoof, the charge straight at the swords. Who gave it that courage? Not Job. Scripture admires the war horse and will not trust it: The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue (Ps 33:17). When Israel's King came, he came humble and mounted on a donkey (Zech 9:9). And when he comes again, John saw him on another horse: behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war (Rev 19:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Upon him rattle the quiver, the flashing spear, and the javelin. With fierceness and rage he swallows the ground; he cannot stand still at the sound of the trumpet. When the trumpet sounds, he says 'Aha!' He smells the battle from afar, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.
verseByVerse.commentary: The rider's weapons clatter on his back; he eats up the ground at a gallop; he cannot stand still when the trumpet blows, and he snorts Aha! as if he loved the fight. The picture is full of life and noise. God delights in the creatures he made, even the fierce ones. Job had thought God's attention was fixed on tormenting him. God's attention is on everything, and much of it is joy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–30 — The Hawk and the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God ends with the hawk and the eagle, which find their way and their food without Job's help (vv. 26-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The birds find their way and their food by the wisdom God gave them. Job did not teach them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads his wings toward the south? Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up and makes his nest on high? On the rock he dwells and makes his home, on the rocky crag and stronghold. From there he spies out the prey; his eyes behold it from far away. His young ones suck up blood, and where the slain are, there is he."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every autumn the hawks fly south. Who taught them the way? Job did not. Even the stork in the heavens knows her times (Jer 8:7), because God built the knowledge into her. The eagle rises and builds where no one can reach. They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles (Isa 40:31).

The speech ends not with a pretty picture but a hard one: the eagle's chicks feeding on blood, the great bird circling wherever there are bodies. God does not hide the harsh side of his world. Jesus used the same picture for the certainty of judgment: Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matt 24:28). The creation God shows Job is not tame or sentimental. It is wild, and beautiful, and sometimes terrible, and all of it is under his hand. That is the God Job must reckon with, and the God Job can trust.

39.theology: Every creature God names is wild and outside man's control, and God knows and tends each one. The world is not arranged around Job, and God's care is wider than Job's case. The one who knows each birth on the mountains is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3), and in Jesus that care came near enough to be seen. God delights in his creatures, and does not hide the harsh side of his world. The King who made the war horse came on a donkey, and will come again on a white horse.
39.examples: This chapter invites a slower look at the world: a walk outside, or a nature film, can become an act of worship when we remember that God saw every birth on the mountains and enjoys the wild donkey's freedom. For a parent whose children have grown and gone, or gone in death, the line about the young who do not return is a reminder that God knew every one of those leavings too.

40.title: Will You Condemn Me That You May Be in the Right?
40.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Job:<sup>2</sup>"Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty? He who argues with God, let him answer it."<sup>3</sup>Then Job answered the LORD and said:<sup>4</sup>"Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth.<sup>5</sup>I have spoken once, and I will not answer; twice, but I will proceed no further."<sup>6</sup>Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:<sup>7</sup>"Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.<sup>8</sup>Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?<sup>9</sup>Have you an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like his?<sup>10</sup>"Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity; clothe yourself with glory and splendor.<sup>11</sup>Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him.<sup>12</sup>Look on everyone who is proud and bring him low and tread down the wicked where they stand.<sup>13</sup>Hide them all in the dust together; bind their faces in the world below.<sup>14</sup>Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you.<sup>15</sup>"Behold, Behemoth, which I made as I made you; he eats grass like an ox.<sup>16</sup>Behold, his strength in his loins, and his power in the muscles of his belly.<sup>17</sup>He makes his tail stiff like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are knit together.<sup>18</sup>His bones are tubes of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron.<sup>19</sup>"He is the first of the works of God; let him who made him bring near his sword!<sup>20</sup>For the mountains yield food for him where all the wild beasts play.<sup>21</sup>Under the lotus plants he lies, in the shelter of the reeds and in the marsh.<sup>22</sup>For his shade the lotus trees cover him; the willows of the brook surround him.<sup>23</sup>Behold, if the river is turbulent he is not frightened; he is confident though Jordan rushes against his mouth.<sup>24</sup>Can one take him by his eyes, or pierce his nose with a snare?
40.overview: Job lays his hand on his mouth (vv. 1-5). God speaks again: will Job condemn God to be in the right, and can his own arm save him (vv. 6-14)? Then God shows him Behemoth, a fellow creature beyond Job's power and wholly in God's (vv. 15-24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Lay My Hand on My Mouth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the faultfinder to answer, and Job falls silent (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who demanded a hearing has nothing to say. It is the beginning of wisdom, not yet the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Job: "Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty? He who argues with God, let him answer it."
verseByVerse.commentary: God pauses and turns to Job directly. Job had said, Then call, and I will answer (13:22), and ended his last speech with Let the Almighty answer me! (31:35). God has called, and asked question after question. Now it is Job's turn: let him answer it. He who argues is one word in Hebrew, mokiach: the arbiter Job longed for: There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both (9:33). In the meantime he has been doing the job himself, sitting in judgment on God. God names it gently and unmistakably.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered the LORD and said: "Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth. I have spoken once, and I will not answer; twice, but I will proceed no further."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who filled chapters with argument has nothing to say. I am of small account: the word means light, of little weight. The princes of his city once laid their hands on their mouths before him (29:9), and he told the friends to do it (21:5). Now he does it before God.

Once ... twice means "more than enough". Elihu used it of God (God speaks in one way, and in two, 33:14), and the psalmist too: Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God (Ps 62:11). Job means: I have said all I had to say, and more. He does not withdraw a word yet; he stops adding to them.

Repentance will come in chapter 42. For now there is silence, the right first response to God. The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (Hab 2:20). David prayed it in his own trouble: I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it (Ps 39:9). Paul says the law's purpose is that every mouth may be stopped before God (Rom 3:19). A believer who has argued with God in the dark may come to the same place: not yet an answer, but a hand over the mouth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Will You Condemn Me That You May Be in the Right?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's second speech: Job has condemned God to justify himself, yet no man's right hand can save him (vv. 6-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart of God's answer: Job has defended himself by accusing God, and no man's right hand can save him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: "Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me. Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Silence is not enough; God is not finished. He speaks a second time, with the same summons as before (38:3).

Here is the real charge against Job. Not that he sinned before his suffering; God never says that. It is that in defending his innocence, Job has put God in the wrong. To make himself right, he has been willing to make God unjust: an enemy, cruel, a God who mocks the innocent. That is exactly what Elihu said: he justified himself rather than God (32:2). Job was right that he was innocent. He was wrong to buy his innocence at God's expense.

The first question turns Job's own words round. Job said, God has put me in the wrong (19:6), and As God lives, who has taken away my right (27:2), where my right is mishpat, justice. God asks: will you put me in the wrong? Literally, will you annul my mishpat?

Every sufferer is tempted here. To keep our own sense of being in the right, we accuse God. Paul will not have it: Let God be true though every one were a liar (Rom 3:4). And the gospel shows that we do not have to choose between God's righteousness and our own acquittal. God set forth Christ so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). In the cross, God is in the right and the believer is declared righteous, both at once: no one has to condemn God to be saved.
verseByVerse.note: “Gird up your loins” means tuck up your robe for action, as a man does before a contest.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like his? "Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity; clothe yourself with glory and splendor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has an arm; he swore it should be broken if he ever raised it against the orphan (31:22). But an arm like God's, that holds up the world and brings down the proud?

No man has, which is exactly why God himself had to act. Isaiah saw it: God saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation (Isa 59:16). And the prophet asked of the suffering Servant, to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? (Isa 53:1), a question John applies to Jesus (John 12:38). The arm of the LORD is a person. Christ is God's arm stretched out to save.

Majesty and splendour are the robes God wears: O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty (Ps 104:1). Put on God's robes, if you can. With holy irony, God invites Job to try being God for a day.

verseByVerse.quote: Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him. Look on everyone who is proud and bring him low and tread down the wicked where they stand. Hide them all in the dust together; bind their faces in the world below. Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has complained for chapters that the wicked prosper and God does nothing (21; 24). Very well: humble every proud man, crush the wicked where they stand, and run the moral government of the world yourself. Job cannot even heal his own sores.

Only God can do this, and he will. The LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty (Isa 2:12); he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts (Luke 1:51). The wicked will be judged, but on God's day and by God's arm.

If Job could do all that, God says, his own right hand could save him, and he would not need God. He cannot, and neither can anyone. His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him (Ps 98:1). By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing (Eph 2:8). The right hand that saves is God's, and the one who sits at it is Christ (Heb 1:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — Behemoth, Which I Made as I Made You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behemoth, made as Job was made, lies at ease where only its Maker can come near (vv. 15-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Behemoth is a creature Job could never master, made by the same hand that made him and wholly in God's power.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, Behemoth, which I made as I made you; he eats grass like an ox. Behold, his strength in his loins, and his power in the muscles of his belly. He makes his tail stiff like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are knit together. His bones are tubes of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now God shows Job two great creatures, and the first is Behemoth. The name is a plural of the ordinary word for beast: the beast of beasts. Many readers see the hippopotamus, a grass-eater of enormous strength living in the marshes; others see a picture of all the untamed power on the land, as Leviathan pictures the power of the sea. One detail keeps the question open: he makes his tail stiff like a cedar, and a hippopotamus has a short, stubby tail. God does not name the beast; he describes it until Job can feel its weight: loins, belly, thighs, bones like pipes of bronze, limbs like iron bars.

Look at the first words: which I made as I made you. Behemoth and Job are fellow creatures, made by the same hand, and God is not threatened by what threatens us.

Is Behemoth a dinosaur? Some young-earth readers think so, pointing to the tail like a cedar and to the first of the works of God (v. 19), and on this commentary’s view of a young creation, in which the land animals and man were made on the same sixth day (Genesis 1:24–27), the idea is not impossible. But God tells Job to behold it, a creature Job could see, made as I made you. This commentary takes the likeliest reading to be a real animal Job knew, perhaps the hippopotamus, drawn larger than life in poetry, as Leviathan is.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV note calls Behemoth a large animal of uncertain identity; the elephant has also been suggested.

verseByVerse.quote: "He is the first of the works of God; let him who made him bring near his sword! For the mountains yield food for him where all the wild beasts play. Under the lotus plants he lies, in the shelter of the reeds and in the marsh. For his shade the lotus trees cover him; the willows of the brook surround him. Behold, if the river is turbulent he is not frightened; he is confident though Jordan rushes against his mouth. Can one take him by his eyes, or pierce his nose with a snare?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the chief of God's land creatures, and only the one who made him can come near him with a sword. The mountains feed him while the wild animals play around him. He lies at complete ease in the shade of the lotus, the river roaring against his mouth, and he does not care (Jordan probably stands here for any torrent).

It is fair to ask why God answers a bereaved and diseased man with a description of a river beast. Here is why. Job has been living as though the power that crushed him were outside God's control, or worse, were God turned enemy. So God takes the most unmanageable thing Job can picture and says: I made that, as I made you; it grazes where I feed it; only my sword comes near it. Whatever is too strong for you is not too strong for me. If you are in a trouble you cannot take by the eyes or lead by the nose, this is the God you are dealing with, and he is not describing his rival. He is describing his livestock.

The New Testament shows the Maker doing exactly that to every power that sets itself up against him: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15). What Job could not approach, Christ has conquered.

40.theology:
God's charge is that Job put God in the wrong to justify himself (v. 8; 32:2). God is true though every man be a liar (Rom 3:4), and in Christ he is both just and the justifier (Rom 3:26).

No man's arm can save him (vv. 9, 14); God's own arm brought salvation (Isa 59:16). Behemoth, beyond Job's power, is wholly in God's (v. 19), and Christ has triumphed over every power (Col 2:15).
40.examples: The man who wanted an arbiter (9:33) has been sitting as God's judge; called to answer, he lays his hand on his mouth. Anyone who has felt wronged by life meets God's question here, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?, and the gospel's answer to it: in Christ God is just and the believer is acquitted.

41.title: King Over All the Sons of Pride
41.text: <sup>1</sup>"Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook or press down his tongue with a cord?<sup>2</sup>Can you put a rope in his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook?<sup>3</sup>Will he make many pleas to you? Will he speak to you soft words?<sup>4</sup>Will he make a covenant with you to take him for your servant forever?<sup>5</sup>Will you play with him as with a bird, or will you put him on a leash for your girls?<sup>6</sup>Will traders bargain over him?
