Who would come near him with a bridle?<sup>14</sup>Who can open the doors of his face? Around his teeth is terror.<sup>15</sup>His back is made of rows of shields, shut up closely as with a seal.<sup>16</sup>One is so near to another that no air can come between them.<sup>17</sup>They are joined one to another; they clasp each other and cannot be separated.<sup>18</sup>His sneezings flash forth light, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn.<sup>19</sup>Out of his mouth go flaming torches; sparks of fire leap forth.<sup>20</sup>Out of his nostrils comes forth smoke, as from a boiling pot and burning rushes.<sup>21</sup>His breath kindles coals, and a flame comes forth from his mouth.<sup>22</sup>In his neck abides strength, and terror dances before him.<sup>23</sup>The folds of his flesh stick together, firmly cast on him and immovable.<sup>24</sup>His heart is hard as a stone, hard as the lower millstone.<sup>25</sup>When he raises himself up, the mighty are afraid; at the crashing they are beside themselves.<sup>26</sup>Though the sword reaches him, it does not avail, nor the spear, the dart, or the javelin.<sup>27</sup>He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.<sup>28</sup>The arrow cannot make him flee; for him, sling stones are turned to stubble.<sup>29</sup>Clubs are counted as stubble; he laughs at the rattle of javelins.<sup>30</sup>His underparts are like sharp potsherds; he spreads himself like a threshing sledge on the mire.<sup>31</sup>He makes the deep boil like a pot; he makes the sea like a pot of ointment.<sup>32</sup>Behind him he leaves a shining wake; one would think the deep to be white-haired.<sup>33</sup>On earth there is not his like, a creature without fear.<sup>34</sup>He sees everything that is high; he is king over all the sons of pride."
41.overview: Can Job hook Leviathan, rope his nose, make a covenant with him, keep him as a pet or sell him to merchants? Let him lay a hand on the creature once and he will not try again; human hope against him is false, and no one dares rouse him (vv. 1-9). Who then is he who can stand before me? Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? (vv. 10-11). God describes the creature at length: shields sealed along his back, terror around his teeth, light and fire and smoke from his mouth and nostrils, a heart hard as the lower millstone, the mighty afraid when he rises (vv. 12-25). Sword, spear, arrow and club are straw to him; he boils the deep and leaves a white wake (vv. 26-32). On earth there is not his like, a creature without fear, king over all the sons of pride (vv. 33-34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Will You Put Him on a Leash for Your Girls?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No hook, rope, covenant or harpoon can master Leviathan; and if no one dares rouse him, who can stand before God (vv. 1-11)?
verseByVerse.theology: If no man can face the creature, no man can face the Creator, and no one has ever put God in his debt.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook or press down his tongue with a cord? Can you put a rope in his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook? Will he make many pleas to you? Will he speak to you soft words? Will he make a covenant with you to take him for your servant forever? Will you play with him as with a bird, or will you put him on a leash for your girls?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second creature is Leviathan, and the questions begin exactly where the last chapter ended: Can one take him by his eyes, or pierce his nose with a snare? (40:24). Its identity is uncertain (ESV note). Much in the description fits the crocodile, and much of it, as we will see, goes far beyond any animal.

Will he make many pleas to you? These are four impossibilities, each a little joke at the expense of human mastery: he will not beg you, negotiate terms, sign on as a lifelong servant, or be walked on a string for the children. Job has spent the book begging for a hearing and asking God for terms; he cannot get either from a beast. The words also cut the other way. It is Job who has been making pleas and speaking soft words: Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser (9:15); I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy (19:16). The beast will not plead with Job; Job has been pleading all along, and with the only one who hears.

But hear what the Psalms say of the same creature: There go the ships, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it (Ps 104:26). The monster no man can leash was made by God for sport, splashing in an ocean God made to hold him. What is unmanageable to us is playful to him.

Texts from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast, tell of a sea dragon, Lotan, fought by their gods. Scripture uses the name in poetry and turns the story upside down: Leviathan is a creature God made, not a rival god.
verseByVerse.note: Job 41:1–8 is 40:25–32 in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Will traders bargain over him? Will they divide him up among the merchants? Can you fill his skin with harpoons or his head with fishing spears? Lay your hands on him; remember the battle—you will not do it again! Behold, the hope of a man is false; he is laid low even at the sight of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No market will handle him and no harpoon will hold him. Then God says something almost amused: try it once, and you will remember the battle. Most of us have a Leviathan we have laid hands on once and remember the battle: a craving, an illness, an enemy, a grief, the death we cannot out-wrestle. The point is not to try harder. It is to notice who is speaking about the creature as casually as a farmer speaks about his cattle.

The hope of a man is false is Job's own theme: he said his days come to their end without hope (7:6) and that God destroys the hope of man (14:19). Hope resting on human strength is a lie, and one look at what is really out there flattens it. That is not cruelty; it is the clearing of the ground. False hope has to die before true hope can be planted.

verseByVerse.quote: No one is so fierce that he dares to stir him up. Who then is he who can stand before me? Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one is so fierce as to stir him up, yet someone did dare, in a manner of speaking. In his first bitter speech Job called for the cursers of days, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan (3:8), to blot out the night he was conceived. Job had summoned the monster as an ally against his own life. God now tells him what he was playing with.

Who then is he who can stand before me? Here is the turn the whole speech has been building towards. God has not been giving Job a lesson in zoology. The argument is: you cannot look this creature in the eye, and I made him. If the works of my hands overwhelm you, what will you do with me, whom you have summoned to court? Every question about ostrich and hawk and Behemoth and Leviathan has been carrying this one question on its back.

Who has first given to me? quietly demolishes Job's case. Job had reasoned that a blameless life put God under some obligation to him. But no one hands God anything first. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine (Ps 50:12). Paul sings this very line at the end of eleven chapters on salvation: Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen (Rom 11:35-36). Nothing we put into God's hands got there except from his hand first. So no believer is ever owed, and none is ever left out: what cannot be earned can be given.
verseByVerse.note: Job 41:9–34 is 41:1–26 in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — His Sneezings Flash Forth Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God describes Leviathan's frame: the armour of sealed shields, the fire and smoke from his mouth, the heart hard as a millstone (vv. 12-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The description reaches past any living animal, towards the evil power that Scripture elsewhere pictures as a sea-dragon.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will not keep silence concerning his limbs, or his mighty strength, or his goodly frame. Who can strip off his outer garment? Who would come near him with a bridle? Who can open the doors of his face? Around his teeth is terror. His back is made of rows of shields, shut up closely as with a seal. One is so near to another that no air can come between them. They are joined one to another; they clasp each other and cannot be separated.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is plainly enjoying the creature he made. Who will pull off his hide as you would a coat, or bridle him like a horse, or reach in and prise open his jaws? The doors of his face is a marvellous phrase for a mouth that opens like a gate, with a ring of terror set round it.

The armour is described the way a soldier would describe a wall of shields: overlapping, sealed, airtight, interlocked and impossible to prise apart. There is no gap in him to strike at. The ESV notes an alternative reading in which the pride of the creature, rather than his back, is in those rows of shields, which fits the end of the chapter, where he is king over the proud. Evil, seen from below, always looks like this: sealed, seamless, no way in.

verseByVerse.quote: His sneezings flash forth light, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn. Out of his mouth go flaming torches; sparks of fire leap forth. Out of his nostrils comes forth smoke, as from a boiling pot and burning rushes. His breath kindles coals, and a flame comes forth from his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A crocodile surfacing and blowing spray in the sunlight could account for some of this, and the eyelids of the dawn is a lovely line: eyes that open like daybreak over the water. But torches, sparks, smoke and burning coals are not natural history. The description has grown into something else, and the reader is meant to notice.

Elsewhere the Bible uses this sea-dragon as its picture of the evil power that God has already broken and will one day destroy. You crushed the heads of Leviathan (Ps 74:14). Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? (Isa 51:9; cf. Job 9:13). And with a date on it: In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent ... and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea (Isa 27:1). John names him: the great dragon ... that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan (Rev 12:9; 20:2).

Job 41 does not say Leviathan is the devil. What it says is that the most terrifying power in the world is a creature God made, described, feeds and governs. The reader of Job, who has seen the Accuser in chapter 1 and knows he is still at large, is being told where such power stands: on the creature's side of the line, under the Maker's sword. And the Maker came in flesh that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:14-15).

verseByVerse.quote: In his neck abides strength, and terror dances before him. The folds of his flesh stick together, firmly cast on him and immovable. His heart is hard as a stone, hard as the lower millstone. When he raises himself up, the mighty are afraid; at the crashing they are beside themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terror goes ahead of him like a dancer: you feel him coming before you see him. His flesh is cast solid, like metal poured in a mould. And his heart is the lower millstone, the one that never moves and takes all the grinding. Nothing in him is soft, and nothing in him can be moved.

He only has to rise out of the water and the strongest men lose their nerve. The ESV notes that the mighty may be read the gods: even the powers the nations feared were said to flinch.

Hold that hard heart beside the man God is speaking to. Job's heart has been broken open, poured out, made bitter, wrung with grief. He might well have envied a heart of stone that feels nothing. But the millstone heart belongs to the beast, and a heart that can be broken is the heart God can teach. God promises to take out hearts of stone, not to give them (Ezek 36:26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–34 — On Earth There Is Not His Like
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every weapon fails against him; he churns the deep and reigns over all the sons of pride (vv. 26-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing God shows Job is the fiercest thing in the world, and it is a creature with a Maker and a sword over it. Then Job answers.

verseByVerse.quote: Though the sword reaches him, it does not avail, nor the spear, the dart, or the javelin. He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood. The arrow cannot make him flee; for him, sling stones are turned to stubble. Clubs are counted as stubble; he laughs at the rattle of javelins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole armoury of the ancient world is laid out and dismissed, weapon by weapon: sword, spear, dart, javelin, arrow, sling, club. Iron might as well be straw; bronze might as well be rotten wood.

There is one weapon the chapter has not dismissed. Of Behemoth God said, let him who made him bring near his sword (40:19), and of Leviathan the prophet says the day is coming when the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will kill the dragon in the sea (Isa 27:1). The Maker's sword is the only sword. Say it to anyone fighting something too big for them with iron and bronze: the arsenal is not the answer, and there is a sword that is.

verseByVerse.quote: His underparts are like sharp potsherds; he spreads himself like a threshing sledge on the mire. He makes the deep boil like a pot; he makes the sea like a pot of ointment. Behind him he leaves a shining wake; one would think the deep to be white-haired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He drags his belly over the mud like a threshing sledge, all broken pottery and edges. He churns the sea until it boils and froths like oil stirred in a pan, and the white water trails behind him so that the deep looks like an old man's head.

In the Gospels there is a boat on such a sea, men certain they are going to die, and a man asleep in the stern. And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. Then: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:39, 41). God asked Job, Who then is he who can stand before me? (v. 10), and the disciples, staring at flat water, ask the same question in the other direction and are looking straight at the answer. Their Scriptures had one answer: the LORD stills the sea (Ps 107:29). The deep that boils under Leviathan lies down at the voice of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: On earth there is not his like, a creature without fear. He sees everything that is high; he is king over all the sons of pride."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has said something like this once before in this book, about a very different creature: there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil (1:8; 2:3). Two have no equal on earth, and the difference between them is one word. The man is unequalled because he fears God. The beast is unequalled because he fears nothing. Fearlessness is not the summit of creation; it is the mark of the monster.

He sees everything that is high: he looks every lofty thing in the eye and is not impressed. Sons of pride: the proud beasts of 28:8 are his subjects, and the phrase makes him the king of everything that will not bow. If pride has a throne, this is who sits on it. The Accuser of chapters 1 and 2, who thought love of God was self-interest in disguise, belongs to that kingdom. So, in a smaller way, does the self-justifying that God has just named in Job (40:8).

And see how God ends. Two whole chapters of questions, and the last word is not about Job's sin at all. It is a creature: enormous, armoured, fearless, crowned over all the proud, and made. Nothing in the speech says that God's power is a reason to stop asking questions; it says the King of all the proud has a Maker who keeps him, feeds him, and will one day run him through. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). The Lion of Judah has conquered, and he did it as a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Rev 5:5-6). That is how the sons of pride are undone, and why a broken man kneeling in ashes is closer to the throne than the king of the fearless will ever be.

Job has heard enough. The next words in the book are his.

41.theology:
No one can stand before the creature, so no one can stand before the Creator (v. 10); and no one has ever given God anything first (v. 11; Rom 11:35-36). Job's case assumed a debt that cannot exist.

The description passes beyond any living animal, and Scripture elsewhere makes the sea-dragon its picture of the evil power God has broken and will destroy (Ps 74:14; Rev 12:9). Job 41 does not identify Leviathan with Satan, but it places every such power on the creature's side of the line, under the Maker's sword, which Christ wielded through death (Heb 2:14-15). The sea that boils under Leviathan lies still at his word (Mark 4:39-41).

The creature is unequalled on earth because he fears nothing (v. 33); the man was unequalled because he feared God (1:8). Fearlessness is the mark of the monster, and pride its kingdom (Jas 4:6).
41.examples: Most of us have laid hands on some Leviathan once and remember the battle: a craving, an illness, a grief. This chapter does not tell us to try harder. It shows us the Maker who speaks of such powers as a farmer speaks of his cattle, whose sword alone does not fail, and whose Son stilled the sea with a word (Mark 4:41).

42.title: But Now My Eye Sees You
42.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered the LORD and said:<sup>2</sup>"I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.<sup>3</sup>'Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.<sup>4</sup>'Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you make it known to me.'<sup>5</sup>I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you;<sup>6</sup>therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes."<sup>7</sup>After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.<sup>8</sup>Now therefore take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and offer up a burnt offering for yourselves. And my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer not to deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has."<sup>9</sup>So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD had told them, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD restored the fortunes of Job, when he had prayed for his friends. And the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.<sup>11</sup>Then came to him all his brothers and sisters and all who had known him before, and ate bread with him in his house. And they showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him. And each of them gave him a piece of money and a ring of gold.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning. And he had 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys.<sup>13</sup>He had also seven sons and three daughters.<sup>14</sup>And he called the name of the first daughter Jemimah, and the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-happuch.<sup>15</sup>And in all the land there were no women so beautiful as Job's daughters. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.<sup>16</sup>And after this Job lived 140 years, and saw his sons, and his sons' sons, four generations.<sup>17</sup>And Job died, an old man, and full of days.
42.overview: Job confesses that no purpose of God's can be thwarted and that now his eye sees him, and he repents in dust and ashes (vv. 1-6). God rebukes the friends for not speaking rightly of him, as Job has, and accepts Job's prayer for them (vv. 7-9). The LORD restores Job twofold, gives him seven sons and three named daughters with an inheritance, and he dies full of days (vv. 10-17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Now My Eye Sees You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job answers without protest: he spoke of things too wonderful for him, and now he has seen God (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job gets no explanation and needs none: he has seen God, and that ends the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered the LORD and said: "I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the first time since chapter 3, Job's answer is not a protest. He begins where the whirlwind left him: God can do all things. That much Job always believed; he said it himself in the worst of his bitterness (9:4-12). What is new is the second half: God's purpose. Job had come to suspect that God's purpose was against him, or that God had no purpose at all and simply crushed whatever came under his hand. Now he says the word purpose without flinching. There is a plan; it is God's; nothing can break it.

Job still does not know why his children died. He has not been told about chapter 1, about the accusation, about the permission given. He walks out of the whirlwind with no more information than he walked in with, and with his questions answered in a way he never asked for: not an explanation, but a Person. Hold that in mind before the restoration begins, because most sufferers get the same thing in the same order.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know. 'Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you make it known to me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job quotes God's first words from the storm, Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? (38:2), and accepts the charge, which is what a man does when he agrees rather than when he is merely cornered. He had spoken about things too wonderful for me as though he had the file in front of him. He did not.

He quotes God a second time (38:3; 40:7), almost humorously: he repeats the summons to answer and then does not argue at all. He demanded a hearing for chapters; given it, he does not present his case.

verseByVerse.quote: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the summit of the book. Job's faith before the test was real: God himself called him blameless and upright and said there was none like him on the earth (1:8). But it was faith by report. He had heard about God from his fathers and from the world and from a lifetime of obedience, and it was true, and it was not enough for this. Now he has met him. Nothing in the whirlwind speeches told Job a fact he could have written down as an answer. They gave him God, and that turned out to be the thing he actually wanted.

Sight of God always has this effect on honest men. Woe is me! For I am lost ... for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts! (Isa 6:5). Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8). Job's own hope had been exactly this: whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another (19:27). He has it early, and standing up, not raised from the dead.

What does he repent of? Not the sins the friends invented; God is about to call those speeches wrong (v. 7), and God never charges Job with the crimes of chapter 22. The verb rendered I despise myself has no object stated in the Hebrew, and the ESV's note says the last words can also be rendered "and am comforted upon" dust and ashes. Job is taking back what he said about God and letting go of the case he had built. Dust and ashes is where he has been sitting since 2:8, and what he called himself in bitterness: I have become like dust and ashes (30:19). The place has not changed. The man in it has.

And with this verse the question that started everything is answered. Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). Job has lost the oxen, the sheep, the servants, the children, the health, the standing, and the explanation. What is left is God, and Job wants him. There is nothing in it for him, and he is on his face. That is the answer, and the Accuser has nothing to say to it.
verseByVerse.note: “Repent” may also be rendered “am comforted” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — You Have Not Spoken of Me What Is Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's verdict on the friends, and their forgiveness through sacrifice and Job's prayer (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God's verdict: the friends' tidy orthodoxy was false speech about him, and Job's anguished honesty was true. The accused man becomes their priest.

verseByVerse.quote: After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns from the sufferer to the counsellors, and his first word to them is anger. Eliphaz is addressed by name, the first to speak and the gentlest (chapter 4); the other two are your two friends. The three of them said many things that would pass in any pulpit: God is great, he does not pervert justice, the wicked come to grief, no man is pure before his Maker. And the verdict on all of it is: you have not spoken of me what is right.

This must be taken at full strength, because the speeches of Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar sit in Scripture and can be quoted like any other verse. They are faithfully recorded; they are not therefore true. Where they described God rightly, they used the description as a weapon to convict an innocent man, which is a lie about God's character even when every sentence parses. Where they went further and told Job what he must have done, they were simply inventing. Never take a sentence from the friends as God's word without asking what 42:7 does to it.

And Job has spoken rightly of God. Job, who called God his enemy, who said God mocks the innocent and laughs at calamity. How can that be right speech? Because Job spoke to God and not merely about him; because he refused to tell a lie in God's favour, and refused to tell a lie against himself; because he kept coming, and his worst words were addressed to the one he could not stop believing in. God prefers a man who shouts at him to a man who explains him away. The friends never once spoke to God in nine chapters of speeches.

One more thing the verse does not say: nothing about Elihu. He is not rebuked and not commended; after chapter 37 the book simply drops him. Some see him as a fourth friend repeating the same formula; others as a forerunner of God's own answer. The likelier reading lies between: Elihu speaks partly truly, and God's answer out of the storm goes beyond him without needing to correct him.
verseByVerse.note: What is right also carries the sense of what is true and firmly grounded.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and offer up a burnt offering for yourselves. And my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer not to deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has." So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD had told them, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends are in real danger, and the remedy has two parts: blood and a mediator. Seven bulls and seven rams is a large offering, larger than anything mentioned in the book; and it is not enough by itself. They must also walk to the ash heap, stand in front of the man they have been lecturing, and ask him to pray. Their theology has been called folly, and their forgiveness comes through the one they accused.

Eliphaz had said it himself without knowing what he was saying. Promising Job a restoration if he would only repent, he ended: He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands (22:30). Eliphaz is now the one who is not innocent, delivered through the cleanness of hands he had called filthy. Job had longed for someone to stand between himself and God: an arbiter (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), a Redeemer who lives (19:25). He never gets a man in the middle for himself; he becomes the man in the middle for the men who wronged him.

So the scene looks like a greater one. The innocent sufferer, vindicated by God, prays for those who accused him: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Christ Jesus is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Rom 8:34); he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25). Job's prayer is heard for three men in one prayer. The prayer of the one Job was waiting for is heard for everyone who comes.

To their credit, they went, named in full one last time, walking with their animals to a man on an ash heap. No apology is recorded, and none is asked for. Job prays for them, which answers everything they had said about his character. Four times in two verses God calls him my servant Job, the name he used of him to the Accuser before any of this began (1:8; 2:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The LORD Restored the Fortunes of Job
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD restores Job when he prays for his friends: his family returns, his flocks are doubled, his daughters are named and given an inheritance, and he dies full of days (vv. 10-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is real, generous, public, and not the whole answer: ten graves remain, and the Redeemer of 19:25 has not yet stood on the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD restored the fortunes of Job, when he had prayed for his friends. And the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing is the message. Not when Job stopped complaining; not when he made his confession; when he prayed for the men who had tormented him. His hands were empty and he used them to hold up Eliphaz. This is not a last condition Job met to earn his goods back. It is the shape of the thing: the blessing comes through the door of intercession, and a man who can pray for his accusers is a man in whom God has already finished the work.

Anyone who has been wronged and is waiting for restoration should look hard at this verse. The waiting is not usually ended by winning the argument. Pray for them, as Christ prayed for us while we were his enemies. It is the last thing the flesh wants to do, it is what the Spirit given to believers makes possible, and it is the first thing that makes a man free. Praying for those who wronged you is not the same as going back to them, trusting them again, or calling the wrong small; anyone who is being abused should seek safety at once, and can pray from there.

Does God always restore the faithful sufferer in this life? No. Many of the faithful did not receive what was promised in this life (Heb 11:39), and Paul says that all who live godly lives will be persecuted (2 Tim 3:12). Job’s restoration is God’s public verdict on his servant, and a foretaste of the final restoration, when every loss will be repaid. It is not a promise of wealth to those who suffer well; the book has spent forty chapters refuting the friends who thought that way.

If your losses have not been given back, this chapter is not a rebuke to you. Christ, the innocent sufferer, had nothing restored to him in this life: he was vindicated by being raised, and his people's restoration waits in him, an inheritance kept in heaven for you (1 Pet 1:4). Job's doubled flocks are a small, early picture of that day, and your restoration is not cancelled because it has not yet come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came to him all his brothers and sisters and all who had known him before, and ate bread with him in his house. And they showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him. And each of them gave him a piece of money and a ring of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These relatives were nowhere to be found in his trouble. He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me (19:13). Now they are at his table eating his bread, sympathising, bringing money and gold rings. Job takes it.

And the narrator writes a sentence that should stop the reader: they comforted him for all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him. Not the evil the Accuser brought, though he struck the blows (1:12; 2:6-7). The book that opened by showing us how the disaster was arranged closes by laying it at God's door. That is Job's own theology from the first day: The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (1:21); Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (2:10). Scripture will not let us protect God from his own sovereignty. It also will not let us doubt his goodness, having shown us his face in the whirlwind and, later, in his Son.
verseByVerse.note: A qesitah was a unit of money of uncertain value (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning. And he had 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys. He had also seven sons and three daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Compare the first page. Job had 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys (1:3). Every figure is exactly doubled. In the law, double is what a thief pays back to the man he robbed (Exod 22:4). God is not paying damages, and no one robbed Job. But the doubling is a public statement in the only language the ancient world read fluently: this man was not under judgment.

And there the doubling stops. Seven sons and three daughters is exactly what he had before (1:2), not twice as many. Some readers have said that the children were doubled after all, because the first ten are not lost but waiting; the book gives grounds for that hope (19:25-27) without saying more, and it is a reason to love the restraint of this verse. The plain point is simpler and harder: livestock can be replaced and children cannot. Ten new children do not cancel ten graves, and the text does not pretend otherwise. And anyone who has buried a child and never been given another may take this from it: the book will not call new children a replacement, and it does not measure God's love by what has been given back.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the name of the first daughter Jemimah, and the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-happuch. And in all the land there were no women so beautiful as Job's daughters. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not one of Job's first ten children is named. Now three daughters are named, and their beauty remarked on; after forty chapters of dust the naming is itself sunlight. These are the names of a man who has come out of the dark and is delighting in his girls. This is the household that had been a graveyard.

Then the quiet, radical line: their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Daughters did not ordinarily inherit at all; under Moses' law they inherited only where there was no son, as the case of the daughters of Zelophehad established: You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers (Num 27:7-8). Job, of his own accord, gives his daughters a share while their brothers are living. A man who has been unjustly treated and has met God does not go back to his house and rule it harshly. Grace received comes out as generosity, and it shows up first in the way a man treats the people with the least claim on him.
verseByVerse.note: Jemimah may mean “dove,” Keziah “cinnamon,” and Keren-happuch “horn of eye-paint.”

verseByVerse.quote: And after this Job lived 140 years, and saw his sons, and his sons' sons, four generations. And Job died, an old man, and full of days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who begged to die (3:21; 7:15) lives 140 years, which the psalm's seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty (Ps 90:10) makes a lavish number. He holds grandchildren and great-grandchildren; the house that lost ten children in one day fills up for four generations. And the last sentence gives him the patriarch's death: Abraham too died an old man and full of years (Gen 25:8). Not emptied. Full. (The Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, adds a line after verse 17 saying that Job will rise again with those the Lord raises up. It is not in the Hebrew and is a later addition, but it shows how early readers heard this ending.)

And still he dies: the book's last piece of honesty. Job never learned why. The children of chapter 1 are not given back. The Accuser is never mentioned again, and Job never knows he was there. The great confession of 19:26 is still in front of him and not behind: after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God. He glimpsed God from the whirlwind while his sores were fresh; he waits, like every believer who has ever closed his eyes, for the day when he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more (Rev 21:4).

Which is why the New Testament can hold this whole book up as an encouragement without softening a line of it: You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful (Jas 5:11). The purpose was there all along, in the silence, in the ash heap, behind the wind. The one who held Job is compassionate and merciful, and he has since stood on this earth himself with a body that could be struck, and let it be struck, and risen. Job's Redeemer lives. That is the answer this book was waiting for, and it has come.

42.theology:
Job receives no explanation and is satisfied: now my eye sees you (v. 5). Sight of God, not information about him, ends the argument, and a man who has lost everything and still wants God is the answer to the Accuser (1:9).

The friends have not spoken of me what is right (vv. 7-8); Job, who said wild things to God's face, spoke rightly, because he spoke to God and would not lie about him or about himself. Their forgiveness comes through sacrifice and the prayer of the man they accused (v. 8), a picture of Christ's intercession (Rom 8:34; Heb 7:25).

The narrator lays the evil at the LORD's door (v. 11) without doubting his goodness. The restoration is real and incomplete. Livestock is doubled; children are not. Job dies (v. 17), and the hope of 19:26 waits for the resurrection (Rev 21:4; Jas 5:11).
42.examples: Most sufferers receive what Job received, and in the same order: not an explanation, but God himself, and only afterwards whatever restoration he gives. The man who longed for a mediator becomes one for the friends who wronged him, and his blessing comes when he prays for them. The restoration is generous and still incomplete: every figure is doubled except the children, and the daughters, named at last, receive an inheritance. Job dies full of days, still waiting for the day of 19:26.
